Weighting by the inverse of the estimated error variance also helped it, by less.
The same count weights made the network worse.
For the network, adding the log of the measurement count as a feature helped instead, and so did shrinking each label toward a prediction by its spread.
NGBoost gained a little from the same extra feature.
The interval model did slightly worse than the point model.
Training on one row per measurement instead of the mean barely changed the score for either model.
The detection of molecules flagged by ChEMBL curators has not run.
Cleaning before the search did best when the fit also used the cleaned labels (Section ).
On expression titer's labels as delivered, deleting the 20% of antibodies the forest residual flags takes the network on the hybrid from 0.155 to 0.562 Spearman this way.
Cleaning only the fit, or only the search, also helps, by less.
On SMAC colloidal stability with a quarter of the labels clipped, deleting the flagged 5% also does best when it reaches both.
Cleaning the search alone does worse than no cleaning.
The largest single gain is on SMAC colloidal stability's labels as delivered.
There the network on the second hybrid goes from -0.014 to 0.560 Spearman when the labels are shrunk toward an out-of-fold prediction for the search alone.
That starts from a score near zero, on one fold of 53 antibodies.

On hERG K_i under Gaussian noise, deleting before the search helped the second hybrid on the first noise draw and hurt it on the second.
On hERG K_i's labels as delivered, the one dataset with a second fold here, label smoothing before the search beat no cleaning on fold 1.
No random-flag control has run for this experiment, and there is no QM9 result.
A separate experiment searched the hybrid on clean or damaged labels, then fitted both on labels with Gaussian noise at level 1.0 and scored them on held-out labels as delivered.
On Caco-2 the network's second hybrid scores within a few thousandths of an RMSE between the two arms on every fold, and neither arm is ahead on all five.
On LogD with the support vector regressor the two arms agree to the third decimal on two of three folds.
The largest loss was on hERG K_i with the network, 0.669 against 0.779 RMSE on the second fold.
On SMAC colloidal stability the two arms swap places from fold to fold.

This thesis set out to handle label noise in molecular data.
This chapter answers the research questions of Chapter , sets out how to choose a noise-handling method, and lists the contributions, limitations and future work.
The first half of the thesis asked four questions about label noise, answered in Chapter .
First, model family decided noise robustness more than the representation did.
On QM9 under Gaussian noise, model family explained 47.2% of the variance in AUCnorm, the representation far less.
The representation mattered more for predictive performance.
Second, random forests were the most consistent model under noise, while LightGBM and XGBoost predicted well on clean labels and lost the most as noise rose.
Third, the type of noise mattered more than the shape of its distribution.
Systematic noise, shared within a scaffold family or clipped at an assay limit, did the most damage, so a study that injects only Gaussian noise misses it.
Fourth, mean predicted uncertainty rose with noise, but no model's uncertainty identified the corrupted labels.
Chapter then asked why published methods for learning with noisy labels did poorly in an earlier exploratory study.
The methods that compared molecules by a distance did worst.
Within one dataset, most features of a standard representation barely vary.
On hERG K_i, 1,815 of the 2,048 ECFP4 features take one value in nearly every molecule.
A distance sums over every feature, so these features dominate it.
The second half asked whether the representation can be adapted to the task.
First, we found that the best set of features depends on the dataset and the downstream model, and a search can find it (Chapter ).
The adaptive hybrid representation beat the best single representation on every small-molecule dataset with both downstream models.
A method built for small molecules also carried over to antibodies, where the gain depended on the dataset.
On two antibody datasets the best single representation was one built for this thesis, which reads only the regions or mutations that vary.
Second, distance in a hybrid tracked the label better on all five small-molecule datasets, and predicting each label from its five nearest neighbors was more accurate (Chapter ).
On antibodies and reactions distance also tracked the label better, but prediction from neighbors was worse on several datasets.
Third, noisy labels could be found and corrected (Chapter ).
With a quarter of LogD's training labels clipped, censored EM removed most of the error that clipping added to the network.
Cleaning guided by a detector beat random deletion or shuffled detector scores on hERG, hERG K_i, Buchwald–Hartwig and three antibody datasets.
On small molecules the hybrid stayed ahead of the single representation through every treatment.
Fourth, importance helped in building the hybrid but not in training.
The hybrid ranks features by importance within each representation.
At the same number of features it beat recursive feature elimination and random features on all but one small-molecule dataset with a result.
Using the importance scores again during training added little.
No single method handled label noise on every dataset.
The forest residual detector fell to chance under clipping, where acting on the known flag did best.
Subtracting scaffold-family offsets made the model worse on Caco-2's labels as delivered.
Deleting the molecules the network fits worst helped on the reactions but almost never on small molecules.
The ranking of the methods also changed between the hybrid and the single representations.
We therefore recommend modeling the noise in a dataset before choosing a method.
Data pooled from several laboratories can carry an offset per source, and an assay with a reporting limit gives clipped labels.
Both come with a flag that a correction can use.
A method that assumes noise that is not there does harm.
Simple methods were often as good as complex ones: random forests were the most consistent model, and on hERG K_i one constant lift for every clipped label beat censored EM.
The contributions on label noise are the following.

Published noise-handling methods adapted to QSAR data, for example censored EM with any downstream model, a random intercept per scaffold family, and the buddy check from meteorology as a detector of noisy labels (Chapter ).
Three methods for which we found no earlier use (Chapter ).
These are the cliff-aware gap, cleaning the labels before the hybrid search, and returning activity-cliff molecules after a cleanup.
Tests of these methods on single representations and hybrids side by side, with three controls: QM9 with no noise added, random deletion and shuffled detector scores (Chapter ).
The ranking of the methods changed with the features.
The contributions on the representation are the following.
The adaptive hybrid representation, which ranks features within each representation, splits a budget of features among them, and searches the selection settings for each dataset and model (Chapter ).
A newly published embedding is added to the search as one more representation.
Hybrids built for distance (Chapter ), and hybrids built from data held at separate sites (Chapter ).

Antibody representations built for this thesis: readouts of the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) and of each region, mutation features, and the change in embedding from the parent antibody (Chapter ).
Most noise results rest on the first outer fold.
QM9 is the only clean control, and most noise methods have no control.
On the labels as delivered there is no ground truth, so a control can show that a gain beats chance but not that a label was corrected.
Every clipped-label result is on injected clipping.

Most DNN results were computed before the DNN began clipping each prediction to the range of its training labels.
We have not tested whether the best hybrid settings follow measurable properties of a dataset (Section ).
The hybrid search needs only several feature matrices for the same samples and a supervised task.
Gene-expression profiles and financial time series are natural next domains, since each has many competing representations of the same samples.
Runs on DNA promoter sequences have started but are not reported here.
The noise methods need more clean controls.
QM9 offers twelve computed properties, and only the HOMO–LUMO gap was used.
In QSAR, a class label usually comes from cutting a continuous measurement at a threshold, so measurement error flips mostly the molecules near that threshold.
Flips of that kind, on more classification datasets, are the next test for the detectors.
A hybrid can also be the input to the model that scores molecules for a generative model; the code exists and has not been run.
Starting the search from the settings found on a similar dataset may save compute, and a deployment across real sites would test the separate-site results of Chapter .
Label noise in molecular data can be handled.
Which method handles it depends on the prediction task, the data, the model and the kind of noise.
No single model, representation or noise-handling method was best on every dataset we tested.
A dataset's noise should be understood before a method is chosen.
The features also matter.
When the noise methods failed, we followed the failure down to the distance between molecules and then to the features that distance is computed over.
The adaptive hybrid representation selects those features for each dataset and model.
On small molecules it predicted better than any single representation, gave better neighbors, and stayed ahead through every noise treatment.
A new foundation model appears every few months in molecular, protein and antibody modeling.
With the hybrid search, a researcher does not need to choose between their current representation and a new one.
They add the new embedding to the search and rerun it, and the search decides whether the embedding contributes features and which.
Chapter tested this on LogD and hERG blocking.
A choice usually made by habit becomes one measured on each task.
New avenues in the drug discovery pipeline have opened up thanks to advances in large dataset collection, analysis, and computation.
Therapeutic targets are identified, potential drug candidates are screened and optimized, and the most promising of these go on to pre-clinical and clinical trials .
However, attrition is high, and roughly 90% of drugs that enter clinical trials are never approved, often due to poor efficacy or toxicity .
Computational methods can remove poor candidates early on in the drug discovery pipeline, long before clinical trials.
This is done through virtual screening, which allows for a large-scale analysis of libraries of compounds .
One standard screening method is the prediction of bioactivities and pharmacological properties of such candidates.

There is a long history of using Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR) models to make these predictions, to act as a filter for compounds with undesirable properties, and thus reduce the time and cost associated with experimental screening .

QSAR models aim to predict the relationship between a molecule's structural and chemical features as encoded by a particular molecular representation and a desired experimental molecular property of interest.
A QSAR model requires a molecular representation and some form of machine learning (ML) model.
An ideal molecular representation will allow a model to learn only the relevant information about each molecule with respect to the target property.

Representations are either `static' hand-crafted descriptors or circular fingerprints that encode structural and physicochemical features ; or learned representations, where the encoding is derived from a predictive model, often taken from the activations of the final layer of a neural network, or a latent space embedding .
QSAR models are of course, sensitive to the quality of the input data on which they are trained.
Experimental noise can arise from measurement errors, variability under experimental conditions, varying provenance of the data, intrinsic biological, chemical variability, and human error.
Even the very measures of model performance may be flawed if test and validation sets are laden with noise.

showed that error in the test labels can make a model look worse than it is: a model trained on noisy data can predict the noise-free values more accurately than an evaluation on the noisy test set indicates.

There is also a limit to how much noise the model can tolerate; argued that once their model's error approached the experimental error, more training data would not be expected to improve accuracy much.

In the context of activity prediction, the inherent variability within experimental setups and assays, batch effects, measurement errors, and biological variability introduce additional layers of complexity .
All of this increases the likelihood of encountering noise in the data.

Even the molecular representations in the training data themselves may be incorrect or misleading , and chemical datasets contain too few repeat measurements of each compound to characterize the distribution the label is drawn from.
Thus, models treat a single label as the population mean .
Here pIC_50 and pK_i are the negative base-10 logarithms of the IC_50 and K_i in molar units, so a difference of one log unit is a tenfold difference in concentration.

Repeat measurements of the same compound-target pair have a standard deviation of about 0.68 log units for pIC_50 and 0.54 log units for pK_i , which is about a 4.8-fold and a 3.5-fold difference in concentration.
For IC_50, keeping only pairs of assays whose recorded conditions match lowers the mean absolute difference from 0.50 to 0.27 log units , or from about a 3.2-fold to a 1.9-fold difference.
This thesis addresses the challenge of conducting molecular property prediction when the underlying experimental data, or ``labels'' are noisy.
Most work on noise in QSAR modeling assumes Gaussian label noise and evaluates either representations or model architectures in isolation.
examined 12 algorithms across multiple noise levels but used fixed representations, and studies that compare representations typically use clean data.

No work has systematically compared the relative importance of representation versus architecture choice for label noise robustness, asked whether probabilistic methods justify their computational overhead under noise, or tested whether findings generalize across different types of injected noise.
This thesis fills that gap.
I will also discuss noise mitigation, using the results of my noise robustness study.
I explore why many noise mitigation techniques underperform in cheminformatics data and methods to address this problem in the form of novel molecular representations.
The first half of this thesis therefore asks four questions.

First, how does the choice of molecular representation and model architecture explain the variance in predictive performance, and does that division change when you instead consider how much performance a QSAR model is able to retain under increasing label noise?
Second, what does the choice of model provide with label noise?
Within this question we compare the effects of deterministic and probabilistic modeling.
Third, does the type of label noise matter, or just the quantity of it?
We explore different techniques of generating and adding label noise to both clean data, as well as data with inherent experimental noise.
Fourth, what is the impact of artificial label noise on a model's uncertainty estimation?
Does the estimated uncertainty rise with increased label noise and can these uncertainty values point to which labels are corrupted?
Together, these questions aim to identify what, if anything, makes a QSAR model robust to noise.
To answer them we introduce NoiseInject, an open-source Python package for benchmarking noise robustness and uncertainty quantification (Section ).
In an early study with Gaussian noise added to QM9 labels, published methods for noisy labels that compared molecules by a distance did worst.
We hypothesized that the fault lay in this distance.

On a given dataset, most features of a general-purpose representation either do not vary or do not relate to the property, yet each adds a term to the distance, so together they dominate it (Chapter ).
We propose instead to compute distances over a hybrid representation: a fixed number of task-relevant features selected from several representations.
A first version showed that the selected features also work as ordinary model inputs, so the question became how to choose them (Chapter ).
The second half asks whether the representation itself can be adapted to the task:
How can the best set of features be selected for a given prediction task?
Does distance in a hybrid representation track the label better than distance in the best single representation, and do methods built on nearest neighbors work better in it?
Can noisy labels be found and corrected, by deletion, sample weighting, label smoothing or other means, and do hybrid representations keep their lead through that cleaning?
Does weighting features by their importance improve the construction of hybrid representations, model training and noise mitigation?

This chapter describes the molecular representations and models we use, molecular similarity and activity cliffs, the sources of label noise, how we inject noise, the methods for learning with noisy labels, the NoiseInject package and how results are evaluated.
The success of machine learning hinges on the quality of input data.
Although the quality can refer to noise, which the majority of our work is centered around, in this case we are talking about the type of input.
Molecular representations provide different features with which QSAR models and noise detection techniques can be learned.
However, a potential bottleneck on larger datasets should be noted; the more complex the data structure, the greater the computational cost.
For smaller datasets, the number of parameters is limited by the size of the training set, to prevent overfitting.

One of the most common and intuitive molecular representations is the Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES) string, which consists of a sequence of ASCII characters generated by a fixed set of rules to specify a given chemical identity .
A common way to use SMILES strings as inputs to QSAR models is to tokenize and one-hot-encode them rather than to use the strings themselves .
The strings are tokenized into atomic branches and symbols and mapped to indices of a vocabulary, and finally converted into binary vectors using one-hot encodings .
This representation, referred to as one-hot-encoded SMILES, allows models to process molecular structures as bit-vector-based fingerprints or as sequences of vectors.
Sequence-based models such as recurrent neural networks and transformers have proven to be particularly successful in capturing text semantics within a sequence.
When applied to raw or one-hot-encoded SMILES strings, these models can effectively capture the structure of the molecule in its textual representation .
Another common representation is the molecular fingerprint, a vector containing information about the properties of the molecule in question.
In a typical bit vector-based fingerprint, each bit accounts for the presence (1) or absence (0) of a given chemical feature or substructure .
One common fingerprint is the Molecular ACCess System (MACCS) key, a substructure key-based fingerprint that encodes predefined atom symbols and properties, as well as bond types .
Another is the Extended Connectivity Fingerprint (ECFP), which encodes local neighborhoods around each atom and bond connectivity in molecules .
ECFPs are typically constructed with a radius of 2, a length of 2048 bits, and no chirality flags.
These existing molecular representations are well established and have been quite successful when coupled with QSAR models .
They are relatively simple, and as the bits can be mapped back to one or more substructures, they are human-interpretable, and furthermore easy-to-compute.
However, hashed fingerprints are subject to information loss due to bit collisions, which happens when two different substructures are encoded at the same bit position .
They are also based on a fixed procedure and are not trainable or adaptable to a particular dataset.
Alternative representations that capture different structural, chemical, or physical features are able to overcome these limitations.
Recent advances have led to the development of new molecular fingerprints.
One such method is the Sort & Slice (SNS) technique, an alternative to hash-based folding for pooling ECFP substructures .
Sort & Slice begins by sorting all circular substructures in the training set according to their frequency of occurrence.
It then ``slices'' away all but the N most frequent substructures, which are subsequently used to generate an N-dimensional, bit-collision-free binary fingerprint.
This approach solves the ambiguity problem of hashed fingerprints, where multiple substructures might be encoded at the same bit position, making it very interpretable .
Sort & Slice fingerprints outperform ECFP of diameter four (ECFP4) with standard hash-based folding methods across various molecular property prediction tasks.
These experiments consisted of different data splitting techniques, machine learning models, fingerprint diameters, fingerprint dimensions, and atomic invariants .
Furthermore, Sort & Slice outperformed advanced substructure selection schemes such as filtered fingerprints and mutual information maximization .
Neural fingerprints are a category of learned representations that overcome the fixed, hard-coded nature of traditional fingerprints.
Unlike ECFP or MACCS keys, which rely on predefined hashing schemes or substructure catalogs, neural fingerprints train on molecular data to capture chemical information .
These representations are the result of deep learning architectures that have learned dense, continuous embeddings which can be used for downstream tasks.
Mol2vec, which adapts the Word2vec algorithm from NLP to molecular substructures , is a common neural fingerprint.
Mol2vec treats molecules like ``sentences'' and circular substructures derived from Morgan fingerprints like ``words''.
The model learns vector embeddings for each substructure through unsupervised training, such that chemically similar substructures are mapped to nearby points in the embedding space .
The embeddings of all present substructures are summed to obtain a full representation.
This approach produces 300-dimensional dense vectors that avoid the sparsity and bit collisions inherent in hashed fingerprints .
Mol2vec has performed strongly on various QSAR benchmarks, matching or exceeding Morgan fingerprints on solubility and bioactivity prediction tasks .
Transformer-based architectures have also been applied to molecular representation learning, similarly stemming from NLP ideas.
MolBERT applies a bidirectional transformer to learn molecular representations from SMILES strings through self-supervised pre-training .

The model has domain-relevant auxiliary adaptations, such as the prediction of calculated physicochemical properties alongside the masked token prediction, to improve the chemical fidelity of the learned embeddings .
MolBERT outperformed count-based ECFP4 (ECFC4), RDKit descriptors and the CDDD neural representation on virtual screening and QSAR benchmarks .
ChemBERTa is another transformer-based approach which pre-trains masked language models on SMILES data from PubChem .
ChemBERTa uses a byte-pair-encoding tokenizer by default and compares it with a SMILES-specific tokenizer .
Attention visualization shows neurons selective for chemically relevant functional groups and aromatic rings, and others that track bracket closures in the SMILES string .
ChemBERTa-2, pre-trained on up to 77 million PubChem compounds, is competitive with existing architectures on MoleculeNet .
Neural fingerprints provide several advantages over traditional fingerprints.
They produce dense continuous vectors that avoid sparseness and information loss from bit collisions .
They can also be pre-trained once on large unlabeled datasets and then fine-tuned for specific downstream tasks, opening the door to transfer learning .
However, pre-training them is computationally expensive, and they are less directly interpretable than fingerprints, although attention visualization offers some insight .
Beyond fingerprints, physicochemical-descriptor vectors (PDVs) are a class of continuous-value molecular descriptors that encode structural and chemical properties of molecules .

Unlike binary fingerprints or graph-based representations, PDVs aggregate atom and bond-level quantities into fixed-length feature vectors that capture a wide variety of information about a molecule and its structure .

PDVs typically consist of hundreds of properties including constitutional descriptors such as molecular weight, atom and bond counts, and heteroatom ratios; topological indices encoding molecular connectivity patterns; physicochemical properties such as logP (lipophilicity), molar refractivity, and topological polar surface area; and electronic descriptors derived from partial charges and polarizabilities .
The RDKit cheminformatics toolkit provides a comprehensive suite of more than 200 molecular descriptors that cover these categories .
Many PDV descriptors, such as logP, molecular weight and partial charges, have a direct physicochemical meaning, although many of the thousands available have no clear interpretation .

They are also less computationally expensive than some 3D methods or neural fingerprints, with many descriptors simply requiring a 2D molecular structure without conformer generation or extensive pre-training.
This efficiency makes PDVs particularly appropriate for high-throughput applications.
Descriptors based on 3D structure can also be used .
However, PDVs have limitations.
The dimensionality of PDV feature spaces can lead to problems with multicollinearity .
This can be mitigated by feature selection or dimensionality reduction techniques .

Additionally, PDVs encode molecular properties as aggregated global features, which may not capture fine-grained structural details such as specific substructure arrangements or local chemical environments, information important for particular endpoints.
One of the more intuitive representations is the molecular graph.
These graphs can be categorized into 2D and 3D graphs.

2D graphs rely on adjacency matrices that encode topological atom- and bond-level features but leave out geometric properties such as bond angles or torsion, meaning they may fail to capture stereochemistry.
3D graphs incorporate these spatial features, but are often limited by remaining in a single conformation .
A standard molecular graph is constructed such that each molecule is represented as G = (V,E) with node features x_i and edge features e_ij.
In one common featurization, nodes encode atom type, chirality, hybridization and aromaticity, and edges encode bond type, ring membership, direction and stereochemistry .
In the standard molecular graph, atoms are mapped to nodes and bonds to edges .
These molecular graphs are typically 2D objects; 3D information such as atomic coordinates and bond angles is not part of the graph unless added as node or edge attributes .

However, there are alternative molecular graph representations such as graphs with quantum 3D embeddings, weight alignment graphs, association graphs containing pairs of molecules, and geometric interaction graph neural networks that incorporate 3D structures and physical interactions .

developed hybrid 2D and 3D graphs, combining 3D data, guaranteeing precision and completeness by providing unabridged information, and 2D data, providing chemical intuitions for guidance, in a zipper-like arrangement.

Voxel-based 3D representations, in which each atom occupies one grid cell, are too sparse for convolutional networks to perform well; instead spread each atom over nearby voxels with a wave transform.
These graph representations do not highlight specific substructures or specific arrangements of atoms and bonds within each molecule.
The substructures contain functional groups that are related to a range of chemical properties and are potentially involved in downstream tasks related to the function of molecules.
developed graph substructure networks, a topologically aware message passing scheme based on substructure encoding.
The method involves encoding structural roles based on the appearance of specific substructures and using them in message passing updates.
Since message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are at most as powerful as the Weisfeiler–Lehman test, they cannot isolate sufficient features from the graph structure .
Graph substructure networks, on the other hand, capture these substructure-related features.
Encoders pretrained on unlabeled molecules, whether graph-based or transformers on SMILES , can also produce embeddings that capture structural features.
There are a wide variety of model architectures that can be used for QSAR modeling.
Starting off with simpler and more explainable models, we have tree-based methods.
Decision trees are non-parametric supervised learning algorithms that perform recursive binary partitioning of the feature space .

A decision tree builds a predictive model by learning a series of if-then rules that recursively split the data based on given feature values, creating a tree where internal nodes represent decision rules, branches represent the results of those decisions, and leaf nodes contain predicted values or class labels .
Each recursive split is chosen to maximize homogeneity within the resulting partitions.
For classification, Gini impurity is commonly used and for regression, mean squared error reduction .
There are several properties that make decision trees a good foundation for QSAR modeling.
First, they handle non-linear relationships between molecular descriptors and target properties without requiring explicit feature engineering or transformation .

They also do not make assumptions about the underlying distribution of the data, making them robust to violations of parametric assumptions that can limit linear regression or other classical methods .
Decision trees handle data in a ``contributory'' rather than ``consensus'' manner.
In consensus methods such as linear regression or neural networks, every data point influences the prediction at every other point in the feature space.
Tree-based methods make predictions based on the subset of training samples that fall into the same leaf node as the test point .
This mechanism essentially quarantines outliers in their respective leaf nodes, limiting their impact on predictions for samples in other regions or chemical domains.
Individual decision trees tend to have high variance and often overfit, particularly at large depths .
Small modifications made to the training data can result in large differences in the structure of the tree, resulting in unstable predictions .
Ensemble methods are used to counteract this instability, aggregating predictions from many trees.
Random forests (RFs) aggregate predictions from trees trained on bootstrap samples of data with random subsets of features at each split .
Bootstrapping ensures that each tree is trained on a slightly different subset of data, which effectively reduces the influence of any individual sample .
This is especially beneficial with noisy samples.
The selection of random features at every node decorrelates the trees, which lowers the generalization error of the ensemble .
The aggregation of trees further prevents overfitting to noise by smoothing out prediction errors from individual noisy labels.
Neural networks (NNs), a very popular family of models, can also be used for QSAR, although with mixed results.
An NN is a system of interconnected nodes which learn by passing information through its layers.
There are weights and biases attached to the nodes and various other parameters which the model optimizes to minimize the difference between the predicted output and the actual target value.
During training, the network parameters are updated using backpropagation, in which gradients of the loss function with respect to each weight are propagated backward through the network .
The structure of these networks and the hyperparameters used depend on the type of NN.

In QSAR, one of the most commonly used architectures is the multilayer perceptron (MLP), an NN containing fully-connected layers with non-linear activation functions which transforms molecular feature vectors (i.e., fingerprints, descriptors) into a property or activity prediction .
A typical MLP for molecular property prediction has a few fully connected hidden layers with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activations and dropout regularization to prevent overfitting.

Training is performed using backpropagation with gradient descent optimizers such as Adam, to minimize a loss function (mean squared error for regression, cross-entropy for classification) on batches of training data.
However, NN performance on QSAR-related tasks has been very mixed.
NNs have a long history in QSAR , and tuned deep networks have outperformed shallow methods such as random forests and support vector machines across diverse activity classes .
Their complexity and use of gradients make them prone to label memorization , which in the context of noise is problematic, as it means that models may memorize the noise themselves.

Although models that are memorizing labels may initially appear to have strong predictive performance, they cannot generalize to out-of-distribution samples properly and often provide inaccurate uncertainty estimates.

Various approaches have been proposed to improve neural network robustness to label noise, including noise-robust loss functions , confident learning to identify mislabeled examples , and regularization techniques such as mixup or label smoothing .
All the models up to this point have assumed a vector-based input.
Molecular graphs, on the other hand, require different types of predictive modeling.
Two standard ML methods on molecular graphs include Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs).
GCNs apply the concept of convolution to graph-structured data.
Instead of operating on grid-based data, such as images, GCNs aggregate information from neighbors of a node to update its representation .
In contrast, GINs address the limitations in GCNs’ ability to differentiate between non-isomorphic graphs.

Unlike GCNs, which normalize and weight the sum of neighboring node features, GINs use a simple sum followed by a trainable MLP, giving the model flexibility to learn complex transformations of node features.
The GIN model’s design is informed by the Weisfeiler–Lehman test for graph isomorphism, enabling it to distinguish between molecular graphs that are structurally similar but differ in subtle ways .

GIN features have been competitive with or better than fingerprints and descriptors at classifying pairs of molecules as activity cliffs (ACs; Section ), where small variations in molecular structure can lead to significant changes in chemical or biological activity .
Descriptor-based models still predicted the potency of cliff molecules better than deep learning methods .
Gradient boosting methods such as eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) sequentially fit trees to the residuals of previous iterations, progressively reducing the prediction error .
We used a handful of gradient-boosted tree ensembles in this thesis including Light Gradient-Boosting Machine (LightGBM) , and Natural Gradient Boosting (NGBoost) .
Support vector regression fits a function that is as flat as possible while keeping training errors small .
It uses the -insensitive loss, under which errors smaller than cost nothing and larger errors cost their size minus .
A constant C trades flatness against tolerance of large errors .
The features enter the model only through the kernel.
With the radial basis function (RBF) kernel, every feature enters the Euclidean distance between two molecules.
In Chapter the continuous representations are standardized and the binary fingerprints are used as built.
Three properties limit the effect of a wrong label: errors inside the tube change nothing, the loss outside it grows linearly, and the weight of each molecule is capped at C .
Under simulated experimental error, the RBF-kernel SVM degraded smoothly and linearly .
Its main limitation is computational cost, because training operates on a kernel matrix that grows with the square of the number of training molecules .
We employed Gaussian process (GP) models using the Gauche framework , which is optimized for cheminformatics tasks.
Standard kernels for GPs are not optimized for the chemical landscape.
Gauche defines such kernels for strings, fingerprints, and graphs that operate on a range of widely used molecular representations .

Standard feed-forward networks are deterministic; however, they can be transformed into probabilistic models (Figure ).
Unlike standard deterministic ML methods, Bayesian methods model distributions over predictions using Bayes' rule, allowing for the quantification of uncertainty within parameters and labels.
Bayesian methods treat the model parameters as random variables with distributions.
Uncertainty can also be estimated from other non-deterministic methods, including deep ensembles and bootstrap modeling .
Much of cheminformatics rests on the similar property principle, which states that structurally similar molecules tend to have similar properties, including biological activity .
Nearest-neighbor prediction, GP kernels and many noise detection methods rely on it.
Similarity is defined only relative to a representation and a coefficient .
Two molecules that are near-identical under a substructure fingerprint may be far apart under a PDV, and a computed similarity value is easily over-interpreted .
The most common measure for binary fingerprints is the Tanimoto coefficient .
For two molecules with fingerprints x, x' 0,1^d,
which is the number of bits set in both molecules divided by the number of bits set in either.
Continuous representations are instead compared with a distance, most often the Euclidean distance _j=1^d(x_j - x'_j)^2.
Both measures are sums over the features, and neither weighs a feature by its relation to the property.
In the Tanimoto coefficient, a bit that is off in both molecules contributes nothing, whereas every bit that is set in either molecule counts.
In the Euclidean distance, every feature that differs between the two molecules counts.
Chapter returns to this point (Equation ).
Distance-based reasoning relies on the assumption that the data embeddings contain quality information.

When the labels are corrupted or the important features are scarce, similarity scores over-rely on compounding false or useless information, and the assumption that similar molecules have similar properties breaks down.
found that the Tanimoto, Dice and Cosine coefficients and the Soergel distance rank molecules almost identically on binary fingerprints.
We take this to mean that changing the formula cannot compensate for a weak representation.
This problem is further complicated by activity cliffs (defined below).
These molecules, which potentially contain the most important information for model prediction, can be confused with noise.
Another barrier to distance-based reasoning is persistent noise across labels.
The task of trying to determine if a molecule's value matches that of its neighbors becomes a lot harder when all of the neighbors have some form of noise as well.
There are many downstream tasks which rely on the concept of similarity.
The second half of this thesis relies on many such tasks, and as such focuses on identifying representations that agree with this principle.
An activity cliff is a pair of structurally similar molecules whose potency differs by a large amount because of a small chemical change .
A cliff also depends on the similarity measure, and there is no widely accepted definition of one .
The MoleculeACE benchmark uses three measures: the Tanimoto coefficient on ECFPs, the Tanimoto coefficient on scaffold fingerprints and a scaled Levenshtein distance on SMILES strings.
A pair counts as highly similar if its similarity exceeds 90% under at least one of them.
Such a pair forms a cliff if the two molecules also differ tenfold or more in K_i or EC_50 .
Across the thirty MoleculeACE targets, molecules in at least one cliff pair make up between 7% and 52% of a dataset .
As the number of dimensions grows, the distances to the nearest and to the furthest point become increasingly similar .
Molecular representations are routinely high-dimensional and sparse.
When many of their features carry no information about the property, distances computed over them are dominated by those features.
Real-world cheminformatics datasets contain label noise arising from multiple sources across the drug discovery pipeline.
Although noise is often modeled as being random, or drawn from a Gaussian distribution, other varieties of noise must be considered when working with experimental data.
To properly model experimental noise, we must first understand where the noise is coming from.

One key issue with QSAR models is the standard ML assumption that labels represent true values, as most chemical datasets lack sufficient replications to provide a robust statistical representation of the underlying distributions .
A single measurement, or even multiple measurements for a given label, will not guarantee that this label accurately reflects the population mean .
Most ML models rely on the assumption that the training data is, in fact, an accurate reflection of the population.
Therefore, they treat these potentially noisy labels as discrete quantities rather than distributions, which opens the door to overfitting to noise.
However, Bayesian methods such as Gaussian processes (GPs), and conformal prediction, do not make this assumption .
Studies involving noise, and specifically the quantification of noise robustness, typically approach label noise by adding independent, zero-mean, Gaussian error to the labels.
However, there's evidence to suggest that noise from experimental assays takes on different forms.

rejected normality of the differences in binding affinity between orthologous targets by Anderson–Darling test, found them approximately Laplace, and found that differences between assays of the same ligand and target closely resemble them.

examined the widest disagreements among 16,844 pairs of repeat pIC_50 measurements and found that in most cases, the wide gap between repeat values was due to annotation error rather than to an imprecise assay.
Although numerous studies have explored the effects of noise on ML algorithms for molecular property prediction, comparisons between different molecular representations remain limited.

examined the predictive limits of QSAR in the presence of noise, showing that by learning the underlying trends rather than fitting to noise, the models can achieve predictions more accurate than those of their training data.

They assumed experimental noise could be modeled as Gaussian-distributed, using the Central Limit Theorem to argue that aggregated experimental measurements from multiple independent error sources exhibit a Gaussian distribution.
However, distinguish random noise, which affects all molecules alike, from systematic noise that differs between regions of chemical space.
Using synthetic noise applied only to nitrogen-containing molecules, they showed that mean-variance estimation can detect it.
Beyond just the distribution, the assumptions of independence and zero mean may fail as well .

examined P-glycoprotein transport measurements from 23 laboratories and found that, among the laboratories using cell lines, 62% of the variance in log digoxin efflux ratio was due to differences between laboratories.
When you pool data from different sources, each source has the potential to carry a shared offset.
These sources usually contain families of related compounds, breaking the independence assumption.
The zero-mean assumption is not assured either, especially when true values fall above or below an assay's detection limit, called censoring.
count censored labels in 15 industrial assays, of which 13 carry censored labels and eight sit between a quarter and two thirds censored.
Chapter tests noise conditions that vary the distribution, the correlation, and the bias of injected error separately, at a matched quantity of noise for every condition except censoring.
Label noise enters bioactivity data at every step from the assay plate to the database.
Table lists these sources, with examples of each and the kind of error each tends to produce.
The kind of error describes how the error is distributed across molecules, which is the property that the noise conditions in Section vary.
These noise sources can interact with each other and present in more ways than a simple Gaussian.
Real noise can be heteroscedastic, larger in some regions of chemical space than others , shared within a laboratory , and non-normal .
We wanted to address this complexity in our research by examining a variety of ways of both modeling and adding noise to datasets.

Although the general assumption in much of the noise analysis and mitigation literature is that noise, specifically label noise, will have a negative effect on the model, this is not necessarily the case.
There are multiple instances of using noise as a method of regularization.
In linear regression, appending observations of pure noise shrinks the coefficient estimates, an implicit regularization, although not an optimal one .
Furthermore, adding artificial noise drawn from a Gaussian distribution to the activation layers of a neural network is considered another form of regularization .
These studies indicate that the presence of noise may act as a form of regularization in some contexts.
It is important to address this potential of regularization from label noise in QSAR and quantitative structure–property relationship (QSPR) models.
Our objective is to evaluate the robustness of QSAR models against label noise.
To do so, we ``inject'' artificial noise into the labels during training while test data remain free of noise.
Validation labels are given noise of the same type and quantity as the training labels, drawn independently.
This artificial noise simulates real-world experimental noise.
The clean target label y_i is replaced by a noisy label y_i = y_i + _i, where _i is the artificial noise injected at the index i, the value of which is determined by a specified noise strategy.
As we increased the quantity of noise, we measured how much predictive performance fell.
We explored seven different ways of adding noise, which we refer to as noise conditions and which are illustrated in Figure and summarized in Table .
Three conditions vary the shape of the distribution from which the error is drawn, and three concentrate the error on some molecules or share it within Bemis–Murcko scaffold families.
The seventh condition, censoring, clips labels at a limit.
The Bemis–Murcko scaffold of a molecule is its ring systems and the chains that link them, with all other side chains removed .
Molecules that share one scaffold form a scaffold family.
For a given label, every condition except censoring delivers the same expected quantity of noise at a set noise level.
These levels are defined as a fraction of the standard deviation of clean training labels.

The problem of training a model when some of its labels are wrong is called learning with noisy labels (LNL).
A method that acts on the training data has two halves: what selects the molecules, and what is then done to them (Table ).
A detector infers from the features and labels how wrong each label looks; the score it gives a molecule is that molecule's suspicion score.
A known flag is recorded in the data, such as a label at the assay limit or the molecule's scaffold family.
Noise detection is a detector alone.
Noise mitigation is a selector followed by deletion, down-weighting or moving the label, after which any model can be fitted; Figure shows how it is evaluated.
Noise-robust training leaves the data untouched and changes the loss, the kernel, a noise term, the training loop or the model, as in co-teaching and Meta-Weight-Net .
A sample-selection step taken out of its training loop and used only to delete molecules before a refit counts as noise mitigation.
sort deep learning methods for noisy labels into five groups: robust architectures, robust regularization, robust loss functions, loss adjustment and sample selection.
All five act during training, so all five are noise-robust training.
No single method is expected to win, since averaged over all problems no learning algorithm outperforms another .
compared 12 algorithms on 12 bioactivity datasets with increasing Gaussian label noise.
Gradient boosting was the least tolerant, the other 11 degraded comparably, and two polynomial-kernel models became sensitive only at high noise.
Neighbor-based cleaning dates back to editing a training set by its nearest neighbors .
It relies on the similar property principle, which activity cliffs break, and QSAR models frequently fail to predict cliffs .
Chapter tests the principle, and Chapter tests neighbor-based noise mitigation with the hybrid as the feature space.
The noise conditions are implemented twice.
NoiseInject, an open-source Python package, injects the noise on the three assay datasets of Chapter and computes the robustness and uncertainty metrics.
QM9 uses a separate Python and Rust pipeline with its own Rust implementation of the same conditions.
Before any cluster run, an automated check compares the two on the same labels, groups and seeds.

Because Rust and NumPy draw different random streams, it compares statistics: the delivered noise, the factor G, the median error, the number of badly corrupted labels and the number of molecules affected.
NoiseInject (version 1.0.0) evaluates model robustness and uncertainty calibration under artificial label noise, for both regression and classification.
It operates on arrays of labels and on the predictions of any externally trained model, which makes it model-agnostic, and its core depends only on NumPy, pandas, SciPy and scikit-learn.
Results are returned as pandas data frames with one row per noise level and one aggregate summary row.
The software is available under an MIT license and archived on Zenodo .
The regression injector sets a noise shape (Gaussian, Student-t or Laplace) and a targeting rule (uniform, grouped-wider, grouped-shifted, outlier or censoring) separately.
Each named condition is one combination of the two with its parameters, and the name is recorded with every result.
The requested noise is the noise level times the standard deviation of the clean training labels.
The injector solves for the scale / G in closed form (Equation ), and a level of zero returns the labels unchanged.
The affected molecules are selected by a separately seeded random number generator, so they are the same at every noise level while the noise draws change.
Under grouped-wider, whole scaffold families are added in random order until they cover as close as possible to 20% of the training molecules.
Censoring is parameterized by the fraction f of labels clipped, with its limit at the (1-f) quantile of the clean training labels.
On the training split the censored set is the k = round(fn) largest labels; on any other split it is whichever molecules lie past the training limit.

Each injection also returns a record of the target and delivered root-mean-square noise, the factor G, the solved scale, the mean of , the fraction of molecules affected, the group sizes and the random seeds.

A second function returns the noise scale each molecule would receive, without drawing noise; we apply it to held-out molecules.
Under uniform and grouped-shifted targeting this scale is the same for every molecule, so the package flags the result as degenerate rather than report a rank correlation of zero.
A separate injector sizes the noise against a unit supplied by the user.
In the KIRBy experiments this unit is the standard deviation of a model's out-of-fold residuals on the clean training labels.
It either adds Gaussian noise with variance equal to the level times the square of the unit, or moves 2%, 5% or 10% of labels by the level times the unit, with a random sign or always upward.
It can also add Gaussian noise whose standard deviation follows a per-molecule covariate or a hidden log-normal draw, scaled to the same mean variance.

The package provides six label-flipping strategies: uniform flips, flip rates set by class frequency, asymmetric flip rates for binary tasks, a random flip rate for each sample, a flip rate for each class, and flips directed by a confusion matrix.
Because the realized flip rate usually differs from the nominal probability, a binary search finds the probability that changes a target fraction of labels.
For regression, the package computes R^2, the root mean squared error (RMSE) and the mean absolute error at every noise level.
For classification, it computes accuracy, together with macro- and weighted-averaged precision, recall and F1 score and a per-class breakdown.
Robustness is read from the retention curve ret(x) = m(x)/m(0), where x is the noise level.
Here m is a bounded metric for which higher values are better: R^2 for regression, and accuracy, F1, precision or recall for classification.
The primary summary is the normalized area under this curve, AUCnorm (Equation in Chapter ), evaluated by the trapezoid rule.
It is the mean fraction of clean performance retained across the noise levels and lies approximately within [0, 1].
It is also less directly correlated with clean-label R^2 than other robustness metrics we tested.
A secondary summary fits ret(x) !(-(x/_W)^) to the curve.
The shape parameter separates curves that hold and then collapse ( > 1) from curves that fall early and then plateau ( < 1).
The parameter _W sets the scale of the decay, and the fit requires at least four noise levels.

The package also reports the clean baseline and the retention at the highest noise level, flags any curve that falls below zero retention, and can withhold the curve summaries for models whose clean baseline is too low.

For a model that returns a predicted standard deviation u_i for each sample, the package computes, at each noise level, the Spearman correlation between u_i and the absolute error |y_i - y_i|, the empirical coverage 1n_i 1[|y_i - y_i| k u_i] at k = 1 and k = 2, against Gaussian targets of 68.3% and 95.4%, the mean interval width 1n_i 2u_i, and the expected calibration error (ECE),
computed over ten equal-count bins B_b of u.
All of these use the clean test labels.
The Spearman correlation between u_i and the injected noise |_i| can only be computed on the corrupted molecules, where the noise is known.
It is reported within each noise level.

A correlation pooled across levels is also returned, but it mostly reflects that uncertainty and noise both rise with the level, so it does not measure whether a model can identify which molecules are corrupted.
Three optional wrappers produce u_i from a point predictor.
The first applies split-conformal prediction to any scikit-learn-compatible model, optionally scaled by the label spread of each molecule's nearest training neighbors.
The second fits an exact Gaussian process with a Tanimoto or RBF kernel through Gauche , and the third applies Monte Carlo dropout to any PyTorch network .
Chapter reports predictive performance as R^2 on held-out molecules and robustness as AUCnorm (Equation ).

This chapter has introduced the two parts of a predictor, the representation and the model.
Similarity depends on the representation and the coefficient, and activity cliffs and uninformative features break the similar property principle.
Real assay noise is often not independent, identically distributed or zero-mean, so our artificial noise model has seven conditions.
Methods for noisy labels fall into noise detection, noise mitigation and noise-robust training, and no single method is expected to win on every dataset.
NoiseInject injects the noise conditions and reports the robustness and uncertainty metrics.
