In this chapter, we inject the noise conditions of Chapter into training labels and measure how much predictive performance each pairing of representation and model keeps.

While there have been many investigations into the effect of noise on molecular property prediction, direct comparisons between how different molecular representations respond to label noise remain limited.
The choice of molecular representation certainly affects predictive performance.
evaluated 62,820 models and found that fixed representations, in most datasets RDKit 2D descriptors, outperformed representations learned from SMILES and molecular graphs.
Whether these conclusions translate to noise robustness is our question.
Between different types of label noise, found no difference in model performance between error distributions with the same mean and standard deviation.
We expand on this by considering alternative patterns of noise, namely noise concentrated in structural groups or on a sparse subset of samples.

This chapter addresses the questions set out in Chapter , specifically how the choice of representation and model architecture explain the variance in predictive performance and in noise robustness, what is the impact of the type of label noise, and whether uncertainty estimates track label noise.
We looked at six representations paired with thirteen models, and several variant models, across four prediction tasks.
Every pairing was run under Gaussian, grouped-wider and grouped-shifted noise at seven noise levels, and the other four noise conditions (Section ) were run on selected pairings.
The hyperparameters of every model are given in Additional file .
Although we are investigating the effects of label noise stemming from experimental settings, for the purposes of testing we inject controlled amounts of artificial noise into clean labels.

Data were extracted from the QM9 molecular property dataset distributed by PyTorch Geometric , which contains 130,831 small organic molecules with pre-computed quantum-mechanical properties obtained from density functional theory (DFT) calculations at the B3LYP/6-31G(2df,p) level of theory.
We selected the gap between the highest occupied and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (HOMO–LUMO gap) as the prediction target in QM9.
We assumed that QM9 labels were free of noise, notwithstanding approximations in the level of theory.

Each experiment was replicated 10 times with a distinct random seed and a randomly selected subset of N = 10,000 molecules, split 80/10/10 into 8,000 training, 1,000 validation and 1,000 test molecules.
All models were fitted on those 8,000 training molecules, except the Gaussian processes, which were fitted on a random subset of 5,000 of them; the validation and test molecules were unchanged.
We repeated these experiments on three molecular property datasets with experimentally determined endpoints.
From the OpenADMET initiative , we used LogD and Caco-2 efflux permeability, with N = 5,039 and N = 2,161 respectively.

We also selected hERG K_i data from ChEMBL , following a protocol inspired by : filter for binding assays, deduplicate by median pChEMBL value, and remove compounds with an inter-assay standard deviation greater than 1.0 log unit, resulting in N = 1,415 compounds.
Each of the three was partitioned into five folds by grouped k-fold cross-validation (CV), and each fold's training block gave up a further grouped fifth as a validation set for early stopping.
A model therefore fits between 3,194 and 3,364 of the 5,039 LogD molecules, depending on the fold, so the Gaussian-process subsample never applies to these datasets.
Unlike QM9's 10 replicates, which are 10 independent draws from one pool, each assay dataset is a single fixed set in which every molecule is tested exactly once and nothing is redrawn.
Log D is the logarithm of the distribution coefficient of a molecule between octanol and water, usually measured at pH 7.4.
It counts every charge state, whereas log P counts only the neutral form, so a basic amine that is protonated at that pH lowers log D below log P.
Caco-2 cells come from a human colorectal carcinoma and grow as a layer that models absorption in the gut.
Permeability across the layer is measured in both directions.
The efflux ratio is the permeability from the basolateral to the apical side divided by that in the other direction.
A ratio above about 2 suggests the compound is pumped out by a transporter such as P-glycoprotein.
The hERG gene encodes a cardiac potassium channel.
Drugs that block it can prolong the QT interval and cause arrhythmia, so hERG binding is screened early in drug discovery.
The hERG K_i dataset holds binding affinities for this channel, as pK_i values.
All splits and CV folds were grouped by the chirality-blind Bemis–Murcko scaffold, implemented such that each distinct acyclic molecule forms its own group, and groups are filled in random order.
Prior to modeling, all molecular structures were sanitized and canonicalized using RDKit to remove invalid valence states and standardize atom and bond typing .
Prediction targets were standardized to zero mean and unit variance.
Experiments that track uncertainty were run once rather than in replicates.

In this study, we evaluated six molecular representations: extended-connectivity fingerprints of diameter four (ECFP4), Avalon, Sort & Slice (SNS), physicochemical descriptors (PDV), ChemBERTa and Molecular Hypergraph Grammar GNNs (MHG-GNNs).
The same six were used on QM9 and on the three assay datasets.
ECFP4 is a Morgan fingerprint with radius r = 2 with d = 2048 bits .
Sort & Slice takes the same substructures as ECFP4, but it ranks them by prevalence and selects the top L (L=1024) .
We fitted the Sort & Slice vocabulary on the training molecules alone, refitting it for each QM9 replicate and for each CV fold.
Avalon is a 2,048-bit fingerprint, generated with the Avalon toolkit through RDKit .

The PDV representation is a vector of 200 physicochemical descriptors computed with RDKit's MolecularDescriptorCalculator ; the 200 are listed in Additional file , and the list is fixed in our code rather than taken from RDKit's default descriptor set, which grows between releases.
ChemBERTa embeddings are the mean over the non-padding token embeddings of the DeepChem/ChemBERTa-77M-MTR checkpoint, producing 384 features .

MHG-GNNs are a GIN-based autoencoder pre-trained on about 1.38 million PubChem molecules using -VAE loss, producing 1024-dimensional embeddings through iterative message passing and found in the published mhggnn_ pretrained_ model_ 0724_ 2023 checkpoint .
We z-score normalized PDV, ChemBERTa and MHG-GNN per feature, using the training molecules' mean and standard deviation; ECFP4, Avalon and Sort & Slice reach the model as built.
To understand model behavior in the presence of label noise, we explored a range of model families.
We fitted tree ensembles, a support vector machine, Gaussian processes and neural networks.
Several are variants of one another, differing in the probabilistic machinery they add, and Additional file gives every configuration with its settings.
Random Forests (RFs) are one of the most common choices for QSAR modeling thanks to their robustness and interpretability .
Quantile Regression Forests (QRFs) hold the distribution of training labels in each leaf and compute quantiles over all trees .
While we used 100 trees for RF, we observed a noisy quantile estimate with 100 trees for QRF, prompting us to use 300 instead.
To observe the effect of the quantile mechanism, we then fit a second RF at 300 trees so the two models were identical in all other settings.
We also used eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) , Light Gradient-Boosting Machine (LightGBM) , and Natural Gradient Boosting (NGBoost) .

NGBoost extends deterministic gradient boosting by treating the parameters of a chosen parametric distribution as regression targets and learns them through boosting with a natural gradient update rule .
NGBoost relies on scoring off validation data, which differs by dataset.
On QM9 the validation split is already held out of every fit.
However, on the three assay datasets the validation set is a scaffold-grouped fifth of the rows NGBoost is handed, which already exclude the validation molecules.
Support vector machines (SVMs) are a well-established baseline in QSAR modeling .
We used a radial basis function (RBF) with C = 1.0 and = scale as the kernel, as it accommodates continuous vectors.
Gaussian processes (GPs) are a non-parametric class of models that use a kernel to produce a Gaussian predictive distribution over every data point .
We fitted three variants of GPs, each with a constant mean and a scaled kernel.
The first uses an RBF kernel and runs on all six representations.
The second uses the Tanimoto kernel and was run on ECFP4 alone.
The third is a heteroscedastic variant in which the RBF process is given a second network that predicts the observation noise of each molecule.
One of the major limitations of using GPs in practice is computational scaling; inference has O(N^3) time complexity and O(N^2) memory, where N is the number of training points .
This can be mitigated with sparse GP approximations, but these introduce approximation error and can be more difficult to tune .
As such, we used a standard GP and only fit on at most 5,000 training molecules, drawn by a seeded sample.
Due to the size of the datasets, this cap only affected QM9.
We implemented these GP models in GPyTorch , with the Tanimoto kernel taken from the Gauche framework .

We tested two deterministic feed-forward architectures, both fully connected and both implemented in PyTorch : (i) NN- with two hidden layers of sizes 128 and 64, and dropout after each hidden layer and (ii) NN- with two hidden layers, each of size 128, with dropout applied before the output layer.
Each model was trained using the Adam optimizer with early stopping on validation loss.
We used Bayesian transformations to convert NNs into Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), and implemented them using PyTorch with ReLU activations and dropout regularization (p=0.2).
Additional file gives their full widths, dropout fractions, learning rates and batch size.
To get these networks producing uncertainty estimates, we applied four probabilistic transformations to each architecture, producing eight probabilistic networks.
The first replaces every linear layer with a Bayesian layer carrying a Gaussian prior N(0, 0.1^2) on its weights, producing BNN- and BNN-.
They are trained on an evidence lower bound whose Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence term is divided by the number of training molecules.
While this is a straightforward approach, it is computationally expensive.
We explored alternative techniques like our second variant, where we add an output head to the standard NN and fit the negative log likelihood of a Gaussian with that variance .

The third, Variational Bayesian Last Layer (VBLL), replaces the output layer with a Bayesian last layer that produces mean-field variational posteriors q(W) = N(_W, diag(_W^2)) over the last-layer weights and trains by maximizing the evidence lower bound.
This can be thought of as minimizing the reconstruction loss plus KL divergence D_KL(q(W) | p(W)) from a standard normal prior, scaled by 1/N .
Because only its output layer keeps a learned observation-noise parameter, VBLL networks report only epistemic uncertainty per molecule, with one aleatoric variance for the whole fit.
The fourth makes observation noise a function of the input.
All eight probabilistic networks estimate their predictive distributions from 100 stochastic forward passes.
Each network and its Bayesian counterpart were tuned to the same set of parameters so that NN- against BNN- and NN- against BNN- differ by the Bayesian layers alone.
The thirteen base models are RF, QRF, XGBoost, LightGBM, NGBoost, SVM, the RBF-kernel GP, and NN, BNN and VBLL in each of the two architectures.

The six variant models are RF (300 trees), the heteroscedastic GP (het.), the Bayesian networks with a variance head, BNN- (var. head) and BNN- (var. head), and the heteroscedastic VBLL- (het.) and VBLL- (het.).
The seven noise conditions used in this chapter are defined in Section .
We controlled noise quantity using noise levels, representing a fraction of the standard deviation of clean training labels.
We ran experiments across seven levels, 0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 and 1.5.
We added the noise to the raw label and standardized the target afterwards, using the clean training mean and spread.

To control the quantity of noise for censoring, we recorded every label above the kth largest clean training label as that limit and used this level as the fraction clipped, at 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5.
Censoring is common in pharmaceutical assays, where a third or more of labels can be censored .
We ran Gaussian, grouped-wider and grouped-shifted noise on every model and representation pairing.
The remaining four conditions ran on selected pairs.
On QM9, Laplace, Student-t and outlier noise were run on eight models, namely RF, NGBoost, SVM, the GP, GP (het.), BNN- (var. head), VBLL- (het.) and VBLL- (het.), each on ECFP4, PDV and ChemBERTa.
Censoring was run on five pairings, namely RF and GP (het.) on ECFP4, and NGBoost, the GP and BNN- (var. head) on PDV.

On the three assay datasets, AUCnorm under censoring was computed for the same five pairings, and the uncertainty statistics under censoring for QRF and the other models that give an uncertainty estimate, on ECFP4, PDV and ChemBERTa.
QM9 , loaded through PyTorch Geometric, was processed by a separate pipeline where the Python code loads and splits the data, and computes several representations.

The data is then passed to the Rust portion of the pipeline which injects the label noise, standardizes the labels, computes the remaining representations, and sends the processed data back to Python which trains and scores the models.
Each replicate, using its own random seed, randomly selects a subset from QM9, split using scaffold splits.
Each of these subsets is split by a new scaffold split (Datasets subsection), and the same grouping defines the scaffold families targeted by the grouped noise conditions.

Rather than parse a CSV or Parquet file into memory for every replicate, our pipeline writes the preprocessed data to memory-mapped binary files (.mmap), which stay on disk and are read record by record (Figure ).
Python writes one file per split.
The Rust program writes a copy in which the processed labels replace the raw ones, and Python reads that copy for training.
Each record holds the isomeric and canonical SMILES, the raw and processed target values, and the requested representations as fixed-width blocks.
Python and Rust read the same pages on disk without deserialization.
The Rust program draws the noise for each split separately, in the order its records are stored.
The amount of noise, the censoring limit and the affected scaffold families are all computed from the clean training labels.
Validation labels get the same amount of noise in label units, the same limit and the same families, from an independent draw seeded from the training seed.
The program checks that validation received as much noise as training.
Test labels are never corrupted, but every split records the noise scale each molecule would have received, so that held-out molecules can be scored against the pattern applied in training.
For every molecule, the Rust program records its canonical SMILES, clean and noisy labels, standardized value, injected noise, noise scale and noise pattern.
Each run also writes a summary of the noise parameters and the amount of noise delivered.

The run halts if a record holds a different molecule when it is written than when its noise was drawn, or if any molecule has an all-zero ECFP4 or Avalon fingerprint, which marks a failed featurization.
A self-test mode runs the same noise checks on a label file alone.
Up to this point we have been concerned with how noise affects the predictive performance of QSAR models.
However, label noise should also affect the uncertainty these models report.
Some models return only a point prediction, while others also return an estimate of uncertainty, either as a predicted distribution or as the spread across an ensemble .
Furthermore, some report a single value of uncertainty while others report one that can be decomposed into an aleatoric and an epistemic component .
The aleatoric component describes underlying noise the model associates with the data, while the epistemic component represents the uncertainty within the model's fit.
We sought to determine if, as expected, the aleatoric component rises with injected label noise while the epistemic component does not.
For the BNN and VBLL transformations, we took the two components over T = 100 stochastic forward passes :
where _t(x) and v_t(x) are the mean and the variance returned for molecule x on pass t, and (x) is the mean over passes.
Here v_t(x) is the predicted observation noise variance.
It varies per molecule in the variance-head and heteroscedastic variants, and is one number for the whole fit in the VBLL transformation.
A full-BNN without a variance head returns no variance, so its uncertainty is epistemic alone.
The other models follow the same split.
For GPs, the epistemic component is the posterior variance of the latent function and the aleatoric component is the learned observation noise .
All variants of the GP produce one number for the whole fit except heteroscedastic.
For QRF models, each tree holds multiple training molecules.
So for a given molecule, the aleatoric component is the variance of the labels in the molecule's given leaf.
The total aleatoric uncertainty is those variances averaged over the trees.
The epistemic component is the variance of the leaf means across the trees.
NGBoost predicts one variance for each molecule from a single fit, which is aleatoric alone .
In every model, the total uncertainty is the sum of the aleatoric and epistemic components.
No held-out label carries injected noise, so every comparison against the injected noise was made on training molecules.
Each training set was divided into five folds grouped on Bemis–Murcko scaffolds, and each molecule was scored by a refit that excluded its own fold.
For NGBoost on QM9, three of the five folds were scored to limit its cost.
No uncertainty was calibrated after fitting.
We compute statistics on the held-out molecules, for QM9 the test split and for three assay datasets the held-out fold of the scaffold CV.
Different combinations of dataset, model, representation, noise condition, and noise level are examined in each scenario.
We used the coefficient of determination (R^2) throughout.
For molecule i, let y_i be the clean label, y_i the prediction, _i the noise injected into its label and u_i the predicted uncertainty.
To evaluate the effect of label noise, we tracked predictive performance retention under increasing artificial noise.
For each QSAR pairing we recorded R^2() at each noise level , and normalized it to obtain the retention ratio R^2()/R^2(0).
To quantify robustness, we used the normalized area under this retention curve,
evaluated using the trapezoidal rule over the seven noise levels, 0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, in the units of Equation .
While we tested other metrics of robustness, we found AUCnorm to be less directly correlated to clean-label R^2 predictions.
For censoring, we sweep over a set of fractions to clip the labels prior to normalization.
An AUCnorm value near 1 indicates that the QSAR model in question has retained predictive performance with artificial noise, meaning it is more robust to noise.
Since we normalize the curve by its own clean-label predictive performance, a model with a low clean R^2 has less to lose, so AUCnorm is reported beside clean R^2.
We excluded replicates with a clean R^2 < 0.3 from the robustness analysis (Additional file ), as performance retention ratios become unstable when the clean-label denominator approaches zero.
On QM9 one AUCnorm is computed per replicate, and we report the median over the 10 replicates.
On the three assay datasets one value is computed per scaffold fold, and the median over the five folds is reported.
To compare the relative effect of the 13 base models across datasets and noise conditions, we compared their rankings using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient () between clean R^2 and AUCnorm.

We compared probabilistic models with their deterministic counterparts using a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test paired on the replicate, at = 0.05, separately for each representation and noise condition.
This test was run only on QM9, as with five scaffold folds the smallest attainable p is 0.0625.

We conducted a separate analysis of variance (ANOVA) for each noise condition to identify the relative contributions of molecular representation and model architecture to both predictive performance and noise robustness.
For a given metric y, either R^2 at a noise level of 1.0 or AUCnorm:

where s_r represents the effect of replicate r, _f represents the effect of model family f, _m(f) represents the effect of model architecture m within its family, _j represents the effect of molecular representation j, ()_fj and ()_m(f)j are the interaction terms, and e_fmjr is the residual.
The proportion of variance explained by each term was calculated as the effect size
using Type I (sequential) sums of squares, entered in the order replicate, model family, model architecture within family, molecular representation, interaction.
The 10 QM9 replicates provide the residual.
The uncertainty on each share is the 95% interval of ^2 over 1,000 bootstrap resamples of whole replicates.
These shares describe the models and representations tested here, not the choice of model or representation in general.
ANOVA relies on the assumption that observations both within and across groups are independent.
Two features of this study break that assumption.

First, each QM9 replicate uses the same data split and the same noise draw for every model and representation, so observations from one replicate are not independent of each other; we therefore entered the replicate as a block.

Second, across the whole set of models in this study, some pairs produced similar predictions that are not independent, so a method present in several near-identical versions would count several times towards the share of model architecture.
To handle this issue, we grouped the models into families.

We considered grouping pairs of models that share a method or an architecture, and compared each pair on clean R^2 and on AUCnorm under the three noise conditions run on every representation, separately on each of the six representations, which gives 24 comparisons per pair.
A pair was grouped when the mean difference between the two models was smaller than their standard deviation across replicates in at least two thirds of these comparisons (Additional file ).

Five families met this criterion: RF with quantile regression forests (QRF; 16 of 24), XGBoost with LightGBM (23 of 24), NN- with BNN- (20 of 24), NN- with BNN- (18 of 24), and VBLL- with VBLL- (20 of 24).

VBLL did not group with the plain or Bayesian network of its own architecture (4 to 10 of 24), as its clean R^2 was lower by 0.02 to 0.09, and NGBoost did not group with XGBoost or LightGBM (2 and 3 of 24).
The two architectures of the plain networks, and of the Bayesian networks, also met the criterion (18 and 17 of 24); we grouped by architecture instead, which the evidence supports equally well.
The 13 base models therefore form eight families.

Within these families, the differences between models accounted for at most 1.0% of the variance in any outcome and noise condition on QM9, and up to 15.1% of predictive performance on clean labels on the three assay datasets.
We also ran Tukey's honestly significant difference test between the members of each family, separately for each representation (Additional file ).
With 10 replicates it detects differences smaller than the variation between replicates, so we report it beside the size of each difference rather than use it to form the families.
Across representations, we considered grouping SNS with the ECFP4 fingerprint, as both encode overlapping circular substructure information.
The two differed by more than their variation across replicates on clean R^2 for every model (0 of 13), so all six representations were kept as separate levels (Additional file ).
To assess the interaction between uncertainty estimation and label noise, we posed three questions.
First, whether uncertainty rises with label noise, as measured by the mean u_i over held-out molecules at the highest noise level divided by its value with no added noise, in each replicate or fold.
The second pertains to models that report separate aleatoric and epistemic components.
We divided the increase of mean epistemic uncertainty between the highest level of noise and clean labels by the mean of the aleatoric component to determine how each responds to label noise.
A ratio near 0 means the added noise was attributed to the labels while a ratio of 1 or above means the epistemic component grew as much or more.
We also compared the mean aleatoric component with the standard deviation of the injected noise.

The third question we had was whether per-sample uncertainty values track injected label noise, as measured by the Spearman correlation between u_i and |_i| over out-of-fold training molecules, per fold and per noise level.
We also report the Spearman correlation between u_i and the absolute error of the prediction.

Finally, we asked whether dividing a molecule's out-of-fold absolute error by u_i ranks the corrupted labels better than the error alone, and report the difference between the two Spearman correlations with |_i|.

Considering the two main components of a QSAR model, the molecular representation and the model architecture, we sought to understand how each contributes to both predictive performance and noise robustness.
ANOVA decomposition divides the variance between model family, model architecture within its family, molecular representation, the pairing of the two, the replicate, and a residual.
We ran this decomposition for Gaussian noise, the standard model, as well as methods whose injected noise is related to the feature space, grouped-wider and grouped-shifted (Figure , Table ).
For predictive performance measured in R^2 at a noise level of 1.0, model family and molecular representation account for comparable shares of the variance, 26.6% and 29.0% under Gaussian noise.

However, for noise robustness, quantified by the normalized area under the R^2 retention curve (AUCnorm; higher values indicate greater robustness), model family accounts for 47.2% of the variance while molecular representation for 8.1%.
This pattern is observed across noise conditions and makes sense, as label noise does not impact the features.

The interaction between model and molecular representation explains 19.9% of the variance in AUCnorm, more than twice the 8.1% explained by representation alone, meaning representation acts on noise robustness mainly through the model it is paired with.
As such, we primarily compare representations within each model.
We compare the variance decomposition on both clean and noisy labels (Figure a).
For predictive performance, the artificial label noise lowers the impact of the choice of model family, while the replicate and residual take more.
This means that the variance is left more up to chance and to the underlying variation within the data itself with label noise, which is the expected behavior.
Robustness divides the variance a bit differently.
Representation explains 8.1% of the variance in AUCnorm, against 31.1% of clean R^2, while model family rises to 47.2%.
The replicate nearly disappears from AUCnorm, likely because each replicate's curve is divided by that replicate's own clean R^2, so a difficult split lowers both and cancels out.
We include two terms which stem from the data rather than the model, the residual and replicate terms.
The replicate measures how much of the variance can be attributed to the train and test split, which in this case is a scaffold split.
On QM9 we replicated each experiment 10 times with different random draws of N=10,000, each time giving a new scaffold split.
On the assay datasets, a replicate refers to one of the five scaffold CV folds.
A large replicate term in ANOVA indicates that the folds differ from one another.
The residual is variance that no other term accounts for.

While we observe similar patterns between noise conditions, the predictive performance of grouped-shifted noise in particular varies significantly between replicates, resulting in a larger share for the replicate.
We find that 28.4% of the variance in AUCnorm and 51.0% of the variance in R^2 are due to the replicate, with model family falling to 32.7% and 8.4%.
This indicates that the offset applied to each scaffold may account for more of the variance in both R^2 and AUCnorm.
The variance decomposition tells us what aspect of QSAR modeling affects predictive performance and robustness, however it does not tell us about the characteristics of individual models.
All models' performance degrades as the labels get increasingly corrupted with noise (Figure ).
The loss remains small until the artificial noise reaches about half the spread of the clean training labels, and then it begins to drop.
The rate it drops and the quantity of noise retained is not necessarily correlated to the model's predictive performance on clean labels.
Across the 13 base models under Gaussian noise at ECFP4, clean R^2 and AUCnorm rank in opposite directions at a Spearman correlation of -0.10 (p = 0.73) (Figure ).
If anything, the lower a model's predictive performance on clean labels, the less it has to lose as the labels get noisier.
The link between predictive performance and noise robustness can be examined by model family (Figure ).
The forests, boosted trees, SVM, and GP all retain relatively high predictive performance on clean labels while maintaining relatively strong robustness to noise.
The plain NNs and BNNs are among the highest in predictive performance on clean labels, and are the four least robust.
The two variational networks sit between these groups, with lower predictive performance on clean labels and middling noise robustness.
Standard feed-forward networks can make strong predictions under clean labels, however they are not a safe bet under noisy ones.
NGBoost is a standout case in the sense it is highly dependent on its paired molecular representation.
Under Gaussian noise it has the highest AUCnorm on every one of the six representations, yet also the lowest in predictive performance on four of the six representations.
It is one of the worst performing models with respect to R^2 on clean data.
Its high robustness is partially due to the fact that when you start with a low predictive performance, you don't have as much to lose.
However, it maintains shallow robustness curves across representations.
On ECFP4 NGBoost's predictive performance ranks lowest up to a noise level of 0.75 and stays in the lower half at every noise level.
However, on PDV it starts second lowest and ends highest, surpassing the other models between noise levels 1.0 and 1.5.
So when paired with the right features, NGBoost has the potential to make better predictions under higher quantities of label noise.
On grouped-shifted noise, RF has higher AUCnorm values than NGBoost on ECFP4, Avalon and ChemBERTa.
Even then, NGBoost reports the highest noise robustness for PDV, MHG-GNN and Sort & Slice.
While NGBoost performs well under higher label noise, LightGBM performs well under smaller quantities of noise.
Its performance drops sharply after noise level 1.0.

As we've seen, the choice of representation can have an impact on noise robustness, but that impact is determined by model family, represented by the interaction term between model and representation in Figure .
Some models are more impacted by representation than others, though.
In general, networks span a wider range of AUCnorm across the six representations than any of the other models.
Between ECFP4 and PDV under Gaussian noise, the four plain and Bayesian networks differ by between 0.037 and 0.065 of AUCnorm, while no tree or kernel model shifts by more than 0.011.
VBLLs are an exception, as no two variational networks differ by more than 0.019.

To further explore the impact of model architecture on noise robustness, we examined deterministic and probabilistic variants of the same core model architecture.
The hypothesis was that a model that reports a distribution rather than a point value may be more robust to small amounts of injected label noise.
We compared variants across three sets of base models: two NNs labeled NN- and NN- and RF (Figure ).
For each NN, we transform a standard deterministic network into a BNN.
The BNNs with a variance head run at different settings from their Bayesian bases, so they are compared only for uncertainty.
We compared RF to its probabilistic counterpart, QRF, with the same baseline architecture and hyperparameters.
Comparisons of this nature are only possible when the variants carry the same underlying settings (Additional files and ).
NN- and BNN- therefore share one setting, as do NN- and BNN-, and QRF is compared with a random forest of the same 300 trees (Additional file ).
We compare RF and QRF directly with the same underlying architecture.
QRF had lower AUCnorm on QM9 under Gaussian and grouped-shifted noise on every representation, and changed it little under grouped-wider noise, with almost no change in clean R^2 (Figure ).
On the assay datasets QRF was less robust than RF under grouped-shifted noise on every dataset and representation, and under Gaussian noise on LogD and hERG K_i (Additional file ).
Under grouped-wider noise it was more robust on Caco-2 and mixed elsewhere.

The Bayesian transformations that we used to transform feed-forward deterministic NNs into probabilistic ones produced a slightly larger AUCnorm, but only because they lowered predictive performance on clean labels.
BNN- kept more AUCnorm than NN- in most combinations on every assay dataset, and BNN- on all assay datasets.
On QM9 the Bayesian transformations made no significant change on either predictive performance or AUCnorm for either network.
Until now we've discussed how much predictive capabilities a model is able to retain while its training labels are corrupted with noise.
Now, we consider how confident the model reports its own predictions are in the presence of noise, and whether or not those estimates match the increased label noise.
found that the mean predicted uncertainty derived from the GPs increases with the amount of label noise in the training data.
We go beyond the population level and instead ask if a model's per-sample uncertainty tracks label noise.
One key sign that a model is able to handle noise is its ability to track it, represented by the per-sample Spearman correlation between predicted uncertainty and noise magnitude.
As expected, mean predicted uncertainty is positively correlated with Gaussian label noise for most models and representations (Table ).
There are a few exceptions, namely BNN- on PDV and VBLL- (het.) on Avalon for QM9.

BNN- fails to rise in at least one fold on every assay dataset, and both full-BNNs with a variance head fail on MHG-GNN for hERG K_i, and BNN- with a variance head also fails on ChemBERTa and on Caco-2.
's finding therefore holds for almost every probabilistic model on the computed property, and for most of them on measured labels.
While this tells us that the models are reportedly less certain under noisy data, we don't know what the model is attributing this uncertainty to.
To answer this question, we decompose uncertainty estimates into their aleatoric and epistemic components wherever possible.

We expect to see aleatoric uncertainty rise with injected label noise, while the epistemic component should remain relatively constant, as it is the aleatoric component that describes uncertainty in the underlying data.
The models whose frameworks allowed for this decomposition include full-BNNs with a variance head, the heteroscedastic GP, and QRF (Table ).
The two heteroscedastic VBLL networks also report both components, and they separate them more often than any other model, though not on every dataset and representation.
They are not drawn in the figures, as they were not scored out of fold.
The full-BNNs with a variance head behave as expected (Figure ), the epistemic component grows by at most 0.43 of the aleatoric growth in every configuration where the ratio can be computed.

Despite QRF's strong predictive performance and noise robustness, both of its aleatoric and epistemic components rise with noise and on some representations, the epistemic component actually rises at a faster rate.
Unlike the predictive performance and robustness, the representation actually dictates whether decomposition works.
For QRF, the epistemic growth is 0.61 to 1.14 times the aleatoric growth on the three fingerprints, 1.02 to 1.44 times on PDV, and 1.29 to 2.04 times on ChemBERTa and MHG-GNN.

Under Gaussian noise the heteroscedastic GP keeps its epistemic growth below a quarter of its aleatoric growth on PDV, ChemBERTa and MHG-GNN except MHG-GNN on QM9, but not on ECFP4 under grouped-shifted noise, where the two grow by similar amounts.

The noise conditions follow the pattern found in robustness, the three conditions which alternate the noise distribution show similar decompositions to those under Gaussian noise, while grouped-shifted raises the epistemic share of the heteroscedastic GP and of QRF in every pairing of dataset and representation.
This scaffold family-based offset may be appearing as structure in the data rather than label noise to the models.
The aleatoric component indicates that label noise increased, but it doesn't tell us by how much (Figure ).
For each unit of added noise it rises by roughly 0.4 to 1 unit, depending on model, dataset and representation.
The aleatoric component can therefore compare noise between datasets or noise levels, but it does not estimate a dataset's internal error.
Uncertainty estimation breaks under censoring as the process of clipping the labels narrows their spread, which in turn shrinks the total uncertainty.
None of the models tested treat a clipped label as a noisy one, so they actually grow more confident while losing information.
Finally, we ask whether a model's uncertainty on one molecule tracks the noise on that molecule's label.
We assess this using the Spearman correlation between predicted uncertainty and the size of the injected noise over out-of-fold training molecules.
Since Gaussian, Laplace, Student-t and grouped-shifted conditions add noise from the same scale to every label, there is not much for uncertainty to find.

It's the same situation with outlier noise, under which a tenth of the data is chosen at random for extra noise, and with grouped-wider in which each scaffold family falls in a single fold, so a model makes predictions based on unseen scaffolds and has no basis for estimating uncertainty.
The only case where per-sample uncertainty tracking is possible is censoring, as the noise is dependent on the value of the label itself.
The correlations are then large and mostly negative, meaning the model is least uncertain on the labels that were clipped most.

On QM9 with half the labels clipped, on PDV, they run from -0.84 to -0.80 across folds for NGBoost and from -0.47 to -0.41 for the GP, and on LogD with half the labels clipped every fold of every model except the two GPs is at -0.29 or lower.
We divided each molecule's error by its uncertainty and found that the division ranked the clipped labels better than the error alone on QM9 and on most of LogD.
Models are most confident on the clipped labels, probably because the clipping piles many labels into one value, which the model learns to tightly predict.

Ironically, per-molecule uncertainty can be used in reverse to identify clipped labels as the labels a model is more certain about, especially when they fall in a certain range, are most likely to have been clipped.
We investigated how a variety of molecular representations and models perform under increasing label noise.

We used ANOVA variance decomposition across three noise conditions on four datasets to show that molecular representation accounts for a larger share of the variance in predictive performance than in robustness.
Robustness to label noise, as measured by AUCnorm, the normalized area under the R^2 retention curve, is more impacted by the choice of model.
The representation each model is paired with explains more variance than the representation alone.

As such, a representation should not be chosen independently of the model it will be used with, and some models benefit from alternative molecular representations across both predictive performance and noise robustness.
Model family was the primary factor in every decomposition except one, Caco-2 under grouped-shifted noise, where the scaffold fold took the larger share.
Grouped-shifted and censored noise, the two conditions in which the error is systematic, corrupt QSAR model predictions the most.
Changing the shape of the distribution from which noise is drawn barely has an impact on model performance, a conclusion which is in agreement with .

Low quantities of noise do not make much of an impact, on the HOMO–LUMO gap every base model keeps at least 93% of its clean R^2 up to a noise level of 0.3, and grouped-shifted noise separates from the other conditions only from a level of 0.75 (Figure ).
Models' performance begins to degrade more rapidly on the assay datasets than on the HOMO–LUMO gap, which makes sense as assay data contain inherent experimental noise.

Tree and kernel models maintained consistent AUCnorm across all representations, while the plain NNs and BNNs depended on the representation they were given, as did the predictive performance of NGBoost.
Across datasets and noise conditions, RF and QRF were reliably robust, although their predictive performance on clean labels was middling and on Caco-2 they struggled under Gaussian noise.
QRF was the slightly less robust of the two, falling below RF under Gaussian and grouped-shifted noise.
Other models performed well only under some conditions.

The GP had the highest predictive performance on clean labels and under independent noise but fell behind when the noise was shared within a scaffold family, NGBoost predicted well only with the right representation, and SVM led in predictive performance under scaffold-shared noise on some datasets.

Transforming a feed-forward network into a Bayesian one increased AUCnorm, but the Bayesian variants never predicted better at any noise level, so switching to a tree-based model is the stronger move under label noise.
With regard to uncertainty estimation, mean predicted uncertainty rose with label noise for almost every probabilistic model on QM9 and for the majority of models on the assay datasets.

Of the models whose aleatoric and epistemic components can be split per molecule, the BNNs with a variance head, the heteroscedastic GP and the heteroscedastic VBLL networks correctly attributed error from the injected noise as aleatoric, while QRF read that error as epistemic.
The success of a split is also dependent on the representation, which is not necessarily the case for predictive performance or noise robustness.

The aleatoric component rises by roughly 0.4 to 1 unit for each unit of noise added, so it can compare noise between datasets or between noise levels, but it does not measure a dataset's internal error.
Outside censoring, no model's per-sample uncertainty identified which labels had been corrupted.
Under censoring the models' most confident predictions are the clipped labels themselves, and dividing a molecule's error by its uncertainty picked out the clipped labels better than the error alone.
QM9 served as a relatively clean baseline as its properties are computed.
The assay datasets containing experimental measurements on the endpoints LogD, Caco-2 , and hERG K_i are smaller and cover a more narrow range of the chemical space.
As the labels in these data are experimentally-derived and pooled from different laboratories, they contain some unknown amount of noise.
We are then adding artificial noise on top of the existing experimental noise.
These validation datasets supported the QM9 findings for the forests, with the boosted trees XGBoost and LightGBM the notable exceptions, degrading on the external datasets.
Future work should extend this type of noise robustness benchmarking to classification tasks and larger experimental datasets with better-known uncertainty estimates.

When training on noisy experimental data in the context of QSAR, it is important to keep in mind that a model's robustness to noise is primarily driven by its own mechanism of training, and to an extent the molecular representation the input data comes in, oftentimes with respect to the model.
Of the models tested, RF was the most consistent choice across the four datasets, ranking between first and eighth for AUCnorm on every dataset, representation and noise condition.
Where a predictive distribution is wanted, its probabilistic counterpart QRF maintains RF's predictive performance and nearly all of its noise robustness.
What QRF cannot do is say where that uncertainty came from.
Beyond the forests, the better choice depends on how much noise there is.
LightGBM and XGBoost predict well on clean labels and lose the most as noise rises, so they suit data you trust, while NGBoost and the VBLL networks start lower and hold what they have.
In this research, we define a noise level as a fraction of the spread of the clean training labels.
It is therefore relative to the dataset rather than an absolute measurement error, and cannot be mapped onto a given dataset exactly.
There are other mechanisms used to estimate the noise in a dataset directly.
When an assay's controls are available, the Z'-factor can be used to estimate noise .
You can also use screening data to test for row, column and plate effects, which produce systematic rather than independent error .
When you lack controls, replicates, and metadata, a label can be checked against the data itself.
Confident learning flags labels by comparing each label to what a model predicts for that molecule when it was left out of training .
You can use the point at which the model error matches the data's error to generate a predictive limit .
Beyond formal methods, you should consider how a dataset was assembled.
How many independent replicates were done, how many laboratories contributed, whether assay protocols were consistently applied, and how varied are the compounds in chemical space?
The first limitation of this study is data availability.
While HOMO–LUMO gap from QM9 is a good baseline as its computed labels carry no measurement error, it is only a single task.
As the noise is meant to replicate experimental data, this analysis would be improved by more quality-controlled, relatively clean and well-replicated experimental data across different targets.
However, data of that nature are hard to find publicly.
Second, AUCnorm is a ratio to clean R^2, so a model that starts from a low clean baseline has less to lose, and a few replicates scored above 1.05.
We tried other measures of noise robustness, but they were either too strongly correlated with clean R^2 or did not capture the right quantity.
The change in R^2 at a single noise level, for example, misses the shape of the curve.
AUCnorm is not a perfect metric, but it describes the whole curve, and across the 13 base models it is unrelated to clean R^2.
Third, it is hard to draw conclusions that hold across so many conditions.
No model or representation wins everywhere, although RF comes closest.
When working with cheminformatics data, you don't know in advance how a model and representation will perform on the given prediction task.
The underlying data is probably noisy, but you don't know how noisy it is or what shape that noise takes.

Given that, our recommendation is to test a handful of models against a handful of representations rather than tuning a single pairing, since on every dataset the pairing explains more of the variance in robustness than the representation does alone.
The pattern of the noise should also guide that choice (Table ).
The same preferences held on all four datasets.
Under Laplace, Student-t and outlier noise, RF was the most robust model and SVM was the second.
NGBoost lost AUCnorm under all three.
Under grouped-wider noise, QRF was the most robust model and SVM was close behind.
Of the boosted trees, XGBoost lost the most.
Grouped-shifted noise was the hardest condition.
Every model lost AUCnorm on every dataset and representation.
RF lost the least of the models that also predicted well, and the GP lost the most.
Gaussian noise was the only condition with a clear specialist.
NGBoost was the most robust model on the HOMO–LUMO gap under Gaussian noise with every representation, but not on Caco-2 or hERG K_i.
These results follow from the loss function each model fits.
NGBoost fits a per-molecule scale under a Gaussian likelihood, so it loses ground when the noise is not Gaussian.
SVM ignores residuals that fall inside its margin, so it gains under the same conditions.
QRF fits conditional quantiles, so a noisy scaffold family widens that family's interval without shifting the fit.
Each boosting stage fits the residuals of the stage before it, and those residuals are largest in the noisy families.
The GP is the most affected by error that is correlated with structure, because its kernel measures structure.
None of this matters if the data are clean, as little separated the models below a noise level of 0.3.
In this chapter each model was given a standard molecular representation, and the choice of representation explained relatively little of the variance in noise robustness.
We observe that this choice does impact the performance of different models to varying degrees, and the representations seem to capture different signals on each dataset that we tested.
Chapter asks how well these representations compare molecules on a single dataset.
The previous chapters have been focused on the impact of label noise.
Before we delve into techniques that are meant to train on, identify, and mitigate such label noise, we first focus on a tangential point, molecular similarity.

All of the aforementioned noise-adjacent methods, as well as the QSAR modeling itself, rest on the similar property principle (SPP; Section ), which posits that structurally similar compounds display similar chemical properties .
This serves as the conceptual foundation for QSAR modeling.
The concept of molecular similarity is also used in various contexts to compare neighboring molecules.
This comes into play when identifying noisy molecules that in theory stick out from their neighbors.
There are some important exceptions to the SPP, namely activity cliffs (ACs) .
Furthermore, there is no single way to define similarity between compounds.
This is where the principle begins to break down in practice.
When defining similarity between two molecules, we typically rely on some pairwise mathematical function, or coefficient, that takes in two molecular representations as input.
Two factors vary here, the representation and the coefficient.

compared eight coefficients and found Tanimoto, Dice, Cosine and Soergel the best and largely equivalent, while similarities derived from Euclidean and Manhattan distances were not recommended on their own.
In this chapter we ask if the standard methods of comparing molecules satisfy the SPP, insofar as they do not sufficiently quantify how similar two molecules actually are.
General-purpose molecular representations are designed to work across chemical domains.
Consequently, when considering data from a specific domain, many of their features show little to no variance.
Some representations assign separate molecules identical feature vectors.
Since common fingerprints do not encode stereochemistry , they are often unable to differentiate stereoisomers, which can have substantially different measured activity .
As these coefficients compare every feature, irrelevant features dilute the result.
Different representations also disagree about which molecules are close based on the information they carry.
The problem of whether neighboring molecules can predict chemical activity has been measured before.

The modelability index of scores a binary dataset by a class-weighted share of nearest-neighbor pairs that share an activity class, producing a single value for how strongly the similarity assumption holds on that particular combination of representation and data.
It is not clear whether a low value is due to the data being intrinsically hard to model or to the representation not capturing adequate features for the task.
Other work in this area relates to activity cliffs.
compared experimental error, activity distribution and activity-cliff metrics as predictors of how well a dataset can be modeled, and found the cliff metrics the strongest of the three.
However, they found that these metrics cannot separate real cliffs from those produced by uncertain activity measurements.
point out that some of these activity cliffs are artifacts of the chosen representation, similarity threshold, or noise in the data.
Activity cliffs are distinct from noise, as they carry some of the most valuable information about the interaction between structure and activity.
None of these measures ask specifically about whether the specific features within these representations matter for the property at hand.
We first consider how much the representation impacts similarity measures.

benchmarked 12 fingerprints and two simple baseline fingerprints for similarity-based virtual screening on 88 targets from three public collections, and found that the screening performance of the 12 fingerprints was highly correlated.
Only the two baselines differed significantly from the rest.
Nearly all of 25 pretrained neural embeddings were found to have a negligible improvement over ECFP across 25 datasets .

However, when looking into the differences between the structure of fingerprints, found that fingerprints which store raw counts are more effective at defining similarity than folded fingerprints when compared against a graph-based structural reference.
Folding introduces bit collisions, which disproportionately distort similarity for molecules with many set bits .

ACs follow the same pattern: across 15 configurations of representation and similarity measures on 3 datasets, the representations disagreed about which pairs form cliffs , supporting the point make about ACs being artifacts of their representation.

Any method that incorporates similarity measures, such as AC detection, or cleaning a training set by comparing each sample's label with its nearest neighbors' labels, whether by removing the samples that disagree or by smoothing their labels, inherits this choice, as do the noise estimation and mitigation methods of this thesis.
learn a molecular similarity from graph embeddings, but independently of any endpoint.
did choose the similarity for the task.

They predict each molecule's activity as the average over its k most similar molecules by Euclidean distance over descriptors, and choose the descriptors by simulated annealing to maximize the leave-one-out q^2.
also optimize the number of neighbors and their weighting.
Both select features for a nearest-neighbor model of one endpoint, whereas this thesis selects features across several representations.
The purpose of this chapter is to establish the problem that Chapter sets out to solve.
Section asks, for a given dataset, how much the features of standard representations vary and how many molecules map to identical feature vectors.

Section asks what happens when these features are used to quantify similarity, and Section follows the consequences for methods built on these similarity measures, including a small sweep of published noise-handling methods (Section ).

General-purpose representations are built to span a broad range of chemical domains.

When your dataset covers only a small region of the chemical space, a lot of the features within these generalized representations become irrelevant, describing chemistry which is absent from the data at hand.
Pairwise comparisons of these representations rely on these irrelevant features.
To investigate similarity estimation, we first look at a simple measure: how many features vary within a dataset.
A single dataset often contains a set of relatively similar molecules.
Many features within a generalized representation contain information that describes all, or almost all, of the molecules in the set, failing to capture the variation between them.
We define a constant feature to be one that takes a single value in every molecule of a dataset and a near-constant feature to be one that carries the same value in at least 95% of the molecules.

We counted constant and near-constant features from a set of representations (described in Table ) across hERG K_i, Caco-2, LogD, QM9, MDR1–MDCK efflux, human liver microsome (HLM) clearance, rat liver microsome (RLM) clearance and the Lhasa hERG blocker training set.
MDR1–MDCK efflux and the two clearance datasets come from Biogen .
HLM clearance and the Lhasa hERG set are not in Table ; their base representations are those with counts in Table .
The substructure-based fingerprints have the most near-constant features.
The learned embeddings, which are taken from the last layers of a NN, have none except MHG-GNN (Tables and , Figure ).
ECFP4 is the worst offender.
On hERG K_i (1,412 molecules) 1,815 of the 2,048 features are near-constant.
That jumps to 1,997 out of 2,048 near-constant features for the HOMO–LUMO gap on QM9.
292 of MHG-GNN's 1,024 features are zero in every molecule across all seven datasets that used it.
They come directly from the saved encoder output rather than the data, and we have not looked into why.
These constant counts are sometimes filtered out by the distance.
Tanimoto similarity (Equation ; the distance is 1-T) ignores bits off in both molecules, but a bit on in every molecule raises every molecule's measured similarity.
It does not use the 105 constant ECFP4 bits on hERG K_i.
Constant features add zero to a Euclidean or Manhattan distance; however, near-constant features are amplified.
That's great behavior if those features define an AC.
If not, they are contributing disproportionately to the measure of similarity.
A standard fingerprint- or descriptor-based representation can produce the same feature vector for two separate molecules.
In turn, models using this representation will produce a single prediction for the molecules with identical features.
Identical feature vectors do not always mean that the representation has merged two different molecules, since a dataset pooled from several sources can hold two measurements of the same molecule.
Many fingerprints are computed without stereochemistry .

In this research, ECFP4 is built with stereochemistry off, and the 2D descriptor sets (PDV, Mordred) also ignore it, so almost every molecule they produce identical representations for is a stereoisomer of another (Table ).
Any representation that reads from these subsequently merges stereoisomers.
Additionally, methods using the Weisfeiler–Lehman relabeling scheme are bounded by the 1-Weisfeiler–Lehman test (Chapter ), so some non-isomorphic graphs also receive the same vector.
This is seen in the graph-kernel features which tie 105 of 1,412 hERG K_i molecules, 56 of which differ only in stereochemistry and 49 in more than that.
Whether or not a learned embedding is able to differentiate stereoisomers is dependent on its input as well as its individual implementation.
SMI-TED, a pretrained SMILES encoder, ties 56 hERG K_i, 633 LogD and 177 Caco-2 molecules, all stereoisomers.
A tokenizer can drop stereochemistry prior to training.

The tokenizer of the ChemBERTa-77M-MTR checkpoint (ChemBERTa-2 in Table , called ChemBERTa in Chapter ) gives 72 of the 1,415 hERG K_i molecules of Chapter the same token sequence as another molecule.
Since stereoisomers can differ in measured activity , these representations lack potentially useful chemical information.
Two molecules are tied when a representation gives them exactly the same feature vector.
We counted ties on hERG K_i, LogD and Caco-2, for each dataset's base representations and augmentation features, the small feature sets added to the hybrid after it is built (Section ).
No tie came from one compound listed twice (checked by InChIKey, which differs between stereoisomers) or from a row of zeros (Table ).
Apart from the MACCS keys, most tied molecules are stereoisomers.
Atom pairs, PDV, Mordred and SMI-TED tie only stereoisomers, and ECFP4, Avalon and topological torsions add a few molecules that differ in more than their stereochemistry.
On hERG K_i, ECFP4, atom pairs, PDV, Mordred and SMI-TED tie the same 56 molecules, so joining any of these five representations leaves all 56 tied.
The WL graph kernel also ties 49 hERG K_i and 26 Caco-2 molecules that are not stereoisomers, and the MACCS keys tie the most molecules on every dataset, mostly not stereoisomers.
The 3D augmentation features and the learned embeddings ChemBERT, GROVER, MHG-GNN, MoLFormer and GraphMVP tie none, and joining all of a dataset's representations leaves no molecule tied.
A model has to give every molecule in a tied group the same prediction.
The best single prediction for a group is its mean label, so ties set an error that no model can go below,
where n is the number of molecules, G runs over the tied groups and y_G is the mean label of group G.
The matching best R^2 is 1 - RMSE_^2 / Var(y).
On hERG K_i this lowest error is at most 0.134 pK_i (MACCS keys), small next to the label standard deviation of 0.915 pK_i.
Single groups can still disagree by a lot.

Independent pK_i measurements of the same compound against the same target differ by 0.44 log units on average, with a standard deviation of 0.54 , so a gap larger than 0.54 inside a tied group is larger than typical measurement noise.
On hERG K_i, 6 of the 26 ECFP4 groups and 38 of the 153 MACCS groups differ by more than 0.54.
The widest ECFP4 group is a pair of stereoisomers 1.14 pK_i apart (Figure ).
An ECFP4 model can at best predict their mean, 5.59 pK_i, which leaves each molecule 0.57 pK_i from its measured value.
A tied pair with different labels is also the most extreme activity cliff possible.
The structure–activity landscape index of molecules i and j,
, is infinite when their similarity is 1 and their labels differ, and here the cliff is made by the representation rather than the chemistry.
A method that judges a label by its nearest neighbors sees a tied neighbor at distance 0 with a different label, and may flag a correct label as noise (Section ).

norm_text: Binary representations were compared by Tanimoto distance, and all others by Manhattan distance on standardized features (Section ), with constant features removed.
Chapter gives the MoleculeACE definition of an activity cliff, which combines three similarity measures.
Here we use one.
Two molecules are similar if their ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity is at least 0.55 , and a molecule is a cliff if a similar molecule has a label that differs from its own by more than a set gap.
We chose the gap on each dataset so that 15% of the molecules are cliffs, so the gap follows the spread of the labels (Table ).
On hERG K_i the gap is 1.76 pK_i, and 211 of the 1,412 molecules are cliffs.
On QM9 only 1,093 pairs of the 9,978 molecules are similar, and the gap is 0.05 eV, 0.06 times the median absolute deviation of the labels.
On the three Biogen datasets (RLM clearance, MDR1–MDCK efflux and HLM clearance) it is 0.20 to 0.34 log units, 0.50 to 0.60 times the median absolute deviation.
The count of cliffs depends on the representation.
We kept each dataset's gap and replaced ECFP4 with each other base representation, calling similar the same number of closest pairs as ECFP4 does.
On hERG K_i the number of cliff molecules then ranges from 138 (atom pairs) to 267 (WL graph kernel).
Of the pairs that ECFP4 calls similar, only 57% to 74% are also among another representation's closest pairs, and on QM9 only 1% to 24% (Additional file ).
We asked whether distance tracks label difference in two ways.

Over all pairs of molecules, we took the Spearman correlation between the distance of a pair and the absolute difference of its labels, a one-number summary of the neighborhood-behavior plot of ; datasets above 2,000 molecules were sampled down to 2,000.

Over each molecule's closest pairs only, we predicted each label as the mean label of the molecule's five nearest neighbors, taken from other scaffold groups, and took the Spearman correlation between predicted and measured labels.
Across the 70 combinations of dataset and representation, the all-pairs correlation ranged from -0.04 to 0.23 and was below 0.10 in 44 of them.
The five-neighbor prediction reached 0.29 to 0.89, higher than the all-pairs correlation in all 70 (Table ; every representation is in Additional file ).
On hERG K_i with ECFP4, the all-pairs correlation is 0.06, while the five-neighbor prediction reaches 0.72, with an RMSE of 0.63 pK_i against a label standard deviation of 0.92 pK_i.
Figure shows why the two differ.
Of the 996,166 hERG K_i pairs, 93% have an ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity below 0.20, and only 1.1% reach 0.55.
Over all pairs the median label difference is 0.81 pK_i, but above a similarity of about 0.4 it is 0.20 to 0.30 pK_i, although 8.3% of the 774 pairs at 0.8 or above still differ by more than 1 pK_i.
Mordred shows the same pattern: the closest 5% of pairs have a median difference of 0.44 pK_i, and every other 5% has 0.78 to 1.11 pK_i.
The useful information sits in the few closest pairs.
The all-pairs correlation is set by the other 95%, whereas the five-neighbor prediction uses only the closest pairs.

We compared the five nearest neighbors of each molecule, from other scaffold groups, under ECFP4, SMI-TED and Mordred (PDV on Caco-2, where Mordred is not a base representation; on HLM clearance ECFP4 is not a base representation and its stored features were used).
On hERG K_i any two of the three share on average 0.47 to 0.52 of each molecule's five neighbors, and on the three Biogen datasets and QM9 only 0.13 to 0.21 (Table ).
For 500 random pairs per dataset we found the maximum common substructure (MCS) with RDKit , allowing 2 seconds per pair and leaving out pairs that ran out of time.
The MCS distance is 1 - n/(a+b-n), where n is the number of atoms in the common substructure and a and b are the numbers of heavy atoms in the two molecules.
Its Spearman correlation with ECFP4 Tanimoto distance ranged from 0.20 (hERG K_i and HLM clearance) to 0.51 (Caco-2 and LogD).
Every method in Section takes a similarity as input and inherits the dilution described here.
We've identified some issues within the representations and similarities computed over them.
While this calls into question the predictive limits of QSAR and other structure-based modeling, it also calls into question downstream applications of molecular similarity.
Nearest-neighbor methods, where a molecule's neighbors, as measured by similarity, are the inputs to several other processes, are by definition sensitive to the quality of similarity measurements.

They are used within other processes like predicting a molecule's activity using its neighbors' labels, detecting outliers, either ACs or noise, defining an applicability domain by distance to the training set , grouping molecules into clusters for data splits , identifying activity cliffs, and, in federated learning, weighting each site's vote on a molecule by that molecule's distance to the site's own data .
If this measure of similarity, or equivalently distance, is flawed, then all of these downstream applications will feel the effects of it.
