norm_text: On LogD with the SVM at 1,000 features, for example, it reaches 0.4303 RMSE against 0.4452 for recursive elimination.

subsection: Selection at a fixed number of features
norm_text: Recursive elimination ranks every feature of the joined representations in one list with one forest, which is the pooled ranking the hybrid avoids (Section ). hERG K_i with the DNN is the exception, where recursive elimination and even random features beat the hybrid at 1,000 features.

subsection: Selection at a fixed number of features
norm_text: On antibodies random features are beaten at most budgets, but recursive elimination is ahead on G with the SVM and on CHO polyreactivity at every budget.
The number of features the search picks depends on the dataset and on the downstream model.
On Caco-2 the search picked more features for the DNN than for the SVM.
On LogD it picked 2,000 for the DNN on every fold, the top of the grid, so the best width for that model may lie above what was searched.
The SVM's smaller picks fit what Chapter showed for distances.
A kernel computed over many features is diluted by the ones that carry nothing, while a network can learn to ignore them.
The small antibody sets pick at most a few hundred features on angiopoietin-2 and G.
On expression titer the random forest's pick varies widely between folds, which is the selection noise of the previous section showing up in the budget.
No one budget or representation count would serve every dataset and model, which is why both are searched (Figures and ).
Across the configurations of a search, the choice of downstream model accounts for more of the variation in score than the budget on most datasets with a result.
On LogD, for example, it accounts for 48.5% of the variance against 1.4% for the budget.
The budget still interacts with the model's own settings.
With the SVM on LogD, rat microsomal clearance, MDR1–MDCK efflux and Caco-2, the search picks the same budget on every fold when the SVM's C is 0.01 or 0.1.
On LogD and rat microsomal clearance it picks larger budgets when the SVM is not (C = 10).
A model that is allowed to fit more can use more features.
The width of the DNN does not move its pick in the same way: on LogD it takes the top of the grid at every width.
Scoring candidate hybrids with the downstream model itself, rather than a model of another family, makes almost no difference on small molecules.
On LogD, Caco-2 and hERG K_i with the SVM the three evaluator settings end within a few thousandths of an RMSE unit of each other.
A cheap evaluator ranks candidate feature sets about the same way as the model that will use them, so on these datasets the search does not need the expensive one.
On some antibody datasets it matters.
On EGFR binding the matched evaluator gives 0.3527 Spearman with the SVM against 0.2993 for a LightGBM evaluator.
It is also best with both models on expression titer and colloidal stability.
Using the importance scores again during training does little on small molecules.
The best of the four conditions gains little over the plain hybrid on any small-molecule dataset, and feature scaling makes LogD with the SVM worse.
The selection has already used the importance scores, so on small molecules there is little left for them to add.
On antibodies some condition helps on most datasets, and by more.
Feature scaling takes colloidal stability with the DNN from 0.2607 to 0.3571 Spearman, and keeping the above-median features also helps G with the SVM.
Both act as further regularization on training sets of a few hundred antibodies.
Which condition helps changes from one dataset and model to the next, so none of them is a default.
Choosing fewer features does not replace tuning the model on small molecules.
A hybrid of up to 2,048 features with the SVM's regularization setting tuned beats the search's smaller hybrid at the default setting.
It does so on all four small-molecule datasets with a result, for example 0.4114 against 0.4299 RMSE on LogD.
On nanobody thermostability, G, expression titer and the Buchwald–Hartwig reactions the smaller hybrid is ahead.
The budget and the model's own regularization both control how much the model can fit.
With thousands of molecules the model's setting does that better, and with a few hundred the budget does.
The hybrid can take in a new embedding as one more base representation, and on small molecules it uses it.
Its selected features beat Gaussian random features put in the same places in the hybrid.
They do so for every embedding on Caco-2 and hERG K_i, and for seven or eight of eight on LogD.
On colloidal stability, expression titer and the Buchwald–Hartwig reactions, they do so for fewer than half of the embeddings.
On the two antibody datasets, one more language model of the same sequence adds little.

With 90% conformal intervals, the hybrid's intervals on small molecules cover close to 90% of the held-out molecules, as the single representation's do, and are narrower: on LogD with the SVM the mean width falls from 1.652 to 1.403 log units.
On several small antibody datasets the hybrid's intervals cover too few held-out antibodies, fewer than the single representation's, for example on angiopoietin-2 binding and G with the SVM.
The calibration set is part of a training fold of a few hundred antibodies.
The hybrid chosen on those antibodies is optimistic about them, the same selection bias as above.
On one fold of each dataset (Figure ), several hybrids draw on all ten representations in similar amounts, for example on LogD with the DNN and on the anti-VEGF expression scan with the SVM.
Elsewhere one or two representations carry the hybrid.
On EGFR binding almost all of its features come from ESM-2 run on the joined chains.
LogD can be read chemically (Figure ).
The SVM's hybrid picked 372 features on all five folds.
Of these, 38 are Mordred descriptors and 36 are ECFP4 bits.
The rest come from eight representations whose features carry no names.
Among the descriptors are Crippen's calculated logP (SLogP), the number of basic groups (nBase) and several surface areas binned by partial charge (PEOE_VSA).
There are also counts of secondary amine and aromatic nitrogen environments.
Among the bits are tertiary amine environments, in which a nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (CN(C)C), and aryl chloride environments.
Unlike logP, which counts only the neutral form of a molecule, logD at pH 7.4 counts every charge state.
At that pH a basic amine is largely protonated, which lowers logD below logP.
A model of LogD should therefore need both lipophilicity and basicity.
The hybrid picked both, on every fold, from two different representations.
The features picked are partly the same from fold to fold.
On the stability index of , the small-molecule hybrids score between 0.27 and 0.50.
The antibody hybrids score between 0.08 and 0.27, and the Buchwald–Hartwig ones fall in the same range.
Many features are correlated within and across representations, so a feature on one fold can stand in for a different one on another.
An index well below 1 therefore does not mean the hybrid is fitting noise.
It does mean a blueprint should be read for what recurs across folds, as for LogD above, rather than from a single fold's list.
On antibodies, features drawn from several language models of one sequence are largely interchangeable, and on a few hundred antibodies which of them is picked changes from fold to fold.
The small-molecule result carries over to the three activity-cliff targets of , data the hybrid was not developed on.
For all but one of the six target and model pairs, the hybrid has a lower error than the single representation the same search ranked first.
With the DNN on factor Xa it goes from 0.7367 to 0.6612 MAE in log units of activity, lower on all five folds.
The exception is factor Xa with LightGBM, where the hybrid is worse.
These targets have many activity cliffs, which is where a single similarity-based representation struggles most (Chapter ).
On Caco-2, MACCS keys and the WL graph kernel both give some molecules a row that another molecule also has (Table ).
Amino-acid composition does the same to 432 of the 659 variants in the EGFR scan, which differ by single mutations.
None of the hybrids built on these datasets leaves two samples with the same row.
On hERG K_i the graph kernel leaves some molecules sharing a row (Table ).
Adding features from ECFP4 and MHG-GNN takes it from 0.6109 to 0.5715 RMSE with the SVM, lower on all five folds, and no two molecules share a row.
Adding ECFP4 and PDV instead improves it almost as much while some molecules still share a row.
So most of the gain comes from the information the added representations give every molecule, and little from breaking the ties.
Search settings found on LogD were reused on hERG K_i, with the features selected again on hERG K_i.
They beat hERG K_i's best single representation with both models (SVM 0.5888 to 0.5665 RMSE, on all five folds).
They stay behind a search run on hERG K_i itself.
Reusing settings saves the search on the smaller dataset at some cost in error.
Feature selection can run where data cannot be pooled.
When each site holds one family of representations, one feature selection over all families beats both the best single family and the best single representation on Caco-2 and LogD, with both models.
On LogD with the SVM it reaches 0.4382 RMSE, against 0.4598 for the best family, and the best single representation is further behind.
Selecting at each site with an even share of the budget does as well as one selection over all families on every dataset and model.
It can, however, build a different number of features.
So each site can select on its own and send only feature indices.
When each of five sites holds a different representation, one hybrid over all sites beats the best single site on both datasets with both models.
It also beats the collaborator's two ensembles, which combine the sites' predictions, in three of the four dataset and model pairs.
The exception is Caco-2 with the DNN, where the ensembles reach 0.2721 and 0.2730 RMSE against 0.2837 for the hybrid.
With two-class labels and up to 30% of each site's labels flipped, selecting features at each site beats the collaborator's ensembles and their student model at every flip level on Caco-2.
With the DNN and no flips it reaches an MCC of 0.5085 against 0.3904 for the better ensemble, and it stays ahead with 30% flipped.
It never beats the same selection made with all molecules pooled, so keeping the data apart still costs something.
With the DNN at 30% flips the two are almost equal.
Only Caco-2 has finished, with three seeds for the DNN and two for the SVM.
We selected features separately in each of five k-means clusters of Caco-2 and fitted one model on all molecules.
This matches one global selection (0.5289 against 0.5316 MCC with the DNN), while fitting a separate model per cluster is worse.
The clusters agree less on which representations matter than random parts of the same size do, measured by mean rank correlation.
This chapter asked how the best set of features can be selected for a given prediction task (Section ).
The answer is that it depends on the dataset and the downstream model, and that a search can find it.
On every small-molecule dataset the hybrid beats the best single representation with both downstream models, on every fold of the six regression datasets.
It also beats the representation that was best in hindsight.
It does so because the representations carry different information.
On hERG K_i, Caco-2 and MDR1–MDCK efflux the hybrids draw on five to seven of them, and no one of them carries more than 29% of the drop in score when its features are shuffled.
On small molecules, this supports the hypothesis behind the hybrid, that the feature set is part of the problem.
At the same number of features the hybrid beats recursive elimination and random features on all but one of the small-molecule datasets with a result.
Drawing on several representations beats drawing on the top one alone on most datasets.
How the budget is split matters less than which representations are drawn on.
No single setting suits every dataset and model.
On Caco-2 and LogD the DNN picked more features than the SVM, and the number of representations ranges from two to all ten.
The cheaper internal evaluators are good enough on small molecules but not on some antibody datasets.
The selected features can also be read: on LogD the hybrid picks lipophilicity and basicity on every fold, from two different representations.
On antibodies the hybrid helps for the same reason it helps on small molecules: the features that matter are few and buried in representations of the whole sequence.
On G, AC-SINS self-association and the 4,275-variant expression scan it beats every single representation.
On the first and last of these, the best single representation is one built here to read the regions and mutations that vary.
On the smaller sets its gains are inconsistent, the search's own scores are optimistic, and an ensemble of one model per representation often does better.
The method also runs on reactions, where it gains nothing on the additive split.
It runs on data held at separate sites, where selecting at each site does as well as one selection over all representations.
It also takes in new embeddings added to the pool.
The fourth question asked whether weighting features by their importance improves the hybrid and model training.
In construction, ranking features by importance within each representation is what makes the hybrid work.
In training, using the importance scores again adds little on small molecules and helps on some small antibody datasets, with no condition that works everywhere.
Whether hybrids keep more of their performance under label noise, and whether their features stabilize noise mitigation, are the subjects of Chapters and .
The hybrid needs data.
Its gains are consistent on datasets of a few thousand samples and inconsistent on datasets of a few hundred.
On those smaller datasets the search's internal scores overstate what the chosen hybrid delivers by up to 0.16 Spearman (Section ), and its prediction intervals cover too few held-out samples.
Most of the antibody datasets in this chapter are of that size.
The antibody results therefore say as much about dataset size as about antibodies, and these datasets cannot separate the two.
Whether the best hybrid settings follow measurable properties of a dataset is the question of the experiment still to be reported in Section .
The hybrid can only select from what the pool offers.
The antibody pools are mostly protein and antibody language models of the same sequence, several of them variants of ESM-2.
The antibody hybrids therefore had few representations of different kinds to combine.
Frozen embeddings also set a ceiling: no signal can be added beyond what the inputs contain.
Integrating many foundation models, each with its own dependencies and hardware, is difficult engineering, and the burden grows with the number of models.
The search is costly and must be rerun when the data, the representations or the downstream model change.
The grid of each dataset was cut to save compute (Section ), so the hybrids reported here are at worst less informative than a full search would find.
The settings found on one dataset carry over to a related one only partly, and we tested this on one pair of datasets.
A downstream model from outside the fixed list of model families gets no matched evaluator.
A full search of one dataset took 0.4 to 38.6 hours of CPU jobs, 8 cores each by default, summed over its 5 outer folds.
A simpler selection is sometimes enough.
Recursive feature elimination over all representations joined beat the hybrid at every budget on G with the SVM and on CHO polyreactivity.
It also beat it on hERG K_i with the DNN at the larger budgets.
On small molecules, tuning the SVM on a wider hybrid did better than a smaller one.
Where one of these is enough, the search costs more than it returns.
Several results are provisional.
Most DNN results were computed before the correction of 8 October 2026.
The Gaussian-process results will change when that model is replaced.
With the DNN, the comparison with PCA at the same number of features disagrees between experiments and waits for the DNN re-runs.
The experiment on adding a new embedding ran on 2,000 molecules of LogD and hERG blocking, and its random control swaps features without a new search.
The separate sites are simulated from one public dataset, so the differences between real sites in curation and chemistry are not tested.
Only Caco-2 has finished the experiment with flipped labels.
This chapter used the hybrid only as input to a model.
Chapter asks whether a feature set chosen for the task also gives better neighbors, which every method that relies on similarity could use, including the detection of noisy labels.
Chapter built the adaptive hybrid representation, a set of features selected from several base representations for one task, as input to a model.
Chapter showed that in most standard representations the distance between two molecules barely rises with the difference in their labels.
Any method that trusts a molecule's neighbors inherits this, such as predicting a label from the nearest neighbors or finding a noisy label by comparing it with its neighbors' labels.
The first idea behind the hybrid was to compute distances on the features relevant to the task alone.
This chapter tests that idea.
There are two ways to use a hybrid for similarity.
In the first, the search of Chapter is run with a nearest-neighbor model as the downstream model, and distances are measured in the hybrid it selects.
In the second, the search ranks each candidate hybrid by how well each molecule's label is predicted from its five nearest neighbors in it, and no downstream model is fitted.
We ask two research questions:
Does distance in a hybrid track label differences better than distance in the best single representation?
Do the methods built on that distance work better in a hybrid?
We test prediction from nearest neighbors, activity cliffs, Bayesian optimization, distance to the training molecules as a guide to prediction error, retrieval of neighbors and clustering.
This chapter uses 13 datasets: five small-molecule, seven antibody and one reaction dataset.
Antibody datasets outnumber small-molecule datasets, so we give every result by domain rather than pooled.
Datasets, folds (grouped by scaffold family for small molecules) and metrics are as in Chapter , with five outer folds.
Some experiments have no result on some datasets because their runs did not finish in time (Section ), and Section lists them.
In each outer fold, everything an experiment compares is chosen from searches on that fold's training molecules alone, and then scored on its held-out molecules.
Features are scaled on the training molecules: features that only take the values 0 and 1 are left as they are, and the rest are standardized.
In the experiments, but not inside the searches, held-out values are also cut to the training range, so a single extreme molecule cannot dominate a distance.
Where a statement covers all 13 datasets, ``molecule'' also stands for an antibody or a reaction.
The fold split, the sample of molecule pairs, the label permutations, the random feature subsets and the k-means starts all use fixed seeds.
So the spread we report is the spread across the five outer folds of one split.
We report the mean over the five folds, and the per-fold values where the spread matters, without significance tests.
The simulation of choosing molecules to measure is repeated over three starting sets instead.
Each outer fold runs three searches on its training molecules.
The first, the general search, is the search of Chapter , run for each of the dataset's two downstream models (Table ).
The second, the distance search, uses a k-nearest-neighbor model as its downstream model, with Euclidean distance and five equally weighted neighbors.
It uses fewer neighbors when a fold has under 25 training molecules.
It has its own lists of importance methods, allocation methods, numbers of representations and budgets.
Its budgets are capped at 500 features, and on some datasets its other lists differ from the general search's too.
On hERG K_i, for example, the general search tries 250, 500, 1,000 and 2,000 features, while the distance search tries 100, 250 and 500.
The third is the similarity search, described in Section .
From these three searches, we take the following feature spaces:
the nearest-neighbor model's best and second-best single representations, ranked by the distance search;
each downstream model's best and second-best single representations, ranked by its general search;
each downstream model's two best hybrids, four in all: the predictive hybrids;
the top hybrid of the distance search: the distance hybrid;
the top hybrid of the similarity search: the similarity hybrid, on the datasets where that search is defined.
Unless stated otherwise, ``the single representation'' in the results means the nearest-neighbor model's best single representation, and ``the hybrid'' means the distance hybrid.
Retrieval and clustering also score one control: the principal components of all representations joined, with as many components as the hybrid has features.
The search of Chapter can be written as follows.
Each configuration fixes an importance method, an allocation method, a number of representations and a budget B.
Given base representations R_1, , R_m, a configuration builds a feature set S_ R_1 R_m with |S_| B.
The search returns S_^*, where ^* = _ s(S_) and s is the search's score.
In the general search, s is a downstream model's score on the search's own held-out folds.
In the similarity search, s(S) = q_5(S), how accurately each molecule's label is predicted from its five nearest neighbors in S (Equation ).
No downstream model is fitted.
All other settings and the folds are shared with the general search.
The neighbor score, computed on a validation set taken from the fold's training molecules, also replaces the internal evaluator when the budget is split.
and chose descriptors to maximize nearest-neighbor prediction within one descriptor set.
We modify this by choosing features across several representations.
The similarity hybrid tests whether choosing features for how well the neighbors predict a label does better than choosing them for a model's prediction.
The score uses the Manhattan distance of Chapter , on features scaled as above.
Each standardized feature adds a term of similar size to this distance.
So a representation's weight in the distance, which the allocation method sets, is roughly its number of features divided by the budget.
A feature that only takes the values 0 and 1 adds less, so a fingerprint weighs less than this per feature.
The neighbor score uses no importance weighting.
We chose Manhattan distance in an earlier comparison of four distances on hERG K_i and LogD, over seven representations each.
It was the only distance never much worse than second on any of three scores: splitting the budget, predicting from neighbors and agreeing with shared structure.
Cosine was better at predicting from neighbors.
The inverse-distance weights were not compared when the score was built.
A later comparison on four datasets used Manhattan distance with 5 neighbors.
There, inverse-distance weights beat equal weights in all 48 pairs of dataset and representation, but lost to inverse squared distance in 39 of the 48.
To rank whole candidates, we compute the score on the held-out molecules of each fold of the search, inside the outer training fold.
These molecules act as each other's neighbors.
Their groups (scaffold families, for small molecules) are split into up to 5 parts, and each molecule's 5 nearest neighbors are drawn from the other parts.
A neighbor from the same scaffold family is an easy match and would inflate the score.
This is the only place in the chapter where a molecule's own group is kept out of its neighbors.
Each neighbor is weighted by the inverse of its distance :
A neighbor at distance 0 receives all of the weight, shared equally if there are several.
On regression data, the score q_5 is the Spearman correlation (y, y).
On binary data, y_i is the distance-weighted fraction of neighbors in class 1, and q_5 = 2(AUROC - 0.5), where AUROC is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.
Both scores put chance at 0.
The budget split needs this, because each representation's share of the budget is its score divided by the sum of the scores.
The modelability index of (Chapter ) is related, but uses a single nearest neighbor and a hard class match.
A fold of the search is undefined when it has fewer than 10 held-out molecules or fewer than 2 groups, or when its labels or predictions are constant.
A candidate hybrid with an undefined fold is refused, rather than ranked on fewer folds.
We do not run the similarity search where its score is undefined:

The four Ginkgo developability datasets in this chapter (AC-SINS self-association, SMAC colloidal stability, CHO polyreactivity and expression titer) use the competition's five folds as their five groups.
Inside an outer fold, each held-out block of the search is then a single group, so no antibody has a neighbor outside its own group.
On the change in binding free energy ( G) caused by a mutation, one protein complex holds 69 of the 429 rows.
On outer folds 1 to 4 it falls alone into one held-out block of the search, and every candidate is refused.
We skip this dataset on all five folds.
Every experiment that predicts from neighbors or measures retrieval scores each feature space at every combination of the settings in Table , instead of at one chosen setting.
A held-out molecule's prediction is the weighted mean of its neighbors' labels,
where N_k(i) is the k training molecules nearest to i under distance d, and w_ij is the neighbor weight.
On classification data, each class receives the summed weight of its neighbors.
A molecule's own group (scaffold family, for small molecules) is never excluded from its neighbors, only the molecule itself.
The one experiment that does not use these settings is the one on all representations joined (Section ).
We found no published source for the rank scheme, so we count it as new.
In a comparison of six schemes on four datasets, 1/rank was best in 27 of 48 dataset and representation pairs and 1/d^2 in 20, while equal weights were never best.
The winning margin was at most 0.0015 RMSE, against a spread across folds of 0.02 to 0.12, so we sweep both.
Importance weighting is feature-weighted nearest neighbors , modified so that the weights come from the importance scores of the hybrid search.
Each feature is multiplied by its weight before the distance is computed, x' = x w.
Negative importances are set to 0.
For a single representation, the importance s is computed on the fold's training molecules, with LightGBM gain in most experiments.
For a hybrid, it is the importance its search used to select the features, with two exceptions.
Distance against label difference refits LightGBM gain on the hybrid's features together, and retrieval recomputes the search's importance on the hybrid as a whole.
We use two formulas for w:
for distance against label difference and the best number of features, w = (s/s)^a, with a = 1 under Manhattan distance, a = 0.5 under cosine and a = 2 under Minkowski with p = 0.5;
for every other experiment that weights, w = s^1/2 under every distance.
The exponent a of the first formula is set so that each feature's term in the distance is multiplied by its relative importance, s_f/s, under all three distances.
The second formula has no such matching.
Under Manhattan distance, a feature with four times the average importance counts four times as much as an average feature under the first formula, and only twice as much under the second.
So the weighted distances of Sections and are the same distance only under cosine.
Some experiments divide the second formula by a constant, which changes neither the ranking of distances nor any prediction from neighbors.
No experiment in this chapter varies the exponent.
The square root was first written for Euclidean distance and kept for the others.
An earlier comparison on four datasets tested it against a power of 1 at every distance.
The square root was better in 34 of 48 dataset and representation pairs, and in 19 of 33 under Manhattan distance.
Table lists every similarity experiment.
The paragraphs below define what each one estimates.
For one feature space, this experiment estimates the Spearman correlation between the distance of two held-out molecules and the absolute difference in their labels.
A positive value means that molecules further apart differ more in their labels.
We estimate it in each outer fold from a sample of up to 50,000 pairs.
We measure it first in each of the dataset's representations alone, under every distance of Table , with no selection and no importance weighting.
We then measure it in the feature spaces of Section , unweighted and weighted.
We predict each held-out molecule's label from its nearest training molecules (Equation ), and make two comparisons.
The first was fixed before the run, so nothing in it is picked on the folds it is scored on.
It compares the distance hybrid against the single representation, both unweighted, under Manhattan distance with 5 neighbors weighted by the inverse of their rank.
The second picks a setting again for each held-out fold, using the other four folds' held-out scores.
On the hybrid side, it picks among up to six hybrids (the four predictive hybrids, the distance hybrid and the similarity hybrid), weighted and unweighted, at every setting of Table .
That gives up to 216 combinations.
On the single side, it picks among the nearest-neighbor model's two single representations, unweighted only, which gives 36.
On the three datasets with two distances, the numbers are 144 and 24, and where the similarity hybrid is undefined they are 180 and 36.
So the two sides differ in two ways at once.
The hybrid side picks from five or six times as many combinations, and only the hybrid side can use importance weighting.
We score every feature space with and without importance weighting, using four models that read a distance.
The first three are prediction from nearest neighbors at every setting, a Gaussian process with an RBF kernel and a support vector regressor with an RBF kernel.
The fourth is each downstream model given four extra features from its nearest training molecules, following q-RASAR .
The four extra features are the neighbors' mean label and its spread, the distance to the nearest neighbor and the mean distance to the neighbors.
They are computed at the three neighbor settings that rank best in a screen on the training molecules.
The Gaussian process and the support vector regressor run on regression data only.
A separate experiment applies the weighting to all representations joined, on regression datasets, once for each importance method.
An activity cliff is a pair of structurally similar molecules with very different activity .
Only the two hERG datasets measure an activity, but we keep the term for the other three small-molecule datasets.
We decide which molecules are cliff molecules in each outer fold, from its training molecules.
We keep the structural side of the rule of : two molecules are similar when their ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity is at least 0.55.
We modify its activity side.
A gap of two log units flags no molecule at all on Caco-2.
Instead, we choose the gap so that 15% of the training molecules are cliff molecules.
A training molecule is a cliff molecule when it is in at least one similar pair whose labels differ by more than the gap.
On classification data, a similar pair counts when its two molecules are in different classes.
A held-out molecule is a cliff molecule when it has at least two similar training molecules whose labels span more than that gap.
Its own label is never read.
Each downstream model is fitted on its two best single representations and its two best hybrids.
Each fit is scored separately on the cliff molecules and on the other held-out molecules.
The main comparison is the first hybrid against the best single representation.
This follows , who showed that a molecule's similarity to the training molecules tracks how well it is predicted.
Each downstream model is fitted twice, on all representations joined and on its own first hybrid, and we record its error on every held-out molecule.
On regression data this is the absolute error.
On classification data it is one minus the predicted probability of the true class.
We then compute the Spearman correlation between that error and the mean distance from the molecule to its nearest training molecules.
This is done at 5, 10 and 20 neighbors and every distance, in each feature space of Section , unweighted and weighted.
Retrieval measures how close a molecule's neighbors are to it in label.
For each held-out molecule, the label gap is the weighted mean absolute difference between its label and those of its nearest training molecules, at every setting of Table .
On classification data, it is one minus the weighted share of neighbors in the molecule's class.
Lower is better.
For clustering, we fit scikit-learn's k-means on the training molecules with 3, 5 and 10 clusters, and assign each held-out molecule to a cluster.
Label coherence is one minus the mean standard deviation of the held-out labels within a cluster, divided by the standard deviation of all held-out labels.
On classification data, it is the mean share of the largest class in each cluster.
Higher is better.
Clusters with fewer than two held-out molecules are left out.
To find the best number of features, we take each downstream model's top hybrid at every budget of its search.
At each budget we record, for that same hybrid, its prediction score and the correlation between distance and label difference, and find the budget where each peaks.
On hERG K_i and Buchwald–Hartwig only, we simulate choosing which molecules to measure, a form of Bayesian optimization.
Starting from a set of whole scaffold families holding at least 5% of the molecules, a surrogate model picks 100 molecules one at a time by expected improvement .
We repeat this from three starting sets, and the score is the area under the best-found-so-far curve.
Last, for each representation a predictive hybrid draws from, we compare the label information in the features it kept against a random subset of the same size.
Each block of features is reduced to at most 50 principal components.
A mutual-information estimate is summed over the components, and the mean over three label permutations is subtracted.
We use scikit-learn's estimators, which follow for continuous labels and for classes.
This sum counts information shared by two components twice.
As in Chapter , distance in a standard representation rises only weakly with the difference in labels.

On the small-molecule datasets, the best of ten representations and distances, picked on the held-out molecules, reaches at most 0.2789 Spearman, on QM9, and varies widely between folds, for example on hERG K_i.
On the small-molecule datasets and Buchwald–Hartwig, no representation has a correlation at or below zero.
On EGFR binding, CHO polyreactivity, AC-SINS self-association and SMAC colloidal stability, at least one representation does.
SMAC colloidal stability is weakest: its best single representation reaches 0.0155 Spearman, and about half of its combinations of representation and distance are at or below zero.
In the distance hybrid, distance tracks label differences more closely on all five small-molecule datasets (Table ).
On LogD the hybrid is higher in every fold, while on Caco-2 it is lower in two folds.
The same holds on all seven antibody datasets and Buchwald–Hartwig, including SMAC colloidal stability.
The predictive hybrids, built for each downstream model rather than for distance, do not always do this.
Some track label differences less closely than their model's best single representation, on Caco-2, EGFR binding, expression titer, SMAC colloidal stability and Buchwald–Hartwig.
On CHO polyreactivity all four predictive hybrids are lower, for example 0.1056 to 0.0644 Spearman for the network's first hybrid.
A hybrid used for distance therefore has to come from the distance search.
Importance weighting on its own closes much of the gap.
On LogD, the single representation with weighting reaches 0.2762 Spearman, which is above the unweighted hybrid (Table ).
On QM9 the weighted single representation stays below the unweighted hybrid.
On both, the weighted hybrid is highest of the three.
The weighted comparison is missing on Caco-2, hERG blocking, hERG K_i, expression titer and SMAC colloidal stability.
The single representation here is the one the nearest-neighbor model ranked first for prediction, not the one whose distance best follows the label.
If we instead pick that representation with hindsight on the held-out molecules, under any of the distances, the distance hybrid is lower on Caco-2.
The similarity hybrid on Caco-2 is higher than that pick.
The same hindsight comparison also goes against the distance hybrid on EGFR binding, expression titer and CHO polyreactivity.
A hybrid's prediction score peaks at more features than the correlation between its distances and label differences does.
On LogD the network's hybrid predicts better at 2,000 features than at 500, while distance in the same hybrid falls from 0.2315 to 0.1535 Spearman.
At the setting fixed before the run, predicting each molecule from its five nearest neighbors is more accurate in the distance hybrid on all five small-molecule datasets (Table ).
The hybrid is better in every fold on LogD, and worse in one fold of five on hERG K_i and Caco-2.
Picking the setting again for each fold does not change this, and the hybrid still wins on all five small-molecule datasets, for example on LogD from 0.6384 to 0.5648 RMSE.
This comparison favors the hybrid (Section ).
On the antibody datasets and Buchwald–Hartwig, the result depends on the comparison.
At the fixed setting the hybrid also wins on most antibody datasets, and loses on G, AC-SINS self-association and Buchwald–Hartwig (Table ).
With the setting picked again for each fold, however, it wins only on EGFR binding, G and SMAC colloidal stability.
It loses on nanobody thermostability, AC-SINS self-association, CHO polyreactivity, expression titer and Buchwald–Hartwig.
The largest gain that holds in both is on SMAC colloidal stability, from 0.0918 to 0.2906 Spearman with the setting picked again.
Multiplying features by their importance mostly helps prediction from nearest neighbors; the exceptions are in bold in Table .
For the other models, weighting gains little or loses.
On hERG K_i the Gaussian process goes from 0.5819 to 0.7115 RMSE, and the support vector regressor also loses there, while on LogD the regressor barely moves.
With neighbor-label features the direction depends on the setting.
On LogD the support vector machine improves with ten neighbors under cosine distance and gets worse with twenty.
Weighting also improves prediction from all representations joined.
With 10 neighbors, weighting by LightGBM gain improves all four regression small-molecule datasets, for example QM9 from 0.5749 to 0.4841 RMSE.
It also helps every antibody dataset and Buchwald–Hartwig with at least one importance method.
It loses with DeepLIFT on Caco-2, and with LightGBM gain on SMAC colloidal stability.
We have not compared the importance weights with shuffled weights, so we cannot say how much of the gain comes from the importance itself.
Whether the hybrid wins depends on the dataset much more than on how the neighbors are found.
Averaged over the other settings, the gain on LogD is similar for each distance and number of neighbors, and the hybrid loses on G under all three distances.
Importance weighting on both sides shrinks the gain on every dataset where the hybrid wins, on LogD from 0.078 to 0.023 RMSE.
Part of what the hybrid does for a distance is therefore what weighting does.
Where the hybrid loses, the spread across folds is larger than the gain, for example on G and AC-SINS self-association.
These datasets have a few hundred training antibodies, against one to eight thousand training molecules for the small-molecule datasets, so we cannot tell size and domain apart here.
The settings the search chose for the hybrid do not line up with winning either.
On LogD and QM9 it picks the same allocation and importance method in every fold, but CHO polyreactivity wins every fold with four different choices.
Retrieval (Section ) shows the same pattern.

On LogD the hybrid's neighbors have closer labels under each distance and number of neighbors, and the hybrid loses on G under all three distances, by less than the spread across folds at the setting fixed before the run.

On the antibody datasets the distance does matter: cosine distance gives the hybrid its smallest lead, and on SMAC colloidal stability it reverses the result, from labels 0.028 closer under Manhattan distance to 0.057 further apart under cosine.
We also tried choosing which molecules to measure next in a hybrid, on hERG K_i and Buchwald–Hartwig only, from three starting sets.
On both the best search is in a hybrid, but on both another hybrid does worse than random picking.
We report activity cliffs on the five small-molecule datasets only.
On the antibody datasets too few held-out antibodies count as cliff antibodies for a score; on G, 11 of the 429 antibodies held out over five folds do.
The rule for held-out molecules is looser than the one that makes 15% of the training molecules cliff molecules, so their share differs.
It is highest on LogD and hERG blocking, where nearly half of the held-out molecules in some folds are cliff molecules, and lowest on hERG K_i.
On LogD, Caco-2, hERG K_i and hERG blocking, each model's first hybrid beats its best single representation on cliff molecules and on the other molecules alike.
On Caco-2, hERG K_i and hERG blocking the gain is larger on cliff molecules than on the rest; on Caco-2 the network goes from 0.3396 to 0.2881 RMSE on cliff molecules.
On LogD the gain on cliff molecules is slightly smaller than on the rest, but both models gain on them in every fold.
A second run with the small-molecule models flags the same cliff molecules and agrees in direction on all four datasets.
QM9 is harder to read.
The hybrid is better on the other molecules for both models.
On cliff molecules only two folds hold the 10 a score needs, and there the hybrid is worse for both models, for the network from 0.2422 to 0.2798 RMSE.
In each model, the hybrid is better in one of those two folds and worse in the other.
With 48 cliff molecules in all, we draw no conclusion from QM9.
A molecule's distance to its nearest training molecules does rise with the error made on it, but weakly.
The distance hybrid tracks error better for both models on QM9, Caco-2, hERG K_i and LogD.
The largest change is on hERG K_i, from 0.1996 to 0.2761 Spearman with the support vector machine's errors, while on LogD it is small.
On hERG blocking the hybrid tracks error worse for both models.
On nanobody thermostability, G, expression titer, CHO polyreactivity and AC-SINS self-association, the hybrid tracks error better for both models.
It tracks error worse for both on SMAC colloidal stability, where the network goes from 0.1360 to 0.0295 Spearman, and on Buchwald–Hartwig.
On Buchwald–Hartwig, G and expression titer, distance in the single representation does not rise with error at all for either model.
The distance hybrid retrieves neighbors with closer labels on all five small-molecule datasets.
With the setting picked again for each fold, QM9's label gap falls from 0.6008 to 0.3928.
Clustering by k-means agrees with retrieval on hERG blocking, LogD and QM9, where the hybrid's clusters are more coherent at 3, 5 and 10 clusters.
On Caco-2 and hERG K_i the answer changes with the number of clusters, and on Caco-2 the hybrid loses at 3 clusters but wins at 5 and 10.
On the other domains it depends on the dataset.

With the setting picked again, the hybrid retrieves neighbors with closer labels on every antibody dataset except G, where the label gap rises from 1.4386 to 1.5072, and Buchwald–Hartwig is worse too.
Principal components of all representations retrieve better than the hybrid only on EGFR binding, and tie on CHO polyreactivity.
Clustering is mixed.
On EGFR binding and SMAC colloidal stability the hybrid's clusters are less coherent at 3, 5 and 10 clusters, although on SMAC colloidal stability its retrieval still wins.
On nanobody thermostability and CHO polyreactivity the hybrid's clusters are more coherent at every count.
The features a hybrid keeps carry no more label information than principal components of the same number.
On LogD the median, summed over single features, is 1.63 nats for the kept features against 1.68 for principal components, and lower for a random subset.
Chapter found that distance in standard representations barely rises with the difference in labels.
On the five small-molecule datasets, distance in a hybrid built for distance tracks label differences more closely than in the single representation (Table ).
Prediction from nearest neighbors improves on all five (Table ), at the setting fixed before the run and with the setting picked again.
Neighbors retrieved in the hybrid have closer labels on all five.
On LogD, Caco-2, hERG K_i and hERG blocking, each model's first hybrid also predicts cliff molecules better than its best single representation.
Weighting features by importance does part of the same work without any selection.
On LogD the weighted single representation tracks label differences better than the unweighted hybrid.
Distance in the hybrid tracks prediction error worse on hERG blocking, and the kept features carry no more label information than principal components of the same size.
On the antibody datasets and Buchwald–Hartwig, the result depends on the dataset.
Distance in the hybrid tracks label differences more closely on all of them.

With the setting picked again, prediction from nearest neighbors is worse in the hybrid on nanobody thermostability, AC-SINS self-association, CHO polyreactivity, expression titer and Buchwald–Hartwig.
Retrieval is worse on G and Buchwald–Hartwig.
These losses agree with the central claim of this thesis, that the right input depends on the data, so a hybrid's benefit has to be measured on each dataset.
Four limitations apply.
QM9 has no result for the best number of features, importance weighting in the four models, or choosing which molecules to measure next.
The weighted comparison of distance against label difference is missing on Caco-2, hERG blocking, hERG K_i, expression titer and SMAC colloidal stability.
The comparison with the setting picked again lets the hybrid side choose among more combinations and use importance weighting, so it favors the hybrid.
Held-out molecules are called cliff molecules by a looser rule than training molecules, so the share of cliff molecules differs between the two.
The hybrid and the single representation are scored on the same cliff molecules, so their comparison is not affected.
On QM9 only 48 held-out molecules are cliff molecules, too few to judge.
Methods that find noisy labels by comparing each label with its neighbors' labels rest on the distance studied here.
Chapter tests whether the hybrid's distance makes noisy labels easier to find and to act on.
Chapter showed that on the five small-molecule datasets, distance in a hybrid built for distance tracks the label more closely than distance in a single representation.
Prediction from nearest neighbors also improves on all five.
This chapter asks whether that helps with label noise.
Can we find the noisy labels in a QSAR dataset, and does doing something about them improve a model's held-out score?
We ask this on two kinds of labels.
The first has damage injected on purpose, so we know which labels were damaged and by how much.
The second is the labels as delivered, which already carry assay error that nobody has marked.
Every method in this chapter reads a feature space.
A detector compares a molecule's label with its neighbors' labels, or with a model's prediction, and both depend on the features.
The adaptive hybrid representation of Chapter leaves out the features that, as Chapter showed, do not relate to the label yet add a term to the distance.
For every method we therefore ask whether it improves the held-out score and, where it does, whether it improves the hybrid more than the best single representation.
The methods fall into the three groups of Table : noise detection, noise mitigation and noise-robust training.
This chapter expands the sweep of twelve published methods in Chapter (Section ).
It also adds methods that select molecules by a known flag, such as a label at an assay limit, which none of the published methods uses.
QM9, whose labels are computed rather than measured, is the clean-label control (Section ).
This chapter uses the datasets of Chapters and (Table ), plus one more, hERG IC_50 (HIC_50 in the figures, Table ), which is used only here.
Its labels are pIC_50 values for the hERG channel from ChEMBL.
The IC_50 is the concentration of a molecule that gives half of the maximal inhibition in an assay, and pIC_50 is its negative base-10 logarithm in molar units.
QM9 is the clean-label control (Section ), and hERG IC_50 is the one dataset with real repeat measurements.
In this chapter, ``hERG'' on its own means the hERG blocking dataset, whose labels are blocker or non-blocker.
Folds and metrics are those of Chapter .
Each dataset has two downstream models.
In each outer fold, a search on that fold's training molecules ranks each model's two best single representations and two best hybrids.
Every method is tested on all four.
In most experiments that search sees the clean training labels.
Only the hybrid's features are then re-ranked, and its budget re-split between base representations, on the damaged labels.
So the hybrid's features move with the damage.
The base representations and the way the hybrid is built, however, are chosen with clean labels, which a real user would not have.
There are two exceptions.
The expanded published sweep repeats the search for every damage kind, level and draw, trained and scored on the damaged labels alone.
The experiment on cleaning before the feature search (Section ) compares cleaning before the search with cleaning after it.
We keep apart three tasks that are often treated as one: finding the damaged labels, sizing the damage, and improving the model's held-out score.
A method can succeed at the first and fail at the third.
Figure shows how one method is run and scored in one outer fold.
We damage a regression dataset in six ways (Table ).
Four are noise conditions from Section : Gaussian, outlier, grouped-shifted and censoring.
Censoring clips labels at a fixed value that imitates an assay's reporting limit, the edge of its measurable range.
The clip is at the top of the label range.
For potency labels such as hERG K_i, real censoring falls mostly at the low end, so the clip imitates the rarer case.
Under outlier noise, a random 5% of molecules get an error three times wider, where Chapter used 10%.
Every other label still gets the ordinary error, so the 5% carry about a third of the squared error, not all of it.
The last two kinds raise a random 10% of the training labels by one fixed amount, in the two units of Table .
The grouped-wider condition and the Student-t and Laplace shapes of Chapter are not used here.
A classification dataset has its labels flipped instead, and the level is the share of training labels flipped.
Six rules decide which labels flip.
A label can flip uniformly, more often in the rarer classes or more often in one direction.
It can also flip at a rate that varies by molecule, in proportion to class frequency, or along a confusion matrix.
With no matrix given, the last rule is the same as the first, so on a two-class dataset five of the six are distinct.
Most experiments first run a screen of two levels: none and 1.0, or none and 25% of labels clipped under censoring.
The screen leaves out the shift sized by model error.
The held-out predictions it produces correlate 0.93 to 0.97 with those of the plain shift in 10%.
Two draws of the plain shift correlate about as closely with each other.
An experiment that is taken further runs all six kinds at levels 0, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 on datasets of 5,000 molecules or fewer.
Under censoring, those levels are 0, 10%, 25% and 40% clipped.
On a classification dataset the screen flips 10% of labels and the full run flips up to 40%.
Each non-zero level is drawn three times, except censoring, which involves no random draw and runs once.
The random seed depends on the damage kind and the draw, not on the level or the fold.
So the levels nest: every molecule's error at level 1.0 is twice its error at 0.5, and a molecule carries the same damage in every fold it trains in.
Only the training labels are damaged.
Unlike Chapter , the held-out labels of the outer fold are left as delivered, so every score in this chapter is against the delivered labels.
Where a search runs on damaged labels, as in the expanded published sweep, the inner folds of that search are scored on damaged labels too.

Three settings involve no injection: the labels as delivered, whose errors nobody has marked; hERG IC_50, where the disagreement between repeat measurements is real noise; and QM9 with no noise added, whose labels are clean.
Three experiments also use damage of their own.
The experiment on break-even precision gives a random 5% of molecules wide errors and leaves every other label alone.
The experiment that changes the model adds Gaussian noise sized by a LightGBM model's error.
The experiment on measuring sources simulates several measurements per molecule.
Each is described where it appears.
A detector gives every training molecule a suspicion score, a number that is high when the label looks wrong (Table ).
It changes no label and fits no final model.
We group the detectors by what they read: an out-of-fold prediction, the neighbors' labels, or a model's predicted spread (Table ).
Every detector of the first two kinds reads the molecule's own label.
Three of the third kind, the heteroscedastic GP, the variance-head network and NGBoost, predict a spread from the features alone and never read it.
Such a detector can only find a wrong label if the damage is tied to structure.
Most detectors only rank molecules.
A few of the third kind return a spread in the label's own units, which can feed a weight or a move.
The gap over neighbor spread is the buddy check used to screen weather-station readings, which divides a reading's gap from its neighbors' mean by their standard deviation .
RegENN applies a similar threshold to filter noisy regression labels .
We found no earlier use of either on molecular labels.
The cliff-aware gap divides by the spread of all labels plus that of the neighbors, so a molecule among neighbors that disagree with each other, as near an activity cliff, scores lower.
SLOM lowers an outlier score in the same way where a neighborhood is unstable, but for spatial data, where neighbors are found by location .
The variance-head network predicts a mean (x) and a variance ^2(x) and is trained with
where = 0.5 keeps the variance from hiding the errors in the mean .
A neighbor detector needs a space to find neighbors in, a neighbor count k and a way to weight the neighbors.
We try k of 5, 10 and 20, and weight each neighbor by 1/rank or by 1/d^2.
The setting is chosen inside each fold, without touching the held-out molecules.
We hold back 20% of the training scaffold families and predict each held-back label as the weighted mean of its neighbors' labels among the remaining training molecules.
The three settings that predict best are kept.
The space is a single representation, a hybrid, or one of the similarity spaces of Chapter .
Two experiments change the space itself.
The first multiplies each z-scored feature by the square root of its importance, rescaled so that the multipliers average 1, before the neighbors are found.
The importance is computed against the damaged training labels, as feature-weighted nearest neighbors do .
The second compares four families of distance for the neighbor detectors.
They are the plain features under Euclidean and Manhattan distance, the features weighted by importance raised to 0.5 or 1.0, forest proximity, and the hybrid's own features.
The forest proximity of two molecules is the share of trees in which they fall in the same leaf , and their distance is one minus it.
The forest has 100 trees with at least 5 molecules per leaf, fitted to the fold's damaged training labels.
One experiment compares several further detectors with the out-of-fold residual.
One is the value of each molecule to a nearest-neighbor predictor, as a Shapley value .
Another is the cleanlab regression score .
The rest divide the residual by a spread for that molecule, from NGBoost, a quantile forest or a conformal interval. cleanlab draws its internal folds at random rather than by scaffold family.
Two experiments test the out-of-fold LightGBM residual under the shift in 10% sized by model error.
The first ranks molecules by the residual itself.
The second divides each residual by a second LightGBM model's out-of-fold estimate of how large that molecule's residual usually is.
It then turns the result into conformal p-values against a calibration set of training molecules .
Molecules are flagged with the Benjamini–Hochberg rule , which bounds the expected share of false flags at 5%, 10% or 20%.
The calibration set is a random 20% or 50% of the training molecules or, where a dataset has repeat measurements, the molecules with three or more measurements that agree.
Both experiments grade the ranking by the area under the ROC curve.
A detector can be graded only where the damage moved some labels and not others, so that it is known which molecules were damaged.
That is outlier noise, censoring, the two shifts in 10% and every label flip.
Under Gaussian and grouped-shifted noise every label moves, and no detection score exists.
We grade a detector by the average precision of its suspicion scores against the set of damaged molecules.
A detector that ranks at random scores the damaged share of the training molecules, so that share is the chance level.
Some experiments report the area under the ROC curve instead, where chance is 0.5.
A noise mitigation method has two halves (Table ).
Something selects the molecules: a detector, a known flag or every molecule.
Then one of three actions follows: delete the molecule, make it count less, or move its label.
Table describes each method this way, so the methods reduce to a few selectors crossed with three actions.
Most methods read the suspicion score rescaled to [0, 1], s_i = (s_i - s)/( s - s).
Deleting drops the molecules above a quantile of s, usually the top 5%, 10% or 20%.
This is the filtering of , which tested on QSAR modeling sets.
Down-weighting gives molecule i the weight 1/(1 + s_i), and all weights are then divided by their mean.
A proportional move takes the label part of the way to a target t_i,
so the most suspect label moves a share of the way and the least suspect does not move.
The target is the weighted mean of the molecule's neighbors' labels , or an out-of-fold LightGBM prediction, which is close to the target blending of .
One further rule, the score-scaled shrink, moves a share 0.5 s_i/(1 + 0.5 s_i) of the way to the out-of-fold prediction.
It was written as James–Stein shrinkage .
The variance it estimates cancels out of the share, so the share depends only on the score.
The main cleanup experiment takes the out-of-fold forest residual as its detector and crosses it with each action above.
It also grades the cliff-aware gap as a detector beside it.
A second experiment asks whether to delete a flagged molecule or keep it, and keeps it either with a lower weight or with a moved label.
Its control deletes the same number of molecules at random, at five seeds.
A third experiment replaces the forest residual with each of five detectors in turn: the cliff-aware gap, and the GP, the heteroscedastic GP, the variance-head network and NGBoost.
Each deletes its top 5%, 10% or 20%.
Where the detector has its own prediction, it also moves every label toward that prediction.
The share moved is given by Equation , or by c_i = s_i/(1 + s_i), which uses the score in its own units.
Four experiments weight molecules by a neighbor or model detector, with no deletion.
Three use the weight 1/(1 + 3 s_i), so the most suspect molecule counts a quarter as much as the least suspect.
They differ in where the neighbors are found: in features scaled by importance on clean labels, in the importance-scaled space above, and in each of the four families of distance.
The fourth uses (-0.1, s_i) with the gap over neighbor spread, the GP or NGBoost as the detector.
With that weight, the most suspect molecule counts about 0.9 times as much as the least suspect.
Close-pair weights look only at pairs of near-identical molecules.
A pair is close if its distance is in the lowest 1% of all training pairs.
The label noise is estimated from the closest fifth of those pairs as ^2 = y^2/2, since two noisy copies of one value differ by twice the noise variance.
Both molecules of any close pair whose labels differ by more than 32, get weight 0.25.
Residual flags give weight 0.25 to the top 5%, 10% or 20% of molecules by out-of-fold LightGBM residual.
The same experiment also asks how precise a detector has to be before acting on its flags helps.
It builds flag sets of the same size with a known share of truly damaged molecules, from none to all.
It then finds the share at which the gain from acting crosses zero.
We call that share the break-even precision.
Cliff put-back runs after a cleanup and undoes it on activity-cliff molecules: deleted molecules return, lowered weights go back to 1 and moved labels go back to their training value.
A training molecule is a cliff molecule if it has a partner with ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity of at least 0.55 whose label is far from its own .
Far means more than twice the median absolute deviation of the labels.
On datasets whose label is not a biological activity, such as LogD, the same test finds pairs that differ sharply in that property, and we keep the name.
The cliff set is rebuilt in every fold from the damaged training labels.
Its control puts back the same number of molecules drawn at random from the non-cliff molecules.
We found no earlier method that puts examples back after a cleanup.
Some cleaning methods exempt a whole class decided in advance , and name the risk of discarding correct exceptions without giving a rule.
The hybrid's features are chosen against the labels, so the labels can be cleaned before the features are chosen or after.
One experiment compares the two orders.
It runs nine cleanups with the out-of-fold forest residual as the detector, under outlier noise and on labels as delivered.
The search and the fit each use the labels as given or the cleaned labels, four combinations in all.
Down-weighting cannot reach the search, because no weight enters the feature ranking or the budget split, so its two cleaned-search arms do not exist.
No source we found crosses features chosen on cleaned or recorded labels with a fit on cleaned or recorded labels.
The nearest design ranks features on one version of the data and fits on another, but its second step is class-imbalance sampling, not label cleaning .
On labels as delivered, nothing says which molecules are wrong, so a gain can come from removing hard molecules rather than wrong ones.
One experiment runs seven cleanups on delivered labels with the neighbor gap and the forest residual as detectors.
Its control shuffles each detector's scores across the training molecules, at three seeds, and reruns the cleanup with the same share and strength.
The same number of molecules is touched, but not the ones the detector picked.
When a label is clipped at an assay limit, we know two things that a detector has to guess: which labels are wrong, and in which direction.
The limit L is read off the clipped training labels as their largest value, if at least two molecules and 1% of the training molecules sit on it.
An out-of-fold LightGBM fit to the clipped labels gives each molecule a prediction p_i.
Let be the standard deviation of y_i - p_i over the molecules below the limit, and m_i the inverse Mills ratio,
where and are the standard normal density and distribution function.
The truncated-normal mean replaces each clipped label by the mean of a normal distribution centered on its prediction and cut at the limit ,
Censored EM repeats this for three rounds, refitting the downstream model out of fold to the current labels each round, after the iterated estimator of .
The constant lift raises every clipped label to L + m, the mean of m_i over the clipped molecules.
That shared amount is larger than the truncated-normal mean's lift by L - p_i on average.
Two arms test what the flag is worth.
Deleting the clipped molecules uses the flag but throws the molecules away.
A per-molecule lift raises each clipped label by its own m_i, and its control deals the same lifts to the wrong clipped molecules, at three seeds.
fitted censored regression to drug-discovery labels, which is the closest precedent.
The same moves run on real censoring in CHO polyreactivity, where 58 of 197 labels sit at 0, the low reference antibody.
That 0 is a floor rather than a ceiling, so the labels are negated, moved as above, and negated back.
Its control moves the same number of labels that are not at the floor by the same amount.
The held-out labels at the floor are censored too, so that experiment adds Harrell's concordance index , which skips the pairs whose order the floor hides.

A scaffold family is also a known flag.
Under grouped-shifted noise every family carries its own offset, so a family's mean out-of-fold residual estimates that offset, and subtracting it from every label in the family undoes it.
Three versions differ in how much they trust a small family.
The first subtracts the whole mean residual from every family.
The second subtracts it only from families of three or more training molecules.
The third is a random-intercept model, fitted by up to five rounds of expectation maximization in the style of mixed-effects random forests .
It shrinks each family's offset toward zero, more for a family with few molecules.
A source is a known flag when each molecule was measured by several of them.
One experiment simulates eight sources.
Each molecule is measured by one to four of them, drawn from hERG IC_50's real counts or uniformly.
Measurement s of molecule i is
where b_s is the source's offset, u_i is an error shared by every measurement of the molecule and v_is is an error of its own.
The value of , 0, 0.3 or 0.7, sets how much of the error the measurements share.
The offsets have standard deviation 0 or 0.5,_e.
The training label is the mean of the molecule's measurements.
The methods remove each source's offset, estimated by a mixed model with the source as a fixed effect and the molecule as a random intercept.
They also weight each molecule by the inverse of its estimated error variance .
Two further arms use the true and _e, which a user never has, so they are bounds and not methods.
hERG IC_50 carries its own known flag: how many times each molecule was measured, and how far apart those measurements are.
A molecule is one canonical SMILES string as given by ChEMBL.
Its count is its number of ChEMBL IC_50 records, and its spread is the variance of their pIC_50 values.
Three methods use the flag.
The first weights each molecule by its count.
The second weights it by the inverse of its estimated error variance, 1/(_u^2 + s_i^2/n_i) .
Here n_i is the number of measurements behind the label, and _u^2 is the error that remains however often a molecule is measured.
Its spread s_i^2 is pulled toward the spread pooled over all molecules, as if the pool were three more measurements.
We do this because a variance from two or three records is unreliable .
The third moves each label toward an out-of-fold LightGBM prediction, further for a less precise label.
The share moved is v_i/(v_i + ^2), where v_i is the molecule's spread over its count and ^2 is the variance of the out-of-fold residual.
Held-out molecules are graded only if they have three or more measurements.
One method moves every label, with no selection at all.
Each label moves halfway toward the out-of-fold prediction of a LightGBM model fitted with a Huber loss , whose threshold is 1.4826 times the median absolute out-of-fold residual.
The Huber loss keeps the outlying labels from pulling that prediction.
A noise-robust training method selects no molecules and leaves the labels alone.
It changes the loss, the model or the training loop instead (Table ).

subsection: Changing the model instead of the labels
norm_text: This experiment ran on Caco-2, hERG K_i and LogD.
The twelve published methods of Chapter are run again (Table ).
Every one uses the same network as the plain model.
It has three hidden layers of 256, 128 and 64 units and dropout 0.2.
It is trained with the Adam optimizer at a learning rate of 10^-3 for up to 200 epochs, with early stopping.
The code is a new implementation of the same twelve, not a rerun of the earlier study.
It is wider in four ways.
It runs on many datasets instead of QM9 alone, under every damage kind instead of Gaussian noise alone, and on hybrids as well as single representations.
It also scores each method against the plain network on the same damaged labels in the same feature space.
Four of the twelve select molecules with a detector and delete them, so under Table they are noise mitigation, and the table marks them so.
Most were built for image classification, and several of our versions differ from their source, as the table states.
The network is also trained with a Huber loss , whose threshold is c times 1.4826 times the median absolute out-of-fold residual, with c of 0.5, 1, 1.5 or 2.
Under the shift in 10% sized by model error, each model's own robust loss is tried at c = 1.5.
That is a Huber loss for LightGBM and the network, a pseudo-Huber loss for XGBoost, and absolute-error splits for the random forest.
Two learners, LightGBM and an SVM, each score every molecule by its out-of-fold error.
For two rounds, each is refitted on the molecules the other finds easiest.
Each then keeps its own easiest 80%, 90% or 95%, and the downstream model is fitted on the molecules both keep.
This follows the exchange of co-teaching , done between whole refits rather than inside one training loop.
Its control deletes the same number of molecules at random, at three seeds.
On hERG IC_50, four methods change what the model sees rather than the labels.
The first trains on one row per measurement instead of one row per molecule with the mean label.
The second adds the log of each molecule's measurement count as an extra feature.
The third gives NGBoost the same extra feature.
The fourth fits an XGBoost accelerated-failure-time model to the interval between each molecule's lowest and highest measurement, instead of to one value.
Each group has its own test, because each makes a different claim.
Noise detection.
Is the suspicion score high on the damaged molecules?
This can only be read where some labels were damaged and others were not (Section ).
On QM9 with no noise added, every flag is a false flag.
Noise mitigation, selected by a detector or a flag.
The held-out score after the action, against the same model on the same features with no action.
Where a control ran, the action must also beat the same action on molecules chosen at random.
Noise mitigation on every molecule.
Against no action.
No random selection is possible, so QM9 with no noise added is the only check.
Noise-robust training.
Against the same model trained normally on the same labels.
A gain on QM9 with no noise added comes from the training change alone, and we set it beside the gain under damage.

Five controls ran, each inside one experiment and described with it: random deletion against deleting flagged molecules, shuffled detector scores against cleaning the labels as delivered, random put-back against cliff put-back, shuffled lifts against the per-molecule lift, and random deletion against the two learners.
Each seed of a control is reported on its own, never averaged.
No other method has a control, and a gain without one is a weaker claim.
QM9 is the clean-label control.
Its HOMO–LUMO gaps are computed rather than measured , so they carry no assay error.
A method that improves QM9 with no noise added is not removing noise.
It is changing the model in a way that would help on any labels.
If deleting never helps on QM9's clean labels, a gain from deleting on a damaged dataset is noise removal.
Methods that weight or move every label may help QM9 too, and their gains elsewhere are read against that.
Each method's QM9 result is given with the method in the results.
Where a clean score exists, we also report how much of the lost score a method wins back.
Each model m is fitted to the clean, the damaged and the treated training labels, giving held-out scores s^m_clean, s^m_damaged and s^m_treated in the dataset's own metric.
The recovery is
which reads the same whether higher or lower values of the metric are better.
It is left undefined when the gap between the clean and damaged score is 2% of the clean score or less.
We report it for single representations only.
A hybrid's features are re-ranked on the damaged labels, so its clean score is not the score of the same features, and the denominator would mix two changes.
Three things hold for every result in this chapter, so we state them once.
Because of time and computational constraints, most results are on the first outer fold only (Section ), and we give the fold count wherever more exist.
Where a method has several settings, such as a share to delete or a strength, we report its best setting on the held-out score.
The single representation and the hybrid it is compared on are picked the same way.
Both picks make every reported gain optimistic.
Third, the network's score changes from one fit to the next.
On QM9 the network's second hybrid scores between 0.3484 and 0.3618 RMSE on the same fold and the same labels, depending on which experiment fitted it.
LightGBM gives one score in every experiment.
A network gain of about 0.01 RMSE or less is inside that spread.
Table shows how often each group of methods improved the held-out score on the first outer fold.
In it, one condition is one dataset, noise condition, model and method.
A row sorts its conditions by outcome: the method improved both the best single representation and the best hybrid, only one of them, or neither.
Where a method has a control, improving both also means beating it.
Mitigation helps most often under injected damage, and least often on the labels as delivered.
The table counts outer fold 0 only.
Six of its experiments also have results on folds 1 and 2, which it does not count.
It also leaves out MDR1–MDCK efflux, which has 24 conditions on fold 0.
