subsection: Changing a label against deleting a molecule
norm_text: So when deleting helps on a damaged dataset and beats random deletion, as it does under the hERG flips, the gain is noise removed.
On the labels as delivered, the control is the same cleanup driven by shuffled detector scores.
On hERG K_i, label smoothing passes this control with both detectors.
Label smoothing with the neighbor gap takes the network on the first single representation from 0.6380 to 0.5775 RMSE, while every shuffled run makes it slightly worse.
With the forest residual, label smoothing also improves the hybrid by more than any of three shuffles.
On hERG, label smoothing beats all its shuffles with gradient-boosted trees on the first single representation and on the second hybrid.
Caco-2 and LogD pass the control too, but by small amounts.
With down-weighting on the network's second single representation, one shuffle wins back more than half of the gain on each.
The hERG K_i smoothing gain on the hybrid holds on three folds.
In a second experiment, label smoothing improved the network's hybrid on each of folds 0, 1 and 2.
The second single representation got worse on fold 0 and better on the other two.
Deleting does not pass its control on the small-molecule labels as delivered.
On Caco-2, hERG K_i and LogD no deletion setting beat both no cleaning and every random deletion.
Buchwald–Hartwig is different.
Deleting the 20% of reactions with the largest neighbor-label gap improves LightGBM on the hybrid and on the second single representation, and beats random deletion on both.
On the hybrid it scores 18.0417 RMSE in percentage points of yield, against 19.8986 for the best random deletion.
Random deletion alone also helped the first single representation, so this score moves between fits as well.
Putting activity-cliff molecules back after a cleanup can be tested on hERG K_i only.
On Caco-2, hERG and LogD more than half of the training molecules count as cliff molecules.
That leaves too few other molecules to draw a random set of the same size.
On hERG K_i, deleting the flagged molecules barely moves the network's hybrid.
Putting the cliff molecules back takes it to 0.5786 RMSE, against 0.5949 with random molecules put back.
Fold 2 agrees, and fold 1 does not.
On three antibody datasets, cleaning the labels as delivered also passes the shuffled-score control, and on those datasets it gave the largest gains (Section ).
This section uses injected damage alone (Section ).
The out-of-fold forest residual finds outliers, shifted labels and flipped classes well above chance on every dataset it ran on.
On Caco-2 under outlier noise its average precision is 0.3381, against a chance level of 0.0512.
Censoring is the exception.
At a clipped share of 0.25 the residual falls below chance on Buchwald–Hartwig and LogD, and is only a little above it on Caco-2.
A model fitted to clipped labels predicts values near the limit for the clipped molecules, so their residuals are small.
This is the behavior Chapter found in the models' own uncertainty, which was lowest on exactly the labels that had been clipped.
The cliff-aware gap does better than the residual when only some labels are shifted.
Under the shift in 10%, its median neighbor setting reaches 0.2686 on Caco-2 against 0.2023 for the residual, and every one of its settings is ahead.
Under outliers only its best setting is ahead, and under censoring it trails the residual on Caco-2, hERG K_i and LogD at every setting.
So no detector is best everywhere.
A neighbor detector is better at a shift that moves a few labels a long way.
A model residual is as good or better at outliers.
The space in which the neighbors are found changes detection little (Section ).
Taking the best setting in each family, the importance-weighted features were best on Buchwald–Hartwig, Caco-2, hERG K_i, LogD and SMAC colloidal stability.
On Caco-2 under outliers the four families reach average precisions close to each other, all far above chance.
The hybrid's own features were the best family on the change in binding free energy ( G) under outliers.
They were also best on SMAC colloidal stability under censoring and on Caco-2 under the shift sized by model error, but on no dataset overall.
Averaged over the detector settings instead of taking the best one, the hybrid's features come out ahead more often, so this ranking depends on how a detector's setting is chosen.
Scaling each feature by its importance before the neighbors are found raised detection under the shift in 10%, and lowered it under censoring on every dataset.
The largest gain was on Buchwald–Hartwig, 0.4647 to 0.5123 average precision, with smaller gains on LogD and SMAC colloidal stability.
Under outliers scaling barely changed detection.
Importance is computed against the damaged labels, so under censoring it likely rewards the features that predict the clipped values, and the clipped molecules then look like their neighbors.
A Gaussian process's own predicted spread plus its residual is the one model-uncertainty detector that could be graded.
The three that predict a spread from the features alone never see a label, and the files mark them as undefined under every damage kind that can be graded.
The GP was slightly ahead of the cliff-aware gap under outliers on Caco-2 and LogD, and behind it under every shift and every hERG flip kind.
Detectors from outside cheminformatics did better than the residual where the residual is weakest.
Under censoring the nearest-neighbor Shapley value reached 0.3906 on Buchwald–Hartwig against 0.1949 for the residual, and was also ahead on SMAC colloidal stability.
Under the shift in 10% the cleanlab score was well ahead of the residual on Buchwald–Hartwig.
The Shapley value's best number is taken over many more settings than the residual's, so these gaps lean in its favor.
Two more experiments graded the plain residual under damage sized by the model's own error.
It ranked the shifted molecules above chance on every dataset there, for example 0.20 to 0.25 against 0.106 on expression titer.
Turning such a ranking into a decision is harder.
Conformal p-values with a false-discovery-rate rule flagged no molecule at all at q = 0.05.
At q = 0.1 they flagged none when the calibration set was drawn from the noisy training labels.
Only with a clean calibration set, which a user would not have, did it flag a few dozen molecules at most in a few passes.
Acting on those flags left the held-out score where it was in almost every pass.
The break-even precision explains when acting on a detector can work (Section ).
Under outliers the residual's top 5% are mostly damaged molecules, and its precision is above the break-even on Caco-2 and hERG K_i.
Under the shift sized by model error, the residual's precision falls below the break-even.
On Caco-2 the residual's top 5% has a precision of 0.17, and deleting them only pays off above 0.62.
On hERG K_i under the plain shift in 10%, the precision of the top 10% is also far below its break-even.
So a detector that ranks the damaged labels above chance can still lead to a worse model.
Acting on its flags helps only above the break-even, which depends on the damage, the action and the model.
Figure applies this test to the two learners.
Each flags the training molecules with the largest loss, and we delete every molecule that either one flags, so slightly more than the flagged share is deleted.
Under the shift in 10% on hERG K_i, the deleted molecules have a precision of 0.23 to 0.26, against a break-even of 0.32 to 0.68.
Deleting raised the RMSE at every share, from 0.6275 to between 0.6913 and 0.7282, on 2 of the 3 noise draws because the run has not finished.
On Caco-2 under the same shift the precision was 0.14 to 0.16, against break-evens of 0.37 to 0.58, and every share again raised the RMSE.
LogD has no break-even yet.
There, under outliers, deleting at 5% with a precision of 0.36 lowered the RMSE from 0.5874 to 0.5571, on 2 of 3 draws.

The shuffled controls are why we still count SMAC, G and expression titer as real results.

subsection: Small molecules and the reaction set
norm_text: Buchwald–Hartwig is the one dataset where deleting flagged reactions from the labels as delivered beats random deletion.
hERG IC_50 is the one dataset whose noise was measured rather than injected.
Weighting each molecule by its number of measurements took the support vector regressor on the hybrid from 0.7598 to 0.7283 RMSE on the first draw.
It helped on all three draws.
Weighting by the inverse of the estimated error variance also helped it, by less.
The same count weights made the network worse.
For the network, adding the log of the measurement count as a feature helped instead, and so did shrinking each label toward a prediction by its spread.
NGBoost gained a little from the same extra feature.
The interval model did slightly worse than the point model.
Training on one row per measurement instead of the mean barely changed the score for either model.
The detection of molecules flagged by ChEMBL curators has not run.
Cleaning before the search did best when the fit also used the cleaned labels (Section ).
On expression titer's labels as delivered, deleting the 20% of antibodies the forest residual flags takes the network on the hybrid from 0.1550 to 0.5619 Spearman this way.
Cleaning only the fit, or only the search, also helps, by less.
On SMAC colloidal stability with a quarter of the labels clipped, deleting the flagged 5% also does best when it reaches both, and cleaning the search alone does worse than no cleaning.
The largest single gain is on SMAC colloidal stability's labels as delivered.
There the network on the second hybrid goes from -0.0143 to 0.5596 Spearman when the labels are shrunk toward an out-of-fold prediction for the search alone.
That starts from a score near zero, on one fold of 53 antibodies.
The same treatment can also go the other way.
Deleting flagged antibodies before the search made the network's first hybrid on SMAC worse.
On hERG K_i under Gaussian noise, deleting before the search helped the second hybrid on the first noise draw and hurt it on the second.
On hERG K_i's labels as delivered, the one dataset with a second fold here, label smoothing before the search beat no cleaning on fold 1.
No random-flag control has run for this experiment, and there is no QM9 result.
A separate experiment searched the hybrid on the clean or on the damaged labels, then fitted both on labels with Gaussian noise at level 1.0 and scored them on the held-out labels as delivered.
On Caco-2 the network's second hybrid scores within a few thousandths of an RMSE between the two arms on every fold, and neither arm is ahead on all five.
On LogD with the support vector regressor the two arms agree to the third decimal on two of three folds.
The largest loss was on hERG K_i with the network, 0.669 against 0.779 RMSE on the second fold.
On SMAC colloidal stability the two arms swap places from fold to fold.
For most datasets, the search itself is not where Gaussian noise does its damage.

norm_text: The tree models and the network ran on different datasets, though, so we cannot say whether the tree models or the datasets are the reason.
Table gives the expanded sweep by domain.
Small-loss selection and multistage cleaning delete the molecules with the largest training loss.
They almost never helped on small molecules, and helped more often on Buchwald–Hartwig and the antibodies.
The reaction side is one dataset, so we read it as one dataset's result and no more.
In Chapter , the heteroscedastic GP was one of the methods that held up under Gaussian noise on QM9, with a retention of 79.0%.
Here it is the only method that helps on G's labels as delivered, from 0.3414 to 0.4475 Spearman on the best single representation.
It also helps the second hybrid, though the first hybrid drops.
Distance-based selection is the only one of the twelve that helps both sides on hERG with 10% of labels flipped one way only.
Its AUROC gains are in the third decimal.
On QM9 with no noise added, every one of the twelve made the network worse on both the best single representation and the hybrid.
DivideMix was the worst, 0.4517 RMSE on the hybrid against 0.3550 for the plain network, and distance-based selection the least bad.
A second run of the same methods inside another experiment scores the network's second hybrid, and there half of the twelve beat the plain network.
The labels are the same in both runs.
The difference is the network's own spread from one fit to the next, which we come back to in Section .
The method that does best on the hybrid is rarely the one that does best on both single representations.

The three exceptions on the first hybrid are Caco-2 under the shift in 10% (distance-based selection), hERG under class-dependent flips (confident learning) and hERG under instance-dependent flips (distance-based selection).
So a ranking of noise-handling methods made on one representation does not carry to another.
Cleaning keeps the hybrid ahead on small molecules.
Before any treatment the hybrid already beats the best single representation in almost every small-molecule condition, and after mitigation it still does.
On LogD with outliers, for example, the network's cleaned hybrid scores 0.5560 against 0.5915 for the cleaned single representation.
Cleaning rarely changes which of the two wins, and when it does it more often moves the win to the hybrid.
On antibodies the hybrid is ahead in about half the conditions, before and after cleaning.
The reaction set sits between the two.
The closest test of the question this thesis started from, whether a better feature set makes noise handling work, is where the detector finds its neighbors.
One experiment down-weights molecules by the neighbor gap and finds the neighbors either in the model's own single representation or in the hybrid, with everything else held fixed.
Finding them in the hybrid helped the same model on the same single representation slightly more often.
The largest differences go both ways.
On LogD under a scaffold-family shift, the network's single representation goes from 0.7051 to 0.6626 RMSE with neighbors in the hybrid, and gets worse with neighbors in its own space.
On nanobody thermostability with outliers, the network barely moves with its own neighbors and gains with the hybrid's.
On expression titer under Gaussian noise the reverse happens, and its own neighbors help more than the hybrid's.
These are the largest cases picked out of many, not typical ones.
No control has run for this comparison.
The network gains from cleaning more often than the support vector regressor on Caco-2, hERG K_i and LogD.
Part of that may be the network's own spread between fits, since a deterministic model with an unchanged score never counts as helped.
On G the support vector regressor gains more often, and on expression titer the random forest gains more often than the network.
On small molecules, a user who builds a hybrid therefore loses nothing by cleaning afterwards.
The ranking of noise-handling methods changed between the hybrid and the single representations in almost every condition.
Whether a noise-handling method works depends on the feature space it runs in, as Chapter found for distance.
On the first outer fold, noisy labels in QSAR data could be found, and in several settings corrected.
Corrections worked best with a flag.
Raising labels clipped at an assay limit won back half to three quarters of the lost RMSE on the small-molecule datasets, with no detector.
With a detector, deleting or relabeling flagged molecules helped under label flips and outliers.
It passed random and shuffled controls on hERG, hERG K_i, Buchwald–Hartwig and three antibody datasets.
On clean QM9 labels deletion never helped, so the deletion gains are noise removed.
The hybrid stays ahead of the single representation on small molecules through every treatment, and the ranking of noise-handling methods depends on the feature space they run in.
Most results rest on the first outer fold.
Further folds exist for the clipped-label corrections on LogD and Caco-2 and for deletion under hERG's flips.
They also exist for label smoothing and cliff put-back on hERG K_i, and for the comparison of searches on clean and damaged labels.
They mostly agree with fold 0, and the text gives the exceptions.
The results to confirm on all folds first are, in order:
SMAC colloidal stability, deletion and relabeling on the labels as delivered.
hERG K_i, relabeling and putting cliff molecules back.
hERG, deletion and relabeling under the flip kinds.
The clipped-label corrections.
The scaffold-family offsets.
Most methods have no control.
Five controls ran, one per experiment (Section ), and none on an antibody dataset under injected damage.
The random put-back control was usable only on hERG K_i.
Three of the methods with large gains have no QM9 result with no noise added: changing the model, cleaning before the search, and moving every label toward a Huber-fitted prediction.
Until those exist, their gains cannot be split into noise removed and a better model.
QM9 is our only clean control, and we tested one of its properties, the HOMO–LUMO gap.
A control on more computed properties would show whether the QM9 results hold beyond that one target.
There is also no way to correct a label without ground truth and know it was corrected.
Nor does any dataset here have a measured floor of assay error below which no model can go.
The following datasets of Chapters and have no noise results yet: rat microsomal clearance, anti-VEGF scan expression, anti-VEGF scan binding, EGFR binding, angiopoietin-2 binding and HIC retention.
MDR1–MDCK efflux has results on outer fold 0, but the tables in this chapter leave them out.
Chapter brings these results together with the rest of the thesis.
This thesis set out to handle label noise in molecular data.
This chapter answers the research questions of Chapter in turn, sets out how to choose a noise-handling method, and lists the contributions.
It closes with the limitations, future work and concluding remarks.
The first half of the thesis asked four questions about label noise, answered in Chapter .
First, model family decided noise robustness more than the representation did.
On QM9 under Gaussian noise, model family explained 47.2% of the variance in AUCnorm and the representation 8.1%.
The representation mattered more for predictive performance.
Second, random forests were the most consistent model under noise, while LightGBM and XGBoost predicted well on clean labels and lost the most as noise rose.
Third, the type of noise mattered more than the shape of its distribution.
Systematic noise, shared within a scaffold family or clipped at an assay limit, did the most damage, so a study that injects only Gaussian noise misses it.
Fourth, mean predicted uncertainty rose with noise, but no model's uncertainty identified the corrupted labels.
Chapter then asked why published methods for learning with noisy labels did poorly in an exploratory study carried out earlier in this project.
The methods that compared molecules by a distance did worst.
Within one dataset, most features of a standard representation barely vary.
On hERG K_i, 1,815 of the 2,048 ECFP4 features take one value in at least 95% of the molecules.
A distance sums over every feature, so these features dominate it.
The second half asked whether the representation can be adapted to the task.
First, the best set of features depends on the dataset and the downstream model, and a search can find it (Chapter ).
The adaptive hybrid representation beat the best single representation on every small-molecule dataset with both downstream models.
On LogD with the SVM it went from 0.4930 to 0.4302 RMSE.
A method built for small molecules also carried over to antibodies, where the gain depended on the dataset.
On two antibody datasets the best single representation was one built for this thesis, which reads only the regions or mutations that vary.
Second, distance in a hybrid tracked the label better on all five small-molecule datasets, and predicting each label from its five nearest neighbors was more accurate (Chapter ).
On hERG K_i the Spearman correlation between the distance of two molecules and the difference in their activity went from 0.0729 to 0.2625.
On antibodies and reactions distance also tracked the label better, but prediction from neighbors was worse on several datasets.
Third, noisy labels could be found and corrected (Chapter ).
With a quarter of LogD's training labels clipped, censored EM took the network from 0.6354 to 0.4795 RMSE, against 0.4314 before clipping.
Cleaning guided by a detector beat random deletion or shuffled detector scores on hERG, hERG K_i, Buchwald–Hartwig and three antibody datasets.
On small molecules the hybrid stayed ahead of the single representation through every treatment.
Fourth, importance helped in building the hybrid but not in training.
The hybrid ranks features by importance within each representation.
At the same number of features it beat recursive feature elimination and random features on all but one small-molecule dataset with a result.
Using the importance scores again during training added little.
Label noise was handled, but no single method handled it on every dataset.
Which method worked depended on the prediction task, the data, the model and the type of noise.
The forest residual detector fell to chance under clipping, where acting on the known flag did best.
Subtracting scaffold-family offsets made the model worse on Caco-2's labels as delivered.
Deleting the molecules the network fits worst helped on the reactions but almost never on small molecules.
The ranking of the methods also changed between the hybrid and the single representations.
We therefore recommend modeling the noise in a dataset before choosing a method.
Data pooled from several laboratories can carry an offset per source, and an assay with a reporting limit gives clipped labels.
Both come with a flag that a correction can use.
A method that assumes noise that is not there does harm.
Simple methods were often as good as complex ones: random forests were the most consistent model, and on hERG K_i one constant lift for every clipped label beat censored EM.
The contributions on label noise are the following.
NoiseInject, an open-source Python package for benchmarking noise robustness and uncertainty in QSAR models (Section ).
Noise conditions beyond Gaussian noise, including noise shared within scaffold families and labels clipped at an assay limit (Chapter ).
A split of the variance in performance and in noise robustness between model family and representation (Chapter ).

Published noise-handling methods adapted to QSAR data, for example censored EM with any downstream model, a random intercept per scaffold family, and the buddy check from meteorology as a detector of noisy labels (Chapter ).
Three methods for which we found no earlier use (Chapter ).
These are the cliff-aware gap, cleaning the labels before the hybrid search, and returning activity-cliff molecules after a cleanup.
Tests of these methods on single representations and hybrids side by side, with three controls: QM9 with no noise added, random deletion and shuffled detector scores (Chapter ).
The ranking of the methods changed with the features.
The contributions on the representation are the following.
The adaptive hybrid representation, which ranks features within each representation, splits a budget of features among them, and searches the selection settings for each dataset and model (Chapter ).
A newly published embedding is added to the search as one more representation.
Hybrids built for distance (Chapter ), and hybrids built from data held at separate sites (Chapter ).

Antibody representations built for this thesis: readouts of the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) and of each region, mutation features, and the change in embedding from the parent antibody (Chapter ).
Most noise results rest on the first outer fold, and where further folds exist they mostly agree with it.
QM9 is the only clean control, with one property tested, and most noise methods have no control.
On the labels as delivered there is no ground truth, so a control can show that a gain is more than chance but not that a label was corrected.
Every clipped-label result is on injected clipping.
CHO polyreactivity is the one dataset here with a floor visible in its labels.
[RESULT NEEDED: whether the same corrections help on CHO polyreactivity's labels at the floor, against the same move applied to labels not at the floor (Chapter , Section )]
The hybrid needs data, and most antibody datasets here hold a few hundred antibodies.
The search is costly and must be rerun when the data, the representations or the model change.
Most DNN results were computed before 8 October 2026, when the DNN began clipping each prediction to the range of its training labels.
We have not yet tested whether the best hybrid settings follow measurable properties of a dataset (Section ).
The hybrid search needs only several feature matrices for the same samples and a supervised task.
Gene-expression profiles and financial time series are natural next domains, since each has many competing representations of the same samples.
Runs on DNA promoter sequences have started but are not reported here.
The noise methods need more clean controls.
QM9 offers twelve computed properties, and only the HOMO–LUMO gap was used.
In QSAR, a class label usually comes from cutting a continuous measurement at a threshold, so measurement error flips mostly the molecules near that threshold.
Flips of that kind, on more classification datasets, are the next test for the detectors.
A hybrid could also be the input to the model that scores molecules for a generative model; the code for this exists and has not been run.
A search that starts from the settings found on a similar dataset could save compute, and a deployment across real sites would test the separate-site results of Chapter .
Label noise in molecular data can be handled.
Which method handles it depends on the prediction task, the data, the model and the kind of noise.
No single model, representation or noise-handling method was best on every dataset we tested.
The noise in a dataset should be understood before a method is chosen.
The features also matter.
When the noise methods failed, we followed the failure down to the distance between molecules and then to the features that distance is computed over.
The adaptive hybrid representation selects those features for each dataset and model.
On small molecules it predicted better than any single representation, gave better neighbors, and stayed ahead through every noise treatment.
A new foundation model appears every few months in molecular, protein and antibody modeling.
With the hybrid search, a researcher does not need to choose between their current representation and a new one.
They add the new embedding to the representations searched and run the search again, and the search decides whether it contributes features and which.
Chapter tested this on LogD and hERG blocking.
A choice usually made by habit becomes one measured on each task.
I present a study of deep learning (DL) approaches for docking small molecules into protein receptors.
This is a mainstay computational problem in structure-based drug discovery, but surprisingly, recent advances in DL techniques have not yet achieved their projected potential for docking.
This chapter introduces structure-based drug discovery (Section), docking (Section), and DL (Section), as well as the motivation for this work (Section) and the structure of the thesis (Section).

Structure-based drug discovery is a paradigm for developing molecules, which when small are often called “ligands”, that bind to other molecules, which are called “targets” or “receptors”, using knowledge of the three-dimensional structures of both molecules.
The central idea is that binding requires the ligand’s shape and chemical features to be complementary to the receptor.

Whether the resulting binding event produces the intended therapeutic effect that makes this compound a drug candidate is determined by the biological target involved, the binding site of the ligand, and the strength of their interaction, in addition to a range of pharmacological constraints (Patrick, 2023, ch.
The ligand’s target specificity, in turn, influences its potential to cause side effects.
Understanding the structural characteristics of target molecules and how to design ligands with complementary features unique to a selected target is a cornerstone of rational drug discovery.
Structure-based drug discovery is only possible because we know the structures of many biomolecules.

Thanks to the continuous improvement of the experimental techniques X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and cryogenic electron microscopy over the past 80 years, we have the structures of increasingly large and biologically important molecules—from small compounds such as penicillin (Crowfoot et al., 1949, 17 atoms) to peptides such as insulin (M. J. Adams et al., 1969, 788 atoms) and even large proteins such as the 2019-nCoV S protein (Wrapp et al., 2020, 4634 atoms).
Access to these structures has led to breakthroughs in drug discovery and production, elucidation of the mechanisms of action, and the very field of rational drug design .
Small molecules, namely organic molecules with up to 100 atoms, which can be administered orally, are a very important and the most used drug modality, and proteins are the most common targets .
Newer drug modalities such as macrocycles, peptides, or antibodies and other targets such as RNA and DNA provide other avenues for drug discovery.
For my thesis I focus on small molecule drugs that target proteins.

Currently, the two most important repositories of experimentally determined structures for proteins and small molecules are the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD) respectively.

The PDB serves as a de facto legal deposit library for protein structures, since most journals require authors to submit structural data upon publication, making it the largest source of protein and protein-complex structures.

The CSD similarly aggregates crystal structures from researchers worldwide, with a strong emphasis on crystallographic data, and contains nearly all known drugs as well as a wide range of drug-like molecules.
In December 2025, the PDB and the CSD contained 246 715 and 1 376 589 unique, experimentally resolved structures, respectively.1 A drug must be produced, stored, and administered.
It must reach its target in a patient and provide a therapeutic benefit with minimal side-effects (Young, 2009, ch.

Because other important properties of drugs have been directly linked to the structures of small molecules, structure-based drug discovery has become a multi-objective optimisation in which favourable interactions are only one criterion.

Examples of computational proxies that link structure to pharmacological properties are estimates of physicochemical parameters such as prediction of log 𝑃 as an estimate of lipophilicity , Lipinski’s ‘rule of 5’ for oral administration effectiveness , and drug-likeness scores .
As we shall see in the next section, docking methods are designed to model molecular interactions and do not help optimise pharmacological properties beyond binding (Young, 2009, ch.
Beyond biological properties, there are other chemical and legal limitations that affect drug design.

Our current chemical knowledge limits which molecules can be synthesised and tested, often delineated by synthetic accessibility estimators , supplier catalogues, synthesis planning tools , and expert chemists.
Patents further limit the design space of small molecules, as one would sensibly exclude all structures patented by others.

Lastly, economic, social, and practical constraints, while also important in drug development, are not directly linked to Statistics retrieved on 17 December 2025 from https://www.rcsb.org/stats for the PDB and https: //www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk/solutions/about-the-csd/csd-statistics/ for the CSD.

structure-based drug discovery, although the favourable mode of administration, i.e. orally administered, the relatively low price of treatment, and long shelf life are certainly important aspects of small molecule drugs.
Docking is a computational approach to predict the binding mode of a ligand when bound to a receptor.
Docking algorithms require as input a 3D structure of the receptor, a description of the ligand, and a search space.
Given these inputs, docking algorithms generate as output the 3D structure of the receptor-ligand binding complex (Figure).
The first input, the 3D receptor structure, should be as close as possible to the holo (ligand-bound) form of the protein.
Using the apo (unbound) form may be appropriate when the structural differences between the apo and holo states are small.

For highly flexible proteins in which the side chains or the backbone undergo conformational changes upon ligand binding, the holo form of the receptor bound to a related ligand may be a more suitable starting point.
In practice, PDB structures are often used, but care must be taken to prepare them, for example by selecting plausible protonation states of the side chains in the binding site .
In certain cases, the use of multiple receptor structures is advantageous, and the use of snapshots generated from molecular dynamics simulations has been demonstrated .
The second input, the ligand molecule, is typically provided with a 3D starting conformation.

Ideally, an unbiased conformation of a ligand is used, one that has not undergone, for example, the minimisation procedure used to generate experimental protein-ligand structures, which would affect the ligand’s bond lengths, angles, and rings.
The PDB provides idealised versions of ligand structures as part of the Chemical Component Dictionary .

Some docking software allow as input 1D string representations (see Appendix A, Section A.1.1) because the software includes a conformation generation module that can generate or regenerate 3D coordinates.

Most docking software requires the user to carefully prepare the ligand by defining the stereochemistry, charges, protonation, and tautomeric state; these are all properties that are typically modelled as fixed during docking .
The third input, the search space restricts the set of solutions that a docking algorithm can output.
Typically, ligand placement is restricted to a defined region of the receptor that encompasses a binding site.
In some cases, the search space is expanded to include the entire protein to perform blind docking.
The search space may be reduced by positional constraints on specific ligand substructures and enlarged by allowing some movement of protein side chains.
Most targets do not undergo large conformational changes and modelling only side-chain flexibility is sufficient .
The two primary outputs of docking methods are the predicted ligand coordinates and an associated docking score.

In principle, a single predicted pose may correspond to any of the many microstates between which a ligand binding mode fluctuates; in practice, however, docking results are typically evaluated by comparison with experimentally determined structures .
Most docking tools, therefore, report a set of ligand poses paired with corresponding scores.
These scores are used by docking programmes to rank poses of the same ligand and externally by users to prioritise a variety of molecular candidates.
Some methods report scores in the units of binding affinity (kcal/mol); for example, AutoDock Vina .

However, docking-derived affinity estimates are generally considered too inaccurate to reliably predict true binding affinities , although improving their accuracy remains an active area of research .
In this thesis, I focus on pose generation.
The main applications of docking are the discovery of potentially new ligands, the optimisation of lead compounds, and the investigation of the mode of action .

Lead discovery by virtual screening with docking proceeds by predicting the binding poses of a (large) set of molecules from a library, measuring the best fit of each molecule, and then ranking the candidates and selecting the top ones as leads.

In ligand optimisation, medicinal chemists inspect lead compounds and their fit with the receptor in order to propose modifications to the molecular structure with the goal of optimising the binding strength or other molecular properties, often iteratively.
For target function analysis, ligands known to elicit biological responses are docked and the differences in the target structure are analysed.
One specialised application of docking explored later in this thesis is the use of docking with constraints in fragment-based drug discovery.

Fragments, ligands with a molecular mass of less than 300 Da, can be used to explore the binding site of a protein effectively, and can be combined into regular sized ligands by growing, linking, and merging .
Docking with substructure constraints derived from fragments can assist in designing ligand elaborations by helping to determine the fit of the added substructures.

Other more specialised applications of docking related to structure-based drug discovery include fitting ligands to electron densities , uncovering reaction mechanisms of enzymes , and studying host-guest systems .
Dedicated software packages, for example PHENIX , which provide pipelines for experimental structure solution, include docking routines to place substructures of the model onto electron maps .
Improvements in docking algorithms therefore impact many aspects of structural biology, and not just drug discovery directly.
The three main requirements for docking algorithms are speed, accuracy, and generalisability.

Speed is needed because virtual screening libraries can be very large, with up to a billion molecules for ‘ultra-large screens’ ; the requirement for speed is further exacerbated by the need to consider multiple structural snapshots of the target when docking into a rigid receptor.
Accuracy in terms of recovering the true binding mode is important for decision making in drug discovery and to avoid taking “duds” further down the drug discovery pipeline.
Generalisation to new protein targets and new ligands is a must because docking for drug discovery, by definition, must predict unknown protein-ligand interactions.
Classical docking algorithms typically break the problem of predicting binding modes into two subroutines: sampling and scoring (Young, 2009, ch.
The sampling subroutine generates co- ordinates for the ligand atoms, and the scoring subroutine grades these coordinates.
Often there is a feedback loop from the scoring to the sampling routine.
In the last 43 years, more than 100 docking methods have been developed , and some examples are listed in Table.

The large number of docking methods reflect the diversity of computational approaches that have been applied to the docking problem: Monte Carlo simulated annealing is a stochastic method from physics that is used for docking in the AutoDock series .
Genetic algorithms are stochastic search algorithms that are used in GOLD and AutoDock 2 .
Fragment- based incremental construction builds solutions step-wise starting from small fragments and is used in HOOK , FlexX , and SEED .
Systematic search approaches exhaustively enumerate poses by discretising the search space and are used by Hammerhead , EUDOC , and in combination with pruning also by Glide .
The diversity of published approaches highlights the amount of algorithmic experimentation done and the maturity of classical docking methods.
Despite the large number of docking approaches, docking as a paradigm remains limited in some important ways.
Being structure-based, the methods require a receptor structure as input.
Rigid docking, that is assuming a rigid receptor structure, is the most common and most reliable approach.
Flexible docking, allowing some movement of the receptor, is slow and often does not perform better than rigid docking .
Further limitations are that the protonation and charge patterns of the ligand and receptor are fixed during the docking and water molecules are only selectively modelled .
Despite these limitations, docking has been and remains an important tool in structure-based drug design.
Possible improvements of docking methods are faster predictions, better control, and richer models.

The first, faster predictions, is for docking ligands into flexible receptors which currently often requires some use of molecular dynamics or docking to a variety of crystal structures of the same target.
The second, better control, is the methods’ flexibility for users to test hypotheses, around, for example, the binding site, substructure positions, and desired interactions (e.g. H-bond, covalent).
The last category, richer models, includes improved modelling of waters, receptor flexibility, charges, protonation, and tautomeric states.
These factors are known to be important in protein-ligand binding and docking programs should more accurately model them.
Deep learning (DL) is a subfield of machine learning.
Machine learning is an approach to build functions, called models, that do not require a programmer to implement all rules by hand.
Rather, the programmer defines parameters that are left to be inferred from data in a process called “training”.
Once the parameters have been determined by training, the model can be used like a regular function.
Supervised learning is one approach to train a machine learning model.
Given pairs of input and desired output, the model is trained to reproduce these data (see Appendix A, Section A.2.1).

The goal is to find parameters that both reproduce the training data and lead to sensible outputs for new, previously unseen inputs that were not shown during training, so that the model can be used to make predictions.
If a model can make satisfactory predictions on new data points, it generalises; a model that does not generalise is said to be overfitting to its training data (Goodfellow et al., 2016, ch.
To assess generalisation when building a model, machine learning engineers split the example data into a training set and a test set.
The training set is used to find the parameters of the model and the test set is used to assess the generalisability of the model.

If there are modelling decisions that cannot be made by the programmer or the model has parameters that cannot be learnt, so-called “hyper-parameters”, then a third split, the validation set, is used to select these To quantify the agreement between a predicted output and ground truth data, a loss function must be specified for supervised training.
Given a data point and the model’s prediction, it returns a positive real number, the loss.
A loss of 0 means that the two data points (actual and predicted) are identical.
The definition of a loss function is an important consideration in supervised machine learning; an underspecified loss function can lead to surprising failure modes of the model.
Often, loss functions combine multiple objectives; for example, by adding different loss components linearly to obtain one main loss.
The loss function is essential because it defines what constitutes good performance on a task.
DL is the sub-set of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with a large number of hidden layers to learn patterns directly from data.
These models typically have a large number of parameters (see Appendix A, Section A.2.2).

DL typically does not rely on human-chosen data representations but uses raw representations of the input to directly learn patterns from the data, including intermediate representations at every layer (Goodfellow et al., 2016, ch.
Neural networks are trained by making small adjustments to the parameters iteratively.
A typical training algorithm involves setting the initial parameter values according to a random initialisation scheme, for example, Xavier initialisation .
Then batches of the data (inputs and outputs) are drawn from the training set.
The model makes predictions on the inputs, and these predictions are compared to the ground truth outputs using the loss function.
The back-propagation algorithm , using the chain rule of calculus, is then used to calculate how much each parameter affects the loss function.
These derivatives are then used to update the parameters, using, for example, gradient descent (Bishop & Bishop, 2024, ch.
7) or more sophisticated stochastic optimisation methods such as Adam .
This procedure is repeated by passing over all the training data multiple times; one pass is called an “epoch”.
Neural networks are highly flexible and, in principle, can approximate any function with enough neurones and hidden layers .
This is particularly useful for non- tabular data for which few other universal modelling approaches exist.
However, this universality does not mean that DL models can be used to solve any problem.

Indeed, no learning algorithm is, in general, the best, when considering all possible problems ; what makes neural networks so useful is that they contain important inductive biases, for example smoothness, that are useful for a large set of relevant problems (Bishop & Bishop, 2024, ch.
In practice, it is possible to include other problem-specific inductive biases such as translation invariance or permutation equivariance, and that makes DL so useful.
However, the main downside of DL models is that they require large amounts of training data to learn from.
In many domains, including structural biology, the input data have an intrinsic structure.
For example, proteins consist of a small set of identical amino acids connected in sequence, forming chains that mostly fold up in repeating patterns.

Understanding the internal structure of the data, the necessary degrees of freedom of a task, and task-specific mathematics have led to new inductive biases, e.g. triangle inequality inspired triangular updates , which have led to breakthroughs.
Choosing a DL framework that follows the structure of the data generating process constitutes an inductive bias that helps a model learn a task more efficiently and using fewer data.
Other examples of common network architectures with strong inductive biases that we will encounter later include convolutional networks, graph neural networks, and diffusion models.
Section A.2 provides technical background on these and other DL–based models that have been applied to docking.
A particularly successful DL model architecture is the transformer .
It is suitable for all types of data, for example sequential data in conjunction with positional encodings (see Appendix A, Section A.2.6).
The transformer has become a universal building block, and many tasks that were solved with more dedicated architectures have now been solved with transformers.
The two main advantages of transformers are that they are well suited for parallel processing and that they are effective at transfer learning.

This has led some researchers to state that, like search, DL represents a paradigm shift and that training (a transformer) with sufficient data is sufficient to build a supervised model for any task, and even reach artificial general intelligence (Bishop & Bishop, 2024, ch.
Whether this is true or not is not yet known.
I can only note that DL-based modelling is still relatively young in comparison to purely mathematical or physics-based modelling.
Deep learning (DL) techniques have led to major breakthroughs in protein structure prediction, recognised by the award of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry .
John Jumper and Demis Hassabis were honoured for developing AlphaFold 2 , a DL-based method capable of generating highly accurate models of protein structures.

AlphaFold 2 won the fourteenth biennial Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction competition (CASP14) in 2020 , and two years later, DL-based methods inspired by AlphaFold 2 dominated CASP15, establishing DL as the dominant method in protein structure prediction .
These advances in computational protein structure prediction are significant for structure-based drug discovery because they can provide structures of more potential drug targets.

While the experimentally determined protein structures in the PDB cover about 35 % of the genes of the human genome , the computationally generated structures in the AlphaFold Data Base cover more than 98 % of human proteins.

This increase unlocks many new targets, for example the computational structure of glucose-6-phosphatase protein is amenable to structure- based drug discovery and they speculate that a ligand that binds to a pocket near the protein’s binding face may help regulate blood sugar levels.
The aforementioned success of DL in protein structure prediction and the implications for structure- based drug discovery motivated me to investigate DL applied in docking.

My guiding hypothesis is that DL-based docking methods are still early on the innovation S-curve , and are less mature than the incumbent methods in functionality and performance, but also that the technology has the potential to replace the incumbent methods.

The first successful application of DL techniques applied to docking that I am aware of is the DL-based scoring function in NNScore that uses a convolutional neural network and takes as input a voxel grid.
The first approaches that used DL also for pose generation include DeepDock that learnt a statistical potential.
Table lists twenty DL-based methods, four of which had been published when I started this work in 2022.

The large number of publications of DL-based docking approaches over the following years demonstrates not only the timeliness of my work but also, in general, the field’s belief that DL could have a large impact on docking.
However, none of the approaches published by 2022 had the level of impact on docking that AlphaFold 2 had on protein structure prediction—and this marks the starting point of my thesis.
In Chapter, I describe a benchmark of classical and DL-based docking methods to investigate their failure modes and make suggestions for their improvement.

In Chapter, I assess the quality of the training and test data sets on which the DL-based docking methods have been trained in an attempt to understand the failure modes of the models relative to the data.
In Chapter, I use experimental data to measure to what extent similar ligands adopt similar poses upon binding.

In Chapter, I explore diffusion guidance using molecular mechanics force field-inspired terms to fix the observed failure modes of a leading DL-based docking method, and I add further terms to constrain substructures and interactions using the insights I gathered in Chapter.
Lastly, Chapter concludes my thesis and introduces the new paradigm of co-folding methods and provides an outlook on DL-based techniques for small molecule docking.
As I discussed in Chapter, the last few years have seen the development of numerous deep learning (DL)-based protein-ligand docking methods.
If AlphaFold 2 is any guide, they offer huge promise in terms of speed and accuracy.

However, despite claims of state-of-the-art performance in terms of root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) to experimentally determined poses, upon closer inspection, I found that they often produce physically implausible molecular structures.
It is therefore not sufficient to evaluate these methods solely by RMSD to a crystallographic native binding mode.
It is vital, particularly for DL-based methods, that they are also evaluated in terms of steric and energetic criteria.

I present PoseBusters , a Python package that performs a series of standard quality checks, built using the well-established cheminformatics toolkit RDKit (Landrum The PoseBusters test suite validates chemical and geometric consistency of a ligand including its stereochemistry, and the physical plausibility of intra- and intermolecular measurements such as the planarity of aromatic rings, standard bond lengths, and protein-ligand clashes.
Only methods that both pass these stereochemical and energetic checks and predict native-like binding modes should be classed as having “state-of-the-art” performance.

I will show that in terms of both physical plausibility and the ability to generalise to examples that are distinct from the training data, none of the DL-based methods I tested outperformed classical docking tools.
In addition, I will show that molecular mechanics force fields contain docking-relevant physics that appears to be missing from DL methods.

PoseBusters allows practitioners to assess docking and molecular generation methods and will help drive innovation in new inductive biases still required to improve DL-based methods and ultimately the development methods that generate more accurate and more realistic predictions.

As described in Chapter, molecular docking, an essential step in structure-based drug discovery , is the task of predicting the predominant binding mode(s) of a protein-ligand complex given an experimentally solved or computationally modelled protein structure and a ligand structure .

The predicted complexes are often used in a virtual screening workflow to help select small molecules from a large library of possible candidates ; or directly by medicinal chemists to understand the binding mode and to decide whether a small molecule is a suitable drug candidate (Patrick, 2023, ch.
Docking methods are designed with the understanding that binding is enabled by interactions between protein and ligand structures.
But due to the complexity of this, methods tend to strike a balance between fast calculation and accuracy (Patrick, 2023, ch.

DL, as described in Chapter, promises to disrupt the dominant design principle of classical docking software, and DL-based docking methods promise to unlock fast and accurate virtual screening for drug discovery.
To this end, several different DL-based docking methods have already been proposed ; see also Table for a more complete list.

Non-DL-based “classical” docking methods include within their search and scoring functions terms that ensure chemical consistency and physical plausibility; for example, limiting the degrees of movement in the ligand to only the rotatable bonds in the ligand and including penalties if the protein and ligand clash .

In this chapter, I show that some current DL-based docking methods still lack such key “inductive biases”, resulting in the creation of unrealistic chemical structures and binding modes despite obtaining root-mean-squared deviation (RMSD) values (see Appendix A, Section A.1.3) from the experimental binding mode that are less than the widely-used 2 Å threshold .

To assess the output of docking methods, I created an independent test suite called PoseBusters that checks the chemical consistency and physical plausibility alongside established metrics, such as the binding mode RMSD.
The problem of assessing the physical plausibility of docking predictions is akin to the structure validation of ligand data in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) .

Structure validation assesses the agreement of each of the ligands’ bond lengths and angles with those observed in related chemical structures and the presence of steric clashes both within the ligand and between it and its surroundings .

While these tests were designed for users to select those ligand crystal structures which are likely to be correct , docking methods are evaluated on their ability to recover crystal structures, so their output should pass the same physical plausibility tests.
Physical plausibility checks are also part of some workflows for conformation generation .

Friedrich, de Bruyn they use geometry checks performed by NAOMI which measures—like the PDB tests just mentioned—the deviation from known optimal values for bond lengths and bond angles, and also tests for divergence from planarity for aromatic rings.
In addition to physical checks, chemical checks are also needed .

Chemical checks proposed for checking PDB structures include the identification of mislabelled stereo assignment, inconsistent bonding patterns, missing functional groups, and unlikely ionisation states .
The problem of checking chemical plausibility has also come up in de novo molecule generation, where they proposed a test suite including checks for the chemical validity of any proposed molecule.

For docking, the focus is less on stability and synthetic accessibility of a generated molecular structure as it is hoped that these have been tested prior to attempting docking, but more on chemical consistency and physical realism of the predicted bound conformation.

Some comparisons of docking methods have included additional metrics based on volume overlap or protein-ligand interactions to supplement pose accuracybased metrics such as RMSD of atomic positions and run time measurements, but the majority of comparisons of docking methods are predominantly based on binding mode RMSD .
The current standard practice of comparing the output conformations of docking methods using on RMSD-based metrics alone also extends to recent new methods.
The five DL-based docking methods that I test in this chapter all claimed better performance than standard docking methods but these claims rested entirely on the sole criterion on RMSD.
None of these methods tested their outputs for physical plausibility.
In this chapter, I present PoseBusters, a test suite that is designed to identify implausible chemical structures, conformations and ligand poses.

I used PoseBusters to evaluate the predicted binding modes generated by the five DL-based docking methods described earlier and listed in Table and two standard non-DL-based “classical” docking methods AutoDock Vina and GOLD .

These poses were generated by re-docking the cognate ligands of the 81 protein- ligand crystal complexes in the Astex Diverse set and 308 ligands of the protein- ligand crystal complexes in the PoseBusters Benchmark set, a new set of complexes released from 2021 onwards, into their cognate receptor crystal structures.

On the commonly-used Astex Diverse set, the DL-based docking method DiffDock appears to perform best in terms of RMSD alone but when taking physical plausibility into account, AutoDock Vina and GOLD perform best.

On the PoseBusters Benchmark set, a test set that is potentially harder for methods that might have overfit to their training data because it contains only complexes that the DL methods have not been trained on, GOLD and AutoDock Vina are the best methods in terms of RMSD alone and, when taking physical plausibility into account, or when proteins with novel sequences are considered.
The DL-based methods make few valid predictions for the “unseen” complexes and their performance degrades the more dissimilar the task is from their training data.
Overall, I show that none of the DL-based methods I considered yet outperforms standard docking methods when physical plausibility is taken into account.
Five DL-based and two classical docking methods were used to re-dock known ligands into their respective proteins, and the predicted ligand poses were evaluated with the PoseBusters test suite.
The following section describes the docking methods, the data sets, and the PoseBusters test suite for checking physicochemical consistency and structural plausibility of the generated poses.

Full details of each can be found in their respective references.
DeepDock learns a statistical potential based on the distance likelihood between ligand heavy atoms and points of the mesh of the surface of the binding pocket.
DiffDock uses equivariant graph neural networks in a diffusion process for blind docking.
EquiBind applies equivariant graph neural networks for blind docking.
TankBind is a blind docking method that uses a trigonometry-aware neural network for docking in each pocket predicted by a binding pocket prediction method.
Uni-Mol carries out docking with SE(3)-equivariant transformers.
All five DL-based docking methods are trained on subsets of the PDBbind 2020 General Set as detailed in Table.
DeepDock is trained on v2019 and the other four are trained on v2020.
It should be noted that I used the DL models as trained by the respective authors without further hyper-parameter tuning.

DeepDock and Uni-Mol require the definition of a binding site while DiffDock, EquiBind, and TankBind are ‘blind’ docking methods that search the entire protein.

The PoseBusters test suite is organised into three groups of tests.
The first checks chemical validity and contains tests for the chemical validity and consistency relative to the input.
The second group checks intramolecular properties and tests for the ligand geometry and the ligand conformation’s energy computed using the Universal Force Field (UFF) .
The third group considers intermolecular interactions and checks for protein-ligand and ligand-cofactor clashes.
Descriptions of all the tests PoseBusters performs in the three sections are listed in Table.
Molecule poses which pass all tests in PoseBusters are ‘PB-valid’.

For evaluating docking predictions, PoseBusters requires three input files: an SDF file containing the re-docked ligands, an SDF file containing the true “reference” ligand(s), and a PDB file containing the protein with any cofactors.
The three files are loaded into RDKit molecule objects with the sanitisation option turned off.
The first test in PoseBusters checks whether the ligand passes the RDKit’s sanitisation.

The RDKit’s sanitisation processes information on the valency, aromaticity, radicals, conjugation, hydridization, chirality tags, and protonation to check whether a molecule can be represented as an octet-complete true molecule.

Passing the RDKit’s sanitisation is a commonly-used test for chemical validity in cheminformatics, for example in de novo molecular generation .

The next test in PoseBusters checks for docking-relevant chemical consistency between the pre- dicted and the true ligands by generating ‘standard InChI’ strings for the input and output ligands after removing isotopic information and neutralising charges by adding or removing hydrogens where possible.

InChI is the de facto standard for molecular comparison , and the ‘standard InChI’ strings generated include the layers for the molecular formula (/), molecular bonds (/c), hydrogens (/h), net charge (/q), protons (/p), tetrahedral chirality (/t), and double bond stereochemistry (/b).
Standardisation of the ligand’s protonation and charge state is needed because the stereochemistry layer is dependent on the hydrogen (/h), net charge (/q) and proton (/p) layers.
These can unexpectedly change during docking even though most docking software considers the charge distribution and protonation state of a ligand as fixed .
The normalisation protocol also removes the stereochemistry information of double bonds in primary ketimines which only depends on the hydrogen atom’s ambiguous location.

The first set of physical plausibility tests in the PoseBusters test suite validates bond lengths, bond angles, and internal distances between non-covalently bound pairs of atoms in the docked ligand against the corresponding limits in the distance bounds matrix obtained from the RDKit’s Distance Geometry module.
To pass the tests, all molecular measurements must lie within the user-specified tolerances.

The tolerance used throughout this manuscript is 25 % for bond lengths and bond angles and 30 % for non-covalently bound pairs of atoms e.g.: if a bond is less than 75 % of the Distance Geometry bond length lower bound, it is treated as anomalous.
This was selected as all but one of the crystal ligands in the Astex Diverse set and all of those in the PoseBusters Benchmark set pass at this threshold.

The PoseBusters test for flatness checks that groups of atoms lie in a plane by calculating the closest plane to the atoms and checking that all atoms are within a user-defined distance from this plane.
This test is performed for 5- and 6-membered aromatic rings and non-ring non-aromatic carbon-carbon double bonds.
The chosen threshold of 0.25 Å admits all Astex Diverse and PoseBusters Benchmark set crystal structures by a wide margin, and as with all other thresholds, can be adjusted by the user.
The final test for intramolecular physicochemical plausibility carried out by PoseBusters is an energy calculation to detect highly strained or unlikely conformations.
Our metric for this is the ratio of the energy of the docked ligand conformation to the mean of the energies of a set of 50 generated unconstrained conformations as in they.
The conformations are generated using the RDKit’s ETKDGv3 conformation generator followed by a force field relaxation using the UFF and up to 200 iterations.
The test suite rejects conformations for which this ratio is larger than a user-specified threshold.
they set a ratio of seven based on the value where 95 % of the crystal ligands in the PDBbind 2020 General set are considered plausible .
I selected a less strict ratio of 100 where only one structure each from the Astex Diverse and PoseBusters Benchmark set is rejected.
Intermolecular interactions are evaluated by two sets of tests in the PoseBusters test suite.
The first set checks the minimum distance between molecules and the second checks the share of overlapping volume.
Both sets of tests report on intermolecular interactions of the ligand with four types of molecules: the protein, organic cofactors, and inorganic cofactors.
For the distance-based intermolecular tests PoseBusters calculates the ratio of the pairwise distance between pairs of heavy atoms of two molecules and the sum of the two atoms’ van der Waals radii.
If this ratio is smaller than a user-defined threshold then the test fails.
The default threshold is 0.75 for all pairings.
For inorganic cofactor-ligand pairings the covalent radii are used.
All crystal structures in the Astex Diverse set and all but one in the PoseBusters Benchmark set pass at this threshold.
The van der Waals and covalent radii used are from the Blue Obelisk open data project that the RDKit uses.

For the second set of intermolecular checks, PoseBusters calculates the share of the van der Waals volume of the heavy atoms of the ligand that overlaps with the van der Waals volume of the heavy atoms of the protein using the RDKit’s ShapeTverskyIndex function.
The tests have a configurable scaling factor for the volume-defining van der Waals radii and a threshold that defines how much overlap constitutes a clash.
A threshold is necessary because many crystal structures already contain clashes.
For example, they found that 81 out of 305 selected high-quality protein-ligand complexes from the PDB contained steric clashes .
The overlap threshold is 7.5 % for all molecule pairings and the scaling factor is 0.8 for protein-ligand and organic cofactor-ligand pairings and 0.5 for inorganic cofactor-ligand pairings.

PoseBusters calculates the minimum heavy-atom symmetry-aware root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between the predicted ligand binding mode and the closest crystallographic ligand using the RDKit’s GetBestRMS function.
Coverage, a metric often used for testing docking methods, is the share of predictions that are within a user adjustable threshold which by default is 2 Å RMSD.
This value is arbitrary but commonly-used and recommended for regular-size ligands .
In this chapter, sequence identity between two amino acid chains is the number of exact residue matches after sequence alignment divided by the number of residues of the query sequence.
The sequence alignment used is the Smith–Waterman algorithm implemented in Biopython using an open gap score of −11 and an extension gap score of −1 and the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix.
Unknown amino acid residues are counted as mismatches.
Post-docking energy minimisation of the ligand structure in the binding pocket was performed using the AMBER ff14sb force field and the Sage small molecule force field in OpenMM .
The protein files were prepared using PDBfixer and all protein atom positions were fixed in space only allowing updates to the ligand atoms’ positions.
Minimisation was performed until energy convergence within 0.01 kJ mol−1 per iteration.
The Astex Diverse set published in 2007 is a set of hand-picked, relevant, diverse, and high-quality protein-ligand complexes from the PDB .

The complexes were downloaded from the PDB as MMTF files and PyMOL was used to remove solvents and all occurrences of the ligand of interest from the complexes before saving the proteins with the cofactors in PDB files and the ligands in SDF files.
I created the PoseBusters Benchmark set, a new set of carefully-selected publicly-available crystal complexes from the PDB.
It is a diverse set of recent high-quality protein-ligand complexes which contain drug-like molecules.
It only contains complexes released since 2021 and therefore does not contain any complexes present in the PDBbind 2020 General set used to train many of the methods.
Table B.1 lists the steps used to select the 308 unique proteins and 308 unique ligands in the PoseBusters Benchmark set.

In this chapter, I discuss PoseBusters, a test suite designed and built to identify chemically inconsistent and physically implausible ligand poses predicted by protein-ligand docking and molecular generation methods.

I show the results of applying the PoseBusters test suite to the output of seven different docking methods, five current DL-based docking methods (DeepDock, DiffDock, EquiBind, TankBind, and Uni-Mol) and two classical docking methods (AutoDock Vina and GOLD).
As mentioned earlier, none of the DL-based docking methods assessed here yet outperforms classical docking methods when both physical plausibility and binding mode RMSD is taken into account.

Our work demonstrates the need for physical plausibility to be taken into account when assessing docking tools because it is possible to perform well on an RMSD-based metric while predicting physically implausible ligand poses (Figure).

Using the tests in the PoseBusters test suite as an additional criterion when developing DL-based docking methods will help improve methods and the development of more accurate and realistic predictions.
In addition, the individual tests in the PoseBusters test suite highlight docking-relevant failure modes.
The results show that Uni-Mol, for example, predicts non-standard bond lengths and TankBind creates internal ligand clashes.

As mentioned earlier, the ability to identify such failure modes in predicted ligand poses makes PoseBusters a helpful tool for developers to identify inductive biases that could improve their binding mode prediction methods.
Our results also show that, unlike classical docking methods, DL-based docking methods do not generalise well to novel data.

The performance of the DL-based methods on the PoseBusters Benchmark set overall was poor and the subset of the PoseBusters Benchmark set with low sequence identity to PDBbind 2020 General set revealed that DL-based methods are prone to overfitting to the proteins they were trained on.

Our analysis of the targets with sequence identity lower than 30 % to any member of PDBbind 2020 General set revealed that across all of the DL-based docking methods almost no physically valid poses were generated within the 2 Å threshold.

The most commonly-used train-test approach for building DL-based docking models is time-based, e.g., complexes released before a certain date are used for training and complexes released later for testing.
Based on our results, I argue that this is insufficient for testing generalisation to novel targets and the sequence identity between the proteins in the training and test must be reported on.
Post-docking energy minimisation of the ligand using force fields can considerably improve the docking poses generated by DL-based methods.
However, even with an energy minimisation step, the best DL-based method, DiffDock, does not outperform classical docking methods like GOLD and AutoDock Vina.
This shows that at least some key aspects of chemistry and physics encoded in classical docking methods and force fields are missing from DL models.

The PoseBusters test suite provides a new criterion, PB-validity, beyond the traditional “RMSD ⩽ 2 Å” criterion to evaluate the predictions of new DL-based methods, and hopefully will help to identify inductive biases needed for the field to improve docking and molecular generation methods, ultimately resulting in more accurate and realistic predictions.

The next generation of DL-based docking methods should aim to outperform standard docking tools on both RMSD criteria and in terms of chemical consistency, physical plausibility, and generalisability.
This chapter introduced the PoseBusters test suite which can check the generated output of docking methods for chemical consistency and physical plausibility.

The main results from our analysis of five DL-based docking methods are that no DL-based method yet outperforms standard docking methods when considerations of physical plausibility are taken into account, that the DL-based docking methods tested do not generalize to novel data, and that force fields contain docking specific information that is lacking from these DL-based docking methods.
The PoseBusters test suite is a new standard to test for physical plausibility alongside native binding mode accuracy.

Since the publication of the results in this chapter , many new DL based docking models, but more broadly also other molecular modelling software, like co-folding methods and de novo molecular generation methods have been assessed using the PoseBusters test suite.

The tests have become a tool for method developers to check that their methods do not egregiously violate stereochemistry and physics, and have helped identify the inductive biases still required to improve DL-based docking methods, as shown by recent improvements .
Since the publication of the first version of the PoseBusters software, additional tests have been added and bugs have been fixed based on suggestions and feedback from various users.
Maria Kadukova contributed settings for a non-flatness test for aliphatic rings.
Guy Durant identified a bug that prevented passing molecule objects into the main function.
In addition, checks for the connectedness of molecules, the absence of radicals, and clashes with water molecules have been added.
Various stability improvements were made for users running the PoseBusters checks on extremely wonky molecules produced by de novo molecular generators.
Other publications have also advanced assessments of protein-ligand models beyond the metrics mentioned here.

For example, they have expanded the set of metrics by monitoring the conservation of intermolecular interactions, showing another way to possibly improve DL-based protein-ligand models, namely by training models directly to learn intermolecular interactions.
This chapter assessed DL-based methods for docking.
The next chapter takes a look at the data behind those models, its quality, the patterns within it, and what that might actually tell us about how good DL models can be.
In the previous chapter, I benchmarked deep learning (DL)-based docking models.
In this chapter, I describe how I used the PoseBusters tests developed in the previous chapter to also assess the models’ training and test data.
The models’ failure modes are present in the commonly used training data set PDBbind 2020 General set, but not as strongly pronounced.
The high quality of the established test sets, the Astex Diverse set, CASF-2016, and PoseBusters Benchmark set, is reconfirmed.
This demonstrates that the models might have learnt these failure modes as biases from the data, but the data do not fully explain them.
A well-known adage in computer science is “garbage in, garbage out.” In the context of machine learning, this principle implies that low-quality training data will tend to produce low-quality models.
This concern is even more pronounced for deep learning, which seeks to learn meaningful latent representations directly from data.
Consequently, a comprehensive evaluation of deep learning-based docking models must also consider the quality of the experimental structures used in training.

Experimentally-solved structures of protein-ligand complexes can vary significantly in quality, and this includes the resolution of the experimental structures (see Appendix A, Section A.1.4), the quality of model fit, and the completeness of the ligand models.

The Protein Data Bank (PDB) , introduced in Chapter as the most important source of experimentally-derived protein-ligand structures, has been continuously growing and now, at the end of 2025, it contains approximately 170 000 protein-ligand structures.
However, not all of these structures are suitable for method development, which is why subsets of relevant, representative, and high quality structures from the PDB are typically selected.
Some data sets that have been used for the training and evaluation of docking methods are listed in Section.
