purposes.
For example, Binding MOAD , applies a resolution threshold of 2.5 Å to collect as many structures as possible.
Not only the quality, but also the volume of the training data is important.
The first method to use linear regression to predict binding affinity in docking was AutoDock 3, which used 30 protein-ligand complexes , for a model with 5 parameters.
DL-based methods, with billions of parameters to be fitted, require far more training data, but it is not yet clear how much data is needed.
The largest data set I have seen used to train DL-base docking models in Section is BindingMOAD, which contains 41 409 protein-ligand complexes.
Not only data selection, but also data preparation is important for many docking workflows.

Ligand preparation includes creating 3D coordinates, adding hydrogen atoms, setting charges, assigning proper bond orders, and generating accessible tautomers, while receptors are typically prepared by removing atom clashes, filling in missing atoms and residues, placing waters, and optimising hydrogen bonds .
For classical docking, data preparation has been shown to critically influence docking success rates, with small preparation errors causing fluctuations of more than 20 % in docking success rates .
The representation and parsing of molecular data is not a trivial problem, in part because several cheminformatics file formats in common use are not open standards.
For example, the widely used MOL2 file format is defined by a closed-source implementation in proprietary software, and no complete public specification exists.
As a result, developers of independent software have had to infer or reconstruct parts of the format, which has led to incompatibilities.
For this reason, the most commonly used open-source cheminformatics library, the RDKit, does not support saving molecules in the MOL2 format.
Another example is the PDB file format, which allows molecules to be stored without explicit bond order information or atomic charges.
This missing information can cause difficulties when parsing molecular structures upon loading.
When DL–based models are trained on such poorly specified data, it is therefore prudent to verify the molecular structures that are actually loaded from the data set.
If problems are identified, the choice of training data and the associated quality criteria should be re-examined.
Benchmarking the RDKit is important because it is the de facto standard cheminformatics library.
It is used by all five DL–based docking methods evaluated in the previous chapter.
The RDKit’s strengths include its robustness, active maintenance, rich feature set, high-performance C++ backend, user-friendly Python API, and extensive documentation.
However, users must exercise caution.

The RDKit performs strict parsing of molecular files and does not attempt to infer missing information, such as atomic charges, bond orders, or valence states, that are not explicitly specified in the input.

While this behaviour increases reliability and transparency, it also means that data sets that cannot be loaded correctly by the RDKit warrant careful scrutiny, particularly given the widespread adoption of the library.
In this chapter, I take a look at the quality of five data sets that have been used to train DL-based docking models.

The PoseBusters tests, introduced in the previous chapter (Chapter), are used to test the data.
Here, the testing scenario is slightly different.
Rather than testing re-docked ligands, as in the previous chapter, the ligand fit in the crystal structures is assessed.
Two changes are made to the test suite to facilitate this scenario: First, the RMSD-based metric is omitted.
Second, rather than checking the identity between the crystal and predicted ligands, the identity of the crystal ligand is checked against its entry in the PDB’s Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) .
For ligands which do not have entries in the CCD, the chemical similarity tests are skipped.

For both Astex Diverse sets, the CASF-2016 set, and the PoseBusters Benchmark set, all ligands are in the CCD; however, the PDBbind 2020 General set has 13.4 % (2611), the PDBbind 2020 General R1 has 13.7 % (2611), and the DockGen set has 7.0 % (23) ligand entries that are not in the CCD.

The commonly used training data set PDBbind 2020 General General contains 19 443 protein- ligand complexes (unique PDB identifiers) and 86.6 % (16 832) passed the intermolecular checks, 69.9 % (13 600) passed the intramolecular checks, and 54.5 % (10 590) structure passed all test (Table).

Not all ligands in this data set had entries in the CCD because 2611 ligands are represented as multimers of CCD entries, for example sugars and small peptides.

The PDBbind 2020 General R1 set had similar failure modes (Figure C.5b), but more structures passed overall (67 %, 12 804) than for PDBbind 2020 General (54.5 %, 10 590); this improvement was mainly due to lower failure rates in the RDKit sanitization test, while the number of protein-ligand clashes remained the same.

The failure modes of the MOL2 ligand and PDB receptor files were mismatches in molecular formula (10, 3.5 %), ligand internal strain (5, 1.8 %), and stereochemistry mismatches (5, 1.8 %).

Although most of the complexes in the PDBbind 2020 General training data pass the tests, most of the predicted poses of the DL-based models fail the intermolecular tests (Table), in particular because they contain protein-ligand clashes and intramolecular ligand clashes (Figure C.7).

Figure further shows that on the more difficult PoseBusters Benchmark set, more than three quarters of the predicted poses have protein-ligand clashes; this is a much higher rate than observed in the training data.
First, I consider what the results show in regards to the ‘garbage in, garbage out’ hypothesis.
As the results show, the PDBbind 2020 General training data set does have a large number of structures that do not pass the tests.
The most severe structural failure mode is protein-ligand clash (Appendix C, Figure C.6a).
This is shared with the five previously benchmarked DL-based models that were trained on subsets of the PDBbind 2020 General General set (Chapter, Table).
However, when comparing failure rates of the methods (Figures C.7 and C.8) to those in the data sets, I observe higher failure rates (Appendix C, Tables).

In particular, the methods generate poses with much higher protein- ligand clash rates from the DL-based methods compared to the training data (Figure) and while the training data does contain systematic structural artefacts, these data issues alone cannot explain the observed error rates in the predicted poses.

In conclusion, there is some evidence that these DL-based models learn protein-ligand clashes from the data, but the quality of the training data does not fully explain the much higher failure rates observed in the models.
To discern the influence of problematic data on model performance, it is not sufficient to examine the training data alone.
One could retrain the models on filtered clean versions of the training data set to see what the effect of the faulty data really is.
However, it is likely that incorrect handling and loading of the data might have caused some of the models to learn from faulty molecular representations.
Indeed, the results show that loading molecular data sets with the RDKit is not trivial.
Depending on which files are chosen and on what options are used, one might get 91 % passing protein-ligand complexes or none when loading the molecules of the CASF-2016 data set.
In general, there is no molecular file type from which the RDKit is guaranteed to load valid molecules.

All file formats admit underspecified or wrong molecular data, and the RDKit parser, as noted, although known for particularly strict parsing, cannot follow the unwritten conventions of other software when dealing with omitted information.
When the RDKit cannot sanitise a molecule, an error is raised.
However, when no error is raised, a molecule can still be wrong.
This is because sanitization does not guarantee that the molecule was correctly loaded.
These silent bugs are logic errors, and they cause molecules to be parametrised wrongly.
This happens when loading the CASF-2016 files.

When loading the SDF files of the ligands instead of the MOL2 files, there are some sanitisation errors, but other ligands load without error but have radicals, non-flat double bonds, and flat non-aromatic rings and their internal energies are much too large (Appendix C, Figure C.4).
This happens despite the two molecular file formats containing identical coordinates and atom types.
The reason is that two different molecules end up being loaded by the RDKit: one is correct, and the other is incorrect.
The wrong chemical representation causes a faulty parametrisation of the UFF in the energy ratio test, leading to a downstream error caused by the file being misinterpreted by the RDKit.

Clearly, the chemical representation of the molecules matters a lot, and much care must be taken to load molecules correctly with the RDKit, because learning from chemically faulty data possibly limits the methods’ performance.

In summary, special care must be taken when loading molecular files with the RDKit - some substructures, such as four valent nitrogens, are never correctly loaded and could lead to systematic blind spots.
Obtaining the latest data from the PDB in mmCIF format and regenerating the data set, as was done for the Astex Diverse, was successful.
The molecular structures loaded from the original files with RDKit were only 60 % PB-valid, but the recreated Astex Diverse set was 92 % PB-valid.

It is apparent that high quality filters (e.g. maximum resolution of 2.5 Å), for example those used to select structures for the Astex Diverse set, the CASF-2016 set, and the PoseBusters Benchmark set, did indeed yield higher quality data selections, even though the PoseBusters tests were not used directly as criteria.
As the PDB continually expands and the RDKit is continually improved, regenerating the data sets periodically will be important.
For future work, it would be interesting to study the diversity and uniqueness of the data.
The PDBbind 2020 General contains 19 443 protein-ligand complexes from the PDB, of which 155 are redundant leaving 19 288 complexes.
For training generative models, it is important not only to have diverse data that do not repeat, but also to have data that cover as much of the input space as possible.
Describing the distribution of the data in terms of diversity measured by protein sequence identity or ligand similarity will be important.
Further work for understanding the trade-off between using all data and selecting only high quality data would be a useful step.

This is because showing that the training data have the same failure modes as the models is only a necessary but not sufficient condition to show that the models have learnt the problems from the data.
Retraining the models with cleaner data would allow this to be measured.
It would be interesting to see what effect retraining the DL-based docking methods on cleaner data sets would have.
This would give a signal of whether efforts to improve the structure models of the PDB, via refitting the models on the electron densities, could be worthwhile for model developers.
In conclusion, the results showed that data sets of molecular structures obtained from the PDB should be carefully inspected, filtered, and errors corrected.
Although the failure modes of the DL-based docking methods resembled those of the training data, I find that the training data were of better quality than the model predictions would make us believe.
To fully discern the influence of problematic data on model performance, the models could be retrained on filtered versions of the data set and their results be compared.
Further, I recommend that all practitioners benchmark and carefully select the training data they choose to build DL-based docking models, maybe less is more in some cases.
In this chapter, I explore common patterns in structure-based drug design using a large collection of protein-ligand complex pairs from the PDB.

The chapter describes the process of selecting high-quality complexes from the PDB, aligning the pairs of PDB structures around ligands bound in the same binding site of the same protein receptors, the measurements calculated on the structures, and the patterns observed in the data.
The chapter provides extensive experimental evidence for an important concept in medicinal chemistry, which is that molecules with similar structures have similar binding modes.
This provides a starting point for the guidance of docking models introduced in the following chapter.
Structure-based drug discovery often relies on the tacit knowledge acquired by practitioners over multiple projects with specific protein-ligand systems.

This knowledge includes the binding modes of existing lead series, the flexibility of the protein and its binding pocket, and the effect of structural changes in the ligand on binding mode and affinity.
Central to this is the dogma that similar molecules with similar structures have similar properties .

Molecular modellers and medicinal chemists with relevant experience can recognise familiar patterns in interactions and substructures, which they use to generate new ideas to improve the binding and properties of lead compounds .
The medicinal chemistry literature makes some of this knowledge explicit.

Individual case studies of success stories in structure-based drug discovery include those of approved drugs such as vemurafenib and current candidates in clinical studies such as AMG 510 and are important reading for practitioners working on the same targets.
Data science approaches have also been applied to make medicinal chemistry knowledge explicit in the context of structure-based drug discovery.

For example, Ferreira de they studied the frequency distribution of non-covalent interactions in a set of 11 016 PDB structures and highlighted how the addition of one interaction may cause structurally similar ligands with conserved binding poses to differ significantly in binding affinity.

they found that only in 14 % of 297 pairs of assembled smaller and larger ligands the binding mode definitely changes upon chemical elaboration, and in many of these the change is due to an expansion of the smaller molecule of the pair into the space occupied by the receptor.

they collected 121 molecular overlays from the PDB that support the pharmacophoric hypothesis, namely that structurally diverse molecules with chemical features arranged similarly in space can bind to the same target.

In the context of fragment-based drug design, they found that in a set of 3672 structures containing fragments and their drug-like superstructures, smaller chemical changes lead to retention of the binding mode more frequently than larger ones.
Although such insights are valuable and can guide practitioners, this is familiar knowledge to expert medicinal chemists.
What such experts need are the right tools to put their structural hypotheses to the test when optimising compounds.
To this end, classical pose prediction tools allow users to bias the predictions .
For example, the Python API of the docking program GOLD allows the specification of distance constraints for individual atoms.
However, many recently developed DL-based docking tools still lack such a capability.

In order to address this limitation, and in preparation for training and testing DL-based methods on the structure-based hypotheses that medicinal chemists employ, I set out to collect a large number of pairs of ligands bound to the same binding site from the PDB.

Although I could start with a data set curated for studying protein-ligand interaction patterns and binding modes, such as the sc-PDB which contains 16 034 carefully protonated and chemically-complete complexes in its latest iteration , I start with the PDB as it is the largest and fastest growing data set of experimentally resolved protein-ligand structures.

By the end of 2017, which is the year of the latest release of the sc-PDB, the PDB contained 111 874 structures obtained by X-ray crystallography and this number has nearly doubled and currently contains 246 715 structures, as noted in Chapter, including more than 450 000 protein-ligand interactions .

In this chapter, I explore the data set with a hypothesis-driven data science approach to test whether the data make sense and to quantify the degree to which molecules with similar structures have similar binding modes.
In the next chapter, I will test and develop machine learning-based drug development tools using these data.

This chapter’s methods are organised into four parts: the selection of protein-ligand complexes from the PDB (Section), the pairing and aligning of these structures (Section), clustering (Section), and the metrics used to describe the final data set (Section).
The Python library RDKit was used for all cheminformatics tasks unless otherwise specified.

The structures were paired by protein chains that share a PDB 70 % cluster identifier 2 , a UniRef 90 % cluster identifier , or UniProt accession number that had small molecule ligands bound to the same binding site.
Ligands within 5 Å after the following alignment are considered to bind within the same binding site.
I aligned the protein chains using PyMOL’s align algorithm which performs a sequence alignment followed by a structural superposition.
The structural superposition was performed on the 𝛼 carbons of the paired chains.

When multiple chain mappings or alternate structures were available for a pair of PDB complexes, only the alignment resulting in the highest overlap of the two ligands, measured with the RDKit shape and colour score SCRDKit , was chosen.
The alignment matrices were stored for further analysis.
Only one pair of structures per PDB CCD—PDB CCD identifier combination was chosen, namely the pair with the highest SCRDKit score.

The metrics based on pairs of complexes are listed in Table and include similarity metrics on the structure (2D) and pose (3D) of the ligands, metrics on changes of the binding pocket, and weight, the difference in the number of heavy atoms, the Tanimoto (Jaccard) similarity on Morgan fingerprints with radius 2 (ECFP4 2048-bit vectors), and the number of atoms in the maximum common substructure (MCS).
The MCS of the ligand pairs were identified using the RDKit’s flexible MCS (FMCS) algorithm with the default settings.
The ligand 3D similarity metrics included the RDKit shape and colour score, SCRDKit , identical to SuCOS , which is similar to the pose similarity metric COS used by they.

The similarity metrics on binding pockets included the number of identical residues between the binding pockets, the RMSD of the C𝛼 atoms of the conserved residues, and the RMSD of the side chains of the conserved residues.
The interaction similarity metrics included the number of conserved ProLIF interactions and the Tanimoto (Jaccard) similarity of the ProLIF interactions.

Because protein chains in PDB structures do not use a standardised residue numbering scheme, residues were mapped between structures using the sequence alignments generated previously for the structural alignments.

The pairs of ligands were categorised according to the following definitions: A pair of ligands is identical if the ligand has the same CCD identifier in the PDB file or if the standard InChI strings generated for the molecules are identical.
A pair of ligands is an elaboration if the MCS is one of the ligands.
Following they, a pair of ligand poses is conserved when SCRDKit is at least 80 %.

Overall, 232 665 unique pairs of PDB structures with ligands bound to the same protein and the same binding pocket were collected, and 53 048 (23 %) of these are pairs of identical ligands bound to the same receptor (but still in different PDB structures).
Of the 179 617 pairs containing non-identical ligands, 99 319 (55 %) pairs contain fragments, 3698 (2.1 %) pairs are elaborations, and 2587 (1.4 %) contain fragment elaborations.
Further, 92 255 (51 %) of the non-identical pairs contain drug-like molecules and 46 159 (26 %) pairs contain a pair of a fragment and a drug-like ligand.
Binding poses are more commonly conserved in pairs of chemically similar ligands.
Figure shows the shape and pharmacophoric similarity, measured by SCRDKit , of all pairs of non-identical pairs of ligands (179 617) versus chemical similarity, measured via chemical fingerprints.
The plot shows that, for more chemically similar pairs of ligands, the binding pose is conserved more commonly.
It also shows a high similarity of H-bond interactions (yellow) for chemically dissimilar ligands.
Figure shows the same set of non-identical pairs (179 617) binned by chemical similarity and in terms of the percentage of poses conserved (SCRDKit ≥ 0.8).
This plot shows the trend more clearly; clearly, there is a steady increase in the percentage of poses conserved as a function of chemical similarity.
For ligand pairs with chemical similarity larger than 80 %, around 90 % of the observed pairs in the data set have conserved binding modes.
Of the 53 048 pairs of identical ligands, 99.0 % are pairs that conserve the binding mode (SCRDKit ≥ 0.8) and 1.0 % (527) do not conserve binding mode (SCRDKit < 0.8).
Six of those pairs of structures containing identical ligands (identical CCD identifiers) with non-conserved poses are shown in Figures D.3 and D.4.
Three of these poses are distinctly different (Figures D.3a and D.4c and Section D.4).

The publications of the PDB structures reveal that ligand DGT in structures 4TNX and 4TO6 is an allosteric binder, ligand DIF binds is shown in different species (6HN0 is ovine and 6HN1 is caprine serum albumin), and ligand OCF receptors 8AYJ and 8ONN differ by a point mutation.
This might explain some pairs of poses scoring lower than expected (Figure D.3b).
Similarly, three of the pairs of ligands with identical CCD identifiers have have non-identical Fingerprints (2048-bit ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity less than 1, for example Figure D.4c).

The ECFPs (2048-bit, radius 2) used here also distinguish ligands with different protonation patterns, resulting in some ligand pairs with identical CCD identifiers scoring less than one in terms of fingerprint similarity.

My analysis shows that chemical similarity correlates strongly with pose conservation, as shown in Figures.
This agrees with the approach often used in structure-based drug design.
Small changes in molecular structures often maintain the binding modes of the original structures more often than larger ones.
In particular, elaborations of molecules maintain binding modes very often; more than 80 % of all observed elaborations maintain the binding pose.
This agrees with the main principle of structural medicinal chemistry, that is making small changes to lead compounds and existing scaffolds.

The statistic that 99.0 % identical ligands conserve their binding pose in the same pocket of different PDB structures confirms how consistent the binding events observed in the crystal structures are.
However, the remaining pairs (1.0 %, 527) include pairs with significant changes in the binding mode when bound to the same receptor (Section D.4).

Slightly different protonation patterns affected the ECFP4 fingerprints, but spot checks revealed that point mutations, difference in pH of the crystal, re- ceptors from different species, and allosteric binding might cause these differences.
The 90 % sequence identity threshold for pairing protein receptors does not filter pose-relevant point mutations.
Identical fragments have been observed elsewhere to adopt multiple binding poses .
Initially, perhaps surprisingly, in our data, pairs of identical fragments have a high rate (99.7 %) of pose conservation.
However, this does not mean that fragments do not adopt multiple poses, because in our pair selection process, I only choose the combination of ligand poses that leads to the highest SCRDKit .
When there were multiple fragments in a binding site, I chose the pair with the pose that was the most similar.
This explains the high rate of pose conservation in identical fragments.
Fragment elaboration pairs showed a similar high rate of pose conservation as all elaboration pairs.
The trends observed for the MCS also agree with intuition: If more of a ligand is conserved, and if fewer atoms are added, then the more similar the smaller and larger ligand poses are.
However, the fitted model on smaller ligand size, relative MCS size, and number of atoms added only explained about 33 % of the variance observed in pose similarity (Pseudo 𝑅2 = 0.33).
The missing variation might be explained by the amount of chemical complementarity removed and added, which was not represented in these models.
Intermolecular interactions are directly related to binding affinity.

For this reason, medicinal chemists count interactions and add up their contributions when designing structures, as can be gleaned from average interaction strength tables (Burnell et al., 2016, Table, p. 32).
The correlations between interactions and pose conservation were lower than expected.
Almost no positive correlation is observed (Figure); the hydrogen bond interaction type has the highest Spearman correlation, which is almost negligible at 𝜌 = 0.08.
This suggests that pharmacophores and interactions contain orthogonal information and should both be considered when designing.

The data set used in this study has a positive selection bias, as I have selected pairs of protein-ligand complexes for which experimentally resolved structures of both ligands bound within the same pocket of the same protein exist.
A modification of a molecule that failed to lead to a binding event in the same binding site (or did not bind at all) would not be represented in our data.
Another bias in our study is that the chemical space represented here is the one explored by structural experiments that led to the submission of structures to the PDB.
These experiments do not explore the proteomic and chemical space uniformly, and only a very small subspace of combinations of ligands and proteins can ever be explored.
A further limitation of this analysis is that most PDB structures do not contain biologically accurate protonation patterns of receptors and ligands.
Similarly, the hydrogen bonds in water networks of binding sites are mostly unresolved in experimental structures.
Although I know that the solvation and protonation patterns strongly contribute to protein-ligand binding, I did not have the data to analyse these here.
In this chapter, I conducted a study of the protein-ligand binding patterns of pairs of structures of similar ligands bound to the same pocket in the same protein from the PDB.
My analysis shows that ligands with high chemical similarity conserve binding modes more frequently and that elaborations, on average, conserve poses more frequently.
Interaction metrics are found to correlate with chemical similarity, but not with pharmacophoric measurements.
This chapter provided some insight into the types of biases that medicinal chemists use when performing structure-based drug design.
It also provides a large data set for the study of protein-ligand patterns that can be further explored.
In the next chapter, I use a diverse subset of these paired data to steer a DL-based docking model to conserve user-chosen interactions and substructures.
Until now, I have explored protein-ligand interactions through docking models (Chapter) and paired crystallographic data (Chapter).
Now we turn to applying our insights and improving deep learning (DL)-based docking.

In this chapter, I start with the DL-based model that performed best in the benchmark in Chapter, namely DiffDock , and apply diffusion guidance to inject user constraints and physical information into the diffusion process.

I first demonstrate on a series of test setups that this approach only produces predictions in the binding site when given the binding pocket location (a user constraint), that the force field information (physical information) improves physical plausibility, and that substructure and interaction constraints (user constraints) can be met with high precision.
In our experiments, I also find that gradient-based guidance performs slightly better than gradient-free guidance.
Next, a realistic docking benchmark is set up in which ligands cross-dock into cognate receptor structures of chemically similar ligands, as is custom in lead optimisation.

I demonstrate the performance of our approach on this task using a new data set of public PDB structures and on a set of unpublished cereblon binding molecular glues with unpublished interactions and an unpublished target.
The resulting method is named GuideDock.

When medicinal chemists use docking for virtual screening, they formulate design hypotheses and select ligands accordingly; for example, they might select ligands that share a certain substructure with a lead molecule for which an experimental protein-ligand complex is available.

For some hypotheses, the medicinal chemists might be able to define constraints; in the previous example, this would be to constrain the atoms of the shared substructures in the same positions during cross-docking.
Such constraints allow a user to test their design hypotheses, but they might also lead to better predicted poses.

Although classical docking methods such as AutoDock 4 and GOLD support atom-wise position constraints suitable for this example, dedicated methods such as EnzyDock , EDock , and FitDock can extract these constraints from template ligands.
DL-based docking models do not yet support any constraints, despite their potential practicality, and even though well-informed constraints can improve docking results.
To test how well DL-based methods might perform with constraints, I integrate constraints into the best DL-based model according to our comparison in Chapter.
The chosen base model is DiffDock, an SE(3) Riemannian diffusion model.
For diffusion models, in general, there are multiple approaches to add constraints.

Due to computational constraints, I restricted myself to training-free approaches, which only modify the inference procedure and avoid the computationally costly training of models by re-using model weights fitted by others.
Of course, this excludes approaches that modify the functional form of the model or propose alternative loss functions .

At the time of starting this work, training-free approaches had not yet been implemented for biological structural models, but I became aware of them in the domain of image generation and I sought to adopt that approach for DiffDock.
However, in the meantime, approaches similar to ours have been implemented in co-folding methods .
Defining constraints when modelling biological structures is a well known procedure in the adjacent field of molecular dynamics.
Here, distance constraints are often used to prevent or enforce interactions, while position constraints can be used to anchor a structure in place to prevent it from drifting out of the frame .

In molecular dynamics simulations, soft constraints are typically implemented as additional terms in the force field, for example, as an additional harmonic term with its minimum at a desired atom location.
Force fields are differentiable scalar functions of the positions of the atoms, and they are parametrised using the molecular structures in the system of interest.
The energy functions in classical force fields are linear functions that sum up terms of various energetic contributions such as bond stretching and steric clashes.
Rather than just adopting the constraint terms, I build a system that can flexibly include any differentiable scalar function on atom positions, which includes all force fields by definition.
Our motivation is two-fold.

First, I hope that guidance with the non-constraint terms will help reduce the number of physically implausible predictions, a problem I identified in Chapter, and second, I hope that this setup will make our model easier to use, as users will be familiar with defining constraints on force fields.

To summarise, I tackle three use cases with inference time guidance, illustrated in Figure: The first is to enable binding site-specific docking with the blind docking model, the second is to allow users to define position and distance constraints, and the third is to improve the physical validity of the predicted poses.
I choose DiffDock-L , the follow-up method to DiffDock that I benchmarked, as the base model.

DiffDock-L is a blind DL-based docking method that decomposes the docking task like most classical docking methods: into a pose generation model for sampling poses, and a scoring model to rank the generated poses.
During inference, the pose generation model is applied 20 times to sample and transform random noise into a ligand binding pose.
This is done in batch to generate 20 ligand poses.
The scoring model is then applied to rank these predictions.

The pose generation model is an SE(3)-equivariant Riemannian diffusion model that defines a diffusion process over the roto-translations and torsions of the typical docking state-space, and it is trained by score-matching with an exploding variance schedule .
The score model has a very similar architecture, but is trained as a classifier that predicts whether a generated pose is within 2 Å RMSD of the crystal pose.
Both models use graph neural networks with equivariant tensor products .

As input, the pose generation model only takes the alpha carbon locations of the receptor proteins into account, ignoring side chains and cofactors, while the scoring model evaluates the poses using all heavy atoms of the protein, also ignoring any cofactors.

Another important limitation, in addition to ignoring anything but protein chains, is the hardcoded limit of 1022 amino acids for the length of the receptor protein chains due to the period of rotary positional embeddings being 1024 for the ESM2 model , which is used to generate embeddings for residues.
In our benchmark of docking methods (Chapter), DiffDock was the best DL-based model.

It showed high physical plausibility in terms of bond lengths, bond angles, and stereochemistry, but protein-ligand clash rates were higher than those of classical docking methods and the main physical failure mode.
DiffDock-L represents an improvement and has 27 % of poses within 2 Å RMSD and PB- valid, relative to 12 % of the poses of DiffDock.
Figure E.1 shows a waterfall plot of the failure modes of DiffDock-L with the most prominent being protein-ligand clash, as it was for DiffDock (Figure B.4e).
In what follows, I apply guidance to the pose generation model of DiffDock-L to control the sampling and improve the quality of the samples generated.
I make no alterations to the pose scoring model.
For both models, I maintain the default inference settings and use the publicly available weights provided by the authors for DiffDock v1.1.3 on the project’s GitHub page.
These weights were generated by they training on BindingMOAD2020 which includes most protein-ligand complexes released to the Protein Data Bank before 2020.
Guidance is a framework for conditioning generative diffusion models on additional information at inference time.
Various authors have already described guidance for different types of diffusion models for various domains, such as images , audio processing , and molecular systems .
For example, in image generation, guidance can be used to condition on a text prompt .
Various guidance frameworks for score-based diffusion models have been proposed recently.
Recall that score-based diffusion models are trained to approximate the score ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥) of a noisy version of the data.

One robust way to create a conditional generative model is to separately train a classifier model on paired data of the form (𝑥, 𝑦) and derive the score ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑦 ∣ 𝑥) from it; the model’s task effectively being to predict the desired property 𝑦 from noisy versions of the data .
By Bayes’ theorem, the sum the two scores ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥) and ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑦 ∣ 𝑥) is the conditional score for ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥 ∣ 𝑦).

Another approach, known as classifier-free guidance, trains on the unconditional and conditional task simultaneously via masking ; this effectively performs score-matching for ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥 ∣ 𝑦) and ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑥).
A disadvantage of these approaches is that they require training and that all particular classes of labels that the model should work with must be specified from the beginning.
Training-free guidance, yet another type of guidance, does not change the model but modifies the iteratively generated intermediate predictions during inference.
Essentially, this form of guidance adds an optimisation task at each intermediate .
When the conditional score ∇𝑥 log 𝑝𝑡 (𝑦 ∣ 𝑥) is tractable or good proxies exists, conditioning can be performed using only the unconditional model .
However, while I adopt this approach for being training-free, it has been mentioned that the training-based forms of guidance lead to better results.
The training-free guidance framework used here is akin to Diffusion Posterior Sampling , Universal Guidance , and Training-Free Guidance but adapted to DiffDock’s latent space and noise schedule.

The three cited frameworks have been developed for variance preserving score-models in Euclidean spaces, but here I apply the same concept to the sampling model of DiffDock-L, a score model with a variance exploding schedule operating on a non-Euclidean state space.

Our goal is not to mathematically derive the general validity of the resulting approach, but to practically show that this approach is possible and to evaluate the merits of guidance for DL-based docking.
A sketch of our approach, using the generic notation of score-based models , follows.
The main idea is that I perform an optimisation of the posterior mean obtained from the latent variables at each inference step.

To clarify, the posterior mean is a point estimate in the target space 𝑥̂0 obtained from the latent 𝑥𝑡 at each inference step using the formula 𝔼 [𝑥0 ∣ 𝑥𝑡 ] = 𝑥𝑡 + 𝜎𝑡2 ∇𝑥𝑡 log 𝑝(𝑥0 ∣ 𝑥𝑡 ), also known as Tweedie’s formula .
I obtain the estimator by plugging-in the score model that was trained to approximate the score, which in mathematical notation is S(𝑥𝑡 , 𝑡) ≈ ∇𝑥𝑡 log 𝑝(𝑥0 ∣ 𝑥𝑡 ).
This way I obtain the formula for our estimator 𝑥̂0 which is This estimator is at the centre of the optimisations in the training-free guidance frameworks cited above.
The next step to setup the optimisations is to define a loss function ℓ which can be any differentiable scalar function on the target space of the model.
All force fields for protein-ligand dynamics including constraints fit this description.
The force fields used for our experiments are described in Section.
I investigate two optimisation schemes.
The first is ‘backward’ guidance, in which 𝑥̂0 is optimised without differentiating through the model.
In mathematical notation, the backward guidance optimisation task is The second optimisation scheme is ‘forward’ guidance in which differentiates through the score model.
This requires evaluating the score model and its gradient and is therefore more costly computationally.
However, I investigate this approach because it might lead to better results.

In mathematical notation, the ‘forward’ guidance optimisation task is In practice, optimisation might not be performed at every inference step due to efficiency considerations and numerical stability.

To illustrate the latter, during early time steps, the mean conditional expectation often does not resemble a valid ligand pose, and the ligand might clash with the receptor, leading to very large values of an energy function due to terms that divide by the distance between atoms, e.g. clash terms based on the Lennard-Jones potential.

An important technical detail for implementing this form of guidance for DiffDock-L is that I re- quire an ‘adapter’ function that converts between updates to the internal coordinates and the external coordinates.
This is because when I optimise 𝑥̂0 , I want to optimise using the internal coordinates (to remain on the manifold), but the force field is written in terms of the external coordinates.
DiffDock-L already includes a function 𝒜𝑐 that maps elements of the tangent space of the internal coordinates and a reference ligand conformation to the external coordinates.
Therefore, I only need to implement its inverse, a new function 𝒫𝑐 , which is a function that maps external coordinates and a reference ligand pose to changes in the internal coordinates.

This function may use the same reference conformation 𝑐 that DiffDock-L uses to define its state space, that is, the space spanned by the roto-translations and torsions applied to the reference pose 𝑐.

Clearly, this function must be a projection onto the tangent space of the internal coordinates (the tangent space of the manifold) because the external coordinates are of higher dimensions than the internal ones.

Based on the definition of the translation, rotation, and torsions, we can define 𝒫𝑐 as the inverse of 𝒜𝑐 such that 𝒫𝑐 ⋅ 𝒜𝑐 = I. Let 𝒫𝑐 be defined as applying the same operations of 𝒜𝑐 but in reverse order: first undo the torsions1 in exactly the reverse order, then use the Kabsch algorithm to remove the translation and rotation components induced by the torsions, and then recover the rotation and translation with another application of the Kabsch algorithm.
For all optimisations, the LBFGS optimiser of PyTorch was used with a set maximum of 10 iterations and a tolerance of 10−5 as an early stopping criterion.

A technical point, and a bit of a warning to the potential user, is that I compute the molecular dynamics force field using the Python API of OpenMM while DiffDock-L is implemented in PyTorch.

While both OpenMM and PyTorch can compute on GPUs, I do not know of any method to share the coordinates between the two frameworks directly on the GPU and I resort to copying the atom coordinates, energies, and forces between the two via CPU NumPy arrays.
Moving these data between the CPU and GPU repeatedly for every optimisation potentially creates a computational bottleneck.

I investigated the application of training-free guidance to DiffDock for three different goals: constrained docking, binding-site specific docking, and improving the physical validity of the base model.
For constrained and pocket-specific docking, I dock a novel ligand into a related ligand’s cognate re- ceptor, which is similar to how docking is used in lead optimisation for drug discovery.
For constrained docking, I provide a set of atom coordinates obtained from the related ligand in its cognate receptor.
These are within 2 Å of the pose of the aligned new ligands and should provide useful constraints.
For pocket-specific docking, I provide the centroid of the aligned novel ligand as a constraint.
I run the constrained and pocket specific docking on an updated Malhotra data set and the new GuideDock data set described in the next section.
For the physical plausibility experiments, I perform re-docking on the PoseBusters data set .

The re-docking experiments show that physical plausibility can be improved to the same extent by a post-prediction energy minimisation, by post-prediction with the simple force field, guidance with the simple force fields, and guidance with molecular dynamics.
Figure shows a comparison of the failure modes of DiffDock-L, DiffDock-L with post-prediction energy minimisation, and guidance with the simple clash terms.
The figure shows that energy minimisation and physical guidance have virtually the same effect: The physical validity is mostly improved due to reducing protein-ligand clashes.
A full list of our experiments re-docking the cognate ligand into the rigid receptor in the PoseBusters data set is provided in Table.

Guidance with OpenFF 2.0.0 and the simpler clash terms yield the same improvement in accuracy and physical validity (45.8 ± 2.9 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid) as the post-prediction minimisation (45.8 ± 2.8 %) applied to DiffDock-L (26.6 ± 2.5 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid).
Performing the post-processing minimisation before or after the scoring makes no difference.
The forward guidance (45.8 ± 2.9 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid) and reverse guidance (45.1 ± 2.8 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid) schemes perform equally well.

However, forward guidance, which differentiates through the model, takes more time (2 min per protein-ligand complex) than the reverse guidance scheme (1.3 min), both significantly longer than DiffDock-L (12 s).

Table also shows that, as expected, providing the centroid location of the docked ligand through guidance improves the accuracy (63.6 ± 2.8 % RMSD within 2 Å) over DiffDock-L (51.9 ± 2.8 % RMSD within 2 Å).
Providing the centroid and running the clash terms results in the overall highest accuracy and physical validity (59.7 ± 2.8 % RMSD within 2 Å and PB-valid).
However, even though the poses are now all within 5 Å RMSD, the 2 Å RMSD threshold is satisfied by only 63.6 % of the generated poses.
Those poses failing this threshold have the centroid in the right location, but the binding pose is still not correct.

Overall, the guidance improved the prediction accuracy by 10 % from around 49 % (DiffDock-L RMSD within 2 Å) to 59 % (GuideDock RMSD within 2 Å).
By implementing simple guidance in DiffDock-L, I demonstrated that the predictions of diffusionbased molecular structure models can be steered in a controlled manner.

Using simple loss functions for guidance was sufficient to increase the physical plausibility of generated poses, as evaluated by PoseBusters, while avoiding the expensive parametrisation required for energy minimisation with a full molecular dynamics force field.
I further showed that guidance improves the performance of DiffDock-L not only in terms of phys- ical plausibility but also in accuracy, as measured by RMSD within 2 Å.

Incorporating prior information from related ligands, sometimes referred to as templates, unsurprisingly improved performance for cross-docking, but only when the underlying assumptions of this approach were satisfied.
Crucially, this requires that the imposed constraints do not interfere with docking and that the rigid receptor does not sterically block the correct ligand pose.
Using guidance to enable pocket-specific and constrained docking was shown to work well in practice.
Revealing additional information about the ligand and its binding pose to the model during inference improved performance relative to the base model.
I showed that the same base model can be applied across these different tasks.
However, when compared to the classical docking method GOLD, our models still performed worse in terms of physical plausibility, though not in terms of RMSD accuracy.
Training the base model to generate only PoseBusters-valid poses may therefore be a promising direction.
Overall, the performance of the resulting method, GuideDock, is at best comparable to that of the classical docking method GOLD, both with and without additional constraints.
A more fundamental paradigm shift, such as moving from docking to co-folding, may be required to surpass traditional physical docking methods in a meaningful way.
Our approach uniquely demonstrates how physical terms derived from force fields and userdefined biases can be integrated with state-of-the-art DL methods for rigid small-molecule docking.
The terms used here improve results by incorporating information that the model either did not learn to exploit (physics) or did not have access to (user biases).
Introducing user biases also enables practitioners to directly test their hypotheses within the docking process.
In this chapter I presented GuideDock, a DL-based docking method that innovates by adding diffusion guidance to the DiffDock-L blind docking method.

This allows reusing the pre-trained model to perform constrained docking and pocket-specific docking, while simultaneously also improving the physical plausibility of the generated poses in comparison to the unguided DiffDock.

Although GuideDock does not surpass classical docking methods, in particular the classical docking method GOLD, the experiments demonstrate that repurposing a single blind docking model for multiple different tasks is possible.
Since I started working on GuideDock, other researchers have implemented guidance terms in biological structure prediction models.
The ‘steering’ approach that was added to the second version of the preprint of Boltz this summer is very similar to our method.
I am excited that I was on the right track with this work, but I suspect that the machine learning community now views co-folding as having superseded docking.
The aim of this thesis was to investigate deep learning (DL)-based protein–ligand docking.

Motivated by the landmark success of AlphaFold2 in protein structure prediction and by the observation that DL- based docking has not yet achieved a comparable impact, I sought to contribute to the advancement of this field.

In particular, this work aimed to assess the current capabilities of existing methods, identify opportunities for improvement, and support the maturation of DL-based docking as a practical technology.
My research improves our understanding of DL-based protein-ligand docking by investigating the shortcomings of common evaluation metrics, training data, and testing setups.
In addition, my research explored the interplay of physics-based and DL-based approaches and showed that diffusion guidance can inject physical biases and user knowledge.
My first key finding is that the established RMSD metric of being within 2 Å of the crystallographic binding mode is insufficient to assess DL-based protein-ligand docking.
Using examples, I showed that the 2 Å RMSD threshold admits physically impossible pretzel-shaped conformations and stark protein- ligand clashes, among others.
As a remedy, I implemented a new metric, PB-validity, which consists of a series of physical and chemical plausibility tests.
This new metric has been adopted by the research community to benchmark docking, de novo molecular generation, and co-folding models.
My most significant contribution is that I have systematically shown that DL-based docking methods have not yet outperformed classical docking methods.
I did this in two independent ways: first, by creating a new, more difficult test set, the PoseBusters test set; and second, by introducing the new metric: PB-validity.
Both provide unique insights into the performance of the models: The PoseBusters tests enumerate chemical and physical failure modes, telling the user what exactly has gone wrong and how badly.
Independently, using a novel out-of-distribution training data test set and splitting it by sequence identity revealed that DL-based methods generalise less well than classical docking methods.
The impact of this contribution has seen a renewed effort of model developers to improve the physical plausibility of docking as well as co-folding models.

Also important is my finding that the very training data, the crystal structures in the PDBbind 2020 General set (and its successor PDBbind 2020 General R1), are polluted with the same failure modes with which DL-based methods struggle.
Filtering, pre-processing, or remediating the training data is rarely done but should be; this includes double-checking that the molecular representations loaded from the data sets are correct.
A simple way to do this is to use the PoseBusters tests also to inspect the training data, but that alone does not guarantee problem-free structures.

Regarding time-based training-test data splits, I found that time-splits are insufficient to demonstrate generalisation because they omit use case-dependent considerations of target and pocket similarity, ligand similarity and known binding modes of congeneric series, and interaction conservation.

Splitting my test set by maximum sequence identity to the training data, I showed that DL-based models perform much better close to the training data and worse on more dissimilar proteins–using the entire PoseBusters tests set without subdivision captures only average performance, which is the weakness of time-based splits.

The lesson for practitioners is to consider receptor sequence identity, interaction similarity, ligand chemical similarity, and pocket similarity of protein-complexes of interest and report such metrics on data splits when benchmarking protein-ligand structure prediction methods.
My thesis also makes a methodological contribution.
The usefulness of guidance for adding physical and user biases to diffusion-based structure models is shown.
The GuideDock approach provides a convenient interface for influencing model predictions via force fields, already familiar to practitioners.
I show that any force field term can be used including soft constraints and clash terms.
GuideDock demonstrates that guidance can improve the physical validity of the predictions and allow the user to define a binding site and substructure constraints.
The same principles are applicable to co-folding methods as well.
I have also shown that the DL-based models analysed here have not yet learnt (neither explicitly or implicitly) some of the rules encoded in the force fields.
This suggests that physics and DL-based methods might still be combined successfully.
I demonstrated two ways of doing this: (i) adding an energy minimisation after pose prediction; and (ii) using diffusion guidance with physics-inspired terms.
Both improve the physical plausibility of the generated poses of the methods.
Further ways of combining force fields and diffusion models are easy to think of and should be explored.
Another practical contribution to the field are two new docking test sets.

The first is the PoseBusters test set that includes data both similar to and different from the training data (PDBbind 2020 General), to highlight the current shortcomings of DL-based models and the way they are benchmarked.
The second is the GuideDock test set, which contains pairs of protein-ligand complexes of small molecules that adhere to the same binding pockets on the same protein chain.

The PoseBusters Benchmark set has already been adopted by the scientific community as a test set; the GuideDock set will no doubt be useful for testing template-based and constrained protein-ligand prediction methods.

Finally, I quantified the relationship between the chemical similarity of related ligands and the similarity of their binding poses; this relationship was found to be even stronger for chemical elaborations of smaller ligands.

This finding is of particular relevance to medicinal chemists, as it provides an empirical basis for the substructure constraints used in constrained docking and, more broadly, in fragment-based drug design.

A drug is a chemical compound designed to produce a desired effect within a living system, such as preventing disease, restoring health, or relieving symptoms.
The field of drug discovery aims to design these molecules to achieve a specific response based on knowledge of a biological target.
Most commonly, this target is a biomolecule like a protein, whose function is modulated by the drug to provide a therapeutic benefit .

For almost all of human history, the discovery of new drugs was guided by a combination of luck and trial-and-error, and relied on the extraction of materials from the local environment: plants, minerals, and animal products 1 .
The 19th century marked the advent of modern drug discovery .

While still mostly relying on the isolation of active ingredients from traditional cures—e.g., morphine (Sertuerner 1817) or quinine (Pelletier 1820)—this era also witnessed the birth of modern chemistry: scientists developed the tools necessary to synthesise molecules in the laboratory, enabling them to modify natural compounds or create entirely new ones from scratch.
This new capability gave rise to the first synthetic drugs, like aspirin (Dreser 1899), and established the modern pharmaceutical industry .
More importantly, though, it marked a fundamental shift in perspective: from merely finding what worked to understanding why it worked.

A pioneering step in this direction was Paul Ehrlich’s early 20th-century concept of a ‘magic bullet’: the idea that a compound could be designed to kill a pathogen, without harming the host, by selectively targeting a mechanism unique to the microbe.
This principle led to the development of arsphenamine , the first antibiotic, and laid the groundwork for the subsequent antibiotic revolution .

This concept of selective targeting was eventually broadened from external pathogens to the body’s own molecular machinery, which led to the first drugs designed with specific human biological mechanisms in mind, like beta-blockers and histamine H2 antagonists .

The development of these drugs constituted the first appearance of rational design: they were purposefully engineered to interact with a known biological target rather than being discovered serendipitously .

Still, a final conceptual leap was required to arrive at the dominant paradigm in modern This traditional form of medicine is actually what gave us the word drug: it is derived from the Old French ‘drogue’, which in turn comes from the Middle Dutch ‘droge vate’, meaning ‘dry barrels’; a reference to medicinal plants preserved as dry matter . pharmacology: structure-based drug design (SBDD) aims to design molecules whose shape and chemical properties are complementary to a target’s binding site by using its 3D structure as a blueprint .

This approach was made possible by advances in biophysical methods, particularly X-ray crystallography, which gave scientists the unprecedented ability to determine the atomic-level structure of proteins.
The method was first successfully demonstrated in the late 1980s with the design of dorzolamide , an inhibitor engineered to treat glaucoma by binding to the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.
SBDD’s most profound impact, however, came shortly after, with the determination of the HIV-1 protease structure in 1989 .
This sparked a monumental effort that led directly to the development of inhibitors like saquinavir and ritonavir , which transformed HIV/AIDS from a fatal disease into a manageable condition.
Despite this enormous progress, developing new drugs remains a challenging process.
The expense of bringing a drug from discovery to market is immense, taking on average over ten years, with recent estimates placing the median cost at $1.3 billion .
This is largely due to the high failure rate of candidate compounds, meaning that each successful drug must offset the financial burden of numerous unsuccessful attempts .
The reasons for these failures are multifaceted.
A 2019 study reported that in Phase II of clinical trials—where a drug’s effectiveness is first tested in patients—a lack of efficacy was the primary cause of failure in over 50% of cases.
In Phase III, this figure rose to over 60%.

Although this statistic may seem to suggest that we are simply bad at designing binders, the reality is slightly more complex; failure can also stem from poor absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) properties (for instance, the drug may be destroyed by stomach acid or be unable to cross the blood-brain barrier) or the initial target identification may have been flawed, meaning that modulating the chosen biomolecule does not produce the desired therapeutic effect.
The other primary cause of failure is safety.
The same 2019 study reported that safety concerns consistently accounted for approximately 20-25% of failures across phases II and III .
These safety issues can be broadly divided into two categories.
The first of these is on-target toxicity, where the drug successfully binds to the target, but causes negative side effects.
This is an inherent and often predictable consequence of the drug’s primary mechanism, and is a common issue that frequently defines the maximum tolerated dose.

Off-target toxicity, on the other hand, arises from unintended interactions with other biological molecules, and can produce severe and unexpected adverse reactions that are a frequent cause of a drug’s outright termination from development .

Accounting for every potential point of ADME or safety failure in clinical trials is practically impossible, not only due to the hugely complex nature of biological systems, but also because negative data from clinical trials is rarely disclosed publicly .
Consequently, there is limited systematic data on the specifics of why and how frequently novel agents fail in late-stage development, making it difficult to learn from failures and reduce them.
A practical strategy to improve the overall success rate is to increase the number of high-quality candidates entering clinical trials.
The goal is to start with molecules that are already high-affinity, specific binders to the target of interest, thereby improving the odds of success from the outset.
An increasingly popular approach to this challenge, and the one adopted in this thesis, is the use of deep learning (DL) algorithms to screen and design drugs in the early stages of development.
For a deep learning model to be effective at structure-based drug design, it must master two fundamental challenges.
First, it must understand the underlying forces of intramolecular bonding; the chemistry and physics dictating the possible arrangements atoms can take within a compound.
This is necessary to produce novel compounds that are chemically valid and stable, ideally with properties similar to those in databases of existing drugs.
Second, it must learn the principles of intermolecular binding to predict or design molecules that bind effectively to a biological target.
The chapters of this thesis are organised around these two challenges.
Chapters address the first challenge, focusing on deep learning methods for generating molecules that are chemically valid and replicate the distribution of known compounds.

Chapter explores the second challenge of protein-ligand bonding, presenting work on a model for virtual screening and then attempting to extract learned information to inform the generation of new candidates.
A prerequisite for structure-based drug design, however, is the availability of an accurate 3D model of the target protein.
While the number of solved protein structures is growing , and prediction methods are improving , obtaining high-resolution structures for novel or complex targets remains a bottleneck.

This motivates the final results chapter of this thesis: chapter 5, where we describe an adaptation of the inference processes of two structure prediction methods (AlphaFold 2 via OpenFold , and AlphaFold 3 via Boltz-2 ) to directly incorporate cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) data, with the goal of providing high-quality predictions that align with experimental data.
First, though, we provide some necessary background and context to frame these research chapters.
We begin by summarising the drug discovery process, focusing on the early stages that this thesis falls within.

We then provide a brief overview of the machine learning (ML) methods used across the different projects within this thesis, and finally describe how computational, and in particular ML-based, methods have been used to screen and design new compounds up until now.
Finally, we outline the structure and key contributions of this thesis.
Small molecule drugs are the most conventional class of pharmaceuticals.
They are organic compounds generally defined by a molecular weight of less than 1000 daltons (Da) .
Their small size and balanced physicochemical properties allow them to cross cell membranes and reach intracellular targets such as kinases .
These features also support oral bioavailability .
This potential for oral dosing and intracellular target access, combined with their stability, and relatively easy, cheap synthesis, are key reasons for their historical dominance in medicine .

While the market shares of peptides and biologics are expanding , small molecules still make up a comfortable majority of new drugs; in 2024, for instance, they accounted for 32 of the 50 novel drugs (64%) approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) .
Despite being the most simple of the different drug types, each approval marks a successful journey through the lengthy, costly, and high-risk drug discovery and development pipeline.
We elaborate on this pipeline below.
This section provides a brief overview of the small molecule drug discovery pipeline2 , before delving into the stages most relevant to this thesis.
As illustrated in Figure, the process can be depicted as a linear sequence of stages from target identification through to clinical trials.
In practice, this process is highly iterative, and characterised by a high rate of attrition, where the vast majority of projects fail to advance from one stage to the next .
Briefly, the journey begins with target identification and validation, in which the biological mechanism to be targeted is found and tested.
Following this, the hit identification stage aims to find initial molecules, or ‘hits’, that can modulate the target’s activity.
These hits then enter the hit-to-lead and lead optimisation stages, where iterative chemical modifications improve key properties.
Promising lead compounds then undergo preclinical testing before potentially advancing to human clinical trials.
The work presented in this thesis falls within the target validation, hit identification and hit-to-lead stages of the drug discovery pipeline.
We go into more detail on these below.

This next phase of the drug design pipeline aims to use knowledge of the validated target to identify a viable chemical starting point, or ‘hit’.
Hit identification strategies can be broadly divided into screening and designing approaches, with fragment-based methods occupying a space between the two.
Screening approaches aim to discover active molecules from large collections.
High-throughput screening (HTS) evaluates libraries of hundreds of thousands to millions of compounds against the target in biochemical or cellular assays.
While it can reveal unexpected chemotypes, HTS is resource-intensive, generates many false positives, and typically yields very low hit rates (between 0.01% and 0.14% ).

The computational counterpart to HTS, virtual screening (VS), evaluates large in silico libraries of molecules to prioritise a smaller, more promising subset for experimental testing (see section 1.4.2 for a more thorough introduction to VS).
In contrast to screening, design approaches instead focus on rationally constructing molecules to complement the target.
Medicinal chemists may design new compounds guided by the features of existing binders (ligand-based design) or by directly analysing the target binding pocket (structure-based design).
Computational de novo design methods parallel these strategies, algorithmically generating novel molecules predicted to have high affinity and selectivity for the binding site (see section 1.4.3).

Fragment-based drug design (FBDD) represents an intermediate strategy that identifies high-quality chemical starting points by screening collections of very small molecules, or fragments, which typically have a molecular weight below 300 Da .
Because these fragments are so small, their binding affinity for a target is usually weak, often in the millimolar (10−3 ) to micromolar (10−6 ) range .
This necessitates the use of highly sensitive biophysical techniques for screening, such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) or X-ray crystallography.
Although they bind weakly, successful fragments are highly efficient binders; they form strong interactions relative to their small size.
This high-quality molecular recognition makes them excellent starting points for chemical elaboration.
Using the 3D structure of the fragment-protein complex as a guide, chemists evolve these initial hits into more potent lead compounds.
This can be achieved by extending the fragment with new functional groups to engage with adjacent regions on the protein surface, a strategy known as fragment growing.

Alternatively, two different fragments which bind in a similar region can be connected through fragment linking, or a single new molecule can be designed that incorporates the key features of multiple overlapping fragments in a process called fragment merging.
Since its adoption in the 1990s, FBDD has proven highly successful, leading to multiple approved drugs such as vemurafenib, venetoclax, and erdafitinib .

These hit-identification strategies are not mutually exclusive and are frequently combined: for example, the chemical structures of hits from a high-throughput screen might be used to build a pharmacophoric profile (a 3D map of the essential features a molecule needs to bind to the target) for generative design, or virtual screening used to prioritise designed compounds for synthesis and experimental testing.
Identified, confirmed hits are not yet drugs.
They are merely starting points that must be refined through two subsequent phases: hit-to-lead (H2L) and lead optimisation (LO).

The H2L phase aims to convert a promising hit into a ‘lead’ by exploring the surrounding chemical space to establish a robust structure-activity relationship (SAR) and improve initial potency and drug-like properties.

The subsequent LO phase is a more intensive, multi-parameter optimisation process that aims to polish the lead compound into a preclinical candidate, balancing high potency and selectivity with a favourable ADME-T profile .
This entire optimisation process is driven by the iterative design-make-testanalyse (DMTA) cycle.

In each cycle, new compound ideas are designed, synthesised, and evaluated in a panel of biological and physicochemical assays, and the resulting data is interpreted to inform the next round of design.
The design and analysis stages of this cycle rely heavily on the ligand-based and structure-based paradigms discussed previously.
In a ligand-based approach, the DMTA cycle is guided by interpreting the SAR from tested compounds.

Quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models might be built to predict the potency of new designs, or a pharmacophore model might be refined to better understand the features required for activity: chemists make iterative changes to the molecule and learn from the resulting data.
The cycle becomes more efficient and rational if a high-resolution target structure is available.
In this structure-based approach, chemists can directly visualise how molecules interact with the target.
For example, if a compound binds weakly, the structure may reveal a nearby hydrophobic pocket that is not being filled.
The next design can rationally add a group to occupy that pocket.
If a molecule is rapidly metabolised, the structure of a metabolic enzyme might show how to block the site of metabolism without disrupting on-target binding.
SBDD thus provides an atomic-level roadmap for solving this multi-parameter optimisation challenge .
The drug discovery stages detailed above present complex challenges.
Navigating the vastness of chemical space and understanding intricate structure-activity relationships are major bottlenecks that make this process slow and resource-intensive.
These problems are particularly well-suited to ML, which has shown promise at learning from complex data.
The following section will introduce the fundamental ML concepts that are applied to these challenges throughout this thesis.
In this section, we provide a very brief overview of the different machine learning architectures used in this thesis.
How they are actually applied to the problems described in section 1.2 will be reviewed in section 1.4.
ML is a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI) focused on the automated detection of patterns in data, which enables computer systems to uncover key insights and predict outcomes.
While the field is vast, most approaches share a common strategy: an algorithm learns to identify patterns from input data without being explicitly programmed.
The primary objective is for the resulting model to generalise from this experience and accurately interpret new, unseen inputs.
The landscape of ML is complex, with methods often stratified by paradigm, architecture, or application.
This can lead to confusion, particularly with terms like ‘AI’, ‘ML’, and ‘DL’ that are often used interchangeably despite their distinct meanings.
To help clarify these relationships and provide a conceptual map, we present a flowchart in Figure outlining the key methods under the umbrella of AI.
Following this flowchart, we will begin by introducing the foundational supervised learning paradigm.
We then move to the fundamental model architecture that forms the basis of modern deep learning: neural networks.
From there, we will explore the two architectures most commonly used in SBDD: convolutional neural networks and graph neural networks.
Finally, we will shift our focus from predictive models to the generative domain with an introduction to diffusion models.
This section is not intended as a comprehensive review of all of these topics; we simply aim to introduce the paradigms, architectures, and applications that are employed in the later chapters.

Supervised learning is a paradigm where the model learns a mapping function from input variables (X) to an output variable (y) based on a set of labelled training examples, D = {(xi , yi )}N the true function f such that y = f (x).
The model, parametrised by weights θ, learns to make predictions ŷ = f (x; θ) by minimising a loss function L(ŷ, y), which quantifies the error between the prediction and the ground truth.
This is typically an optimisation problem aimed at finding the optimal parameters θ∗ that minimise the expected loss over the entire data distribution.
In practice, this expectation is approximated by the empirical mean over the training data, which provides the objective used for gradient-based optimisation.
The primary tasks within supervised learning are regression, where y is a continuous value, and classification, where y is a discrete category.

They are composed of interconnected nodes, or neurons, typically organised in layers.
Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies a non-linear activation function, σ(·), to produce an output.

These models are trained using optimisation algorithms like stochastic gradient descent, with gradients calculated via the backpropagation algorithm .
Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule of calculus to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every model parameter θ, enabling updates according to the objective defined in eq.
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a specialised type of deep neural network designed for processing grid-like data, such as images .
Their key innovation is the convolutional layer, which leverages the principles of local connectivity and parameter sharing.
Instead of each neuron connecting to all neurons in the previous layer, it only connects to a small local region.
A filter, or kernel (K), with a set of learnable weights is slid across the input data (I), computing a dot product at each position.
This operation, known as a convolution, produces a feature map that highlights specific patterns like edges or textures.

By stacking these layers, CNNs can build a hierarchical representation of visual data.

Distinct from CNNs that operate on regular grids, graph neural networks (GNNs) are designed to work directly with data structured as graphs, G = (V, E), where V is a set of vertices (nodes) and E is a set of edges (connections) .
The core principle of GNNs is message passing, where each node aggregates information from its local neighbourhood to update its own state representation.

GNNs are thus able to learn from both node features and the graph’s topology.
While standard GNNs operate on abstract graph structures, many scientific applications require reasoning about physical systems in 3D space—like molecules.
For these, E(n) E(n) equivariant graph neural networks (EGNNs) are a critical extension.

A model is ‘equivariant” to a transformation (like rotation or translation) if transforming the input and then passing it through the model yields the same result as passing the original input through the model and then transforming the output (see Appendix A.1 for a more detailed explanation of invariance and equivariance).
This property is crucial because the physical properties of a system should not change based on its position or orientation in space.
EGNNs achieve this by explicitly incorporating node coordinates xi ∈ R3 into the message passing mechanism.
The updates are designed to be equivariant to isometries of Euclidean space (E(n)), meaning rotations, translations, and reflections.

where messages mij are made invariant to rotation by depending only on the squared distance between coordinates.
The feature updates ϕh and coordinate updates ϕx are learned functions, allowing the model to reason about both the graph structure and its physical geometry simultaneously.
As illustrated in Figure, diffusion models are not tied to a specific network architecture, but are instead a class of deep generative models.
These models aim to approximate the data distribution and generate new samples that are statistically indistinguishable from the training data.

Earlier approaches such as adversarial models (where a generator and discriminator compete to produce increasingly realistic samples) dominated generative modelling for several years, but were often limited by unstable training dynamics and mode collapse.
In contrast, diffusion models benefit from stable, likelihood-based training and have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a range of domains .
At their core, diffusion models learn to reverse a gradual noising process that transforms data into (approximately) Gaussian noise.
The procedure consists of two stages:
Forward process (fixed): A Markov chain that progressively corrupts a clean sample x0 into noise over T timesteps.
At each step t, the noised data xt is sampled from a Gaussian distribution:
where βt is a small, pre-defined variance schedule.
After sufficient steps, xT is close to isotropic Gaussian noise .
Reverse process (learned): A neural network (commonly a U-Net, though other architectures such as transformers are also used) is trained to denoise.
It predicts the added noise, ϵθ (xt , t), and thereby approximates the reverse conditional distribution pθ (xt−1 |xt ).
Training typically minimises a mean- squared error between the true noise ϵ and the prediction ϵθ .

Several variants of diffusion models exist, including continuous-time score-based models formulated via stochastic differential equations , deterministic samplers such as denoising diffusion implicit models , and alternative parameterisations (e.g. x0 - or v-prediction ).

A fuller taxonomy also distinguishes models by their training objectives, sampling strategies, and choice of architecture, but all share the same underlying principle: modelling data by learning to denoise corrupted samples.
