This suggests we might be able to use it to identify important bonds—and therefore atoms—involved in binding.

Having shown that PointVS is potentially capable of identifying important binding interactions, we next assessed whether it can be used as a method for extracting structural information from a number of bound structures, and hence used to guide molecule design.

To do this, we extracted hotspot maps from PointVS by performing edge attention attribution on fragment screen data, and compared the resulting hotspots to those found using a data-driven approach, the Hotspots API .
Our first test used the non-covalent bound structures available for Mpro.
The dataset available for this target is far more extensive than most targets will benefit from, as it is comprised of not only fragment-like molecules, but also follow-up compounds.
These follow-up compounds, which have been curated with the specific intention of targetting important protein atoms, consist of closely related compounds with the same basic scaffold.

Intuitively, the presence of high-quality compounds should result in PointVS being able to extract higher-quality hotspots, as the bound ligands were designed to interact with protein atoms that have been experimentally validated to be important.

We used this dataset as a starting point to verify that, given a selection of bound structures, PointVS can be used to identify these important protein atoms in a way that is useful for fragment elaboration.
The data was extracted from the fragalysis platform .
A full list detailing the structures used is given in Appendix A.3.
The hotspots identified by the Hotspots API and attribution with PointVS are shown in Fig 2.5a and b.
The hotspots of the two methods will not fall on exactly the same points, as the PointVS hotspots correspond to protein atoms, and the API hotspots to points in the binding pocket.
Still, the two methods clearly highlight very separate regions of the binding pocket as important.
As mentioned previously, the Mpro dataset contains a significant number of closelyrelated follow-up compounds with the same basic scaffold.

To ensure that PointVS is providing a novel insight into important binding regions in the pocket of Mpro and not highlighting important protein atoms by simply counting the number of times they are within close proximity of a ligand donor or acceptor atom, we used PLIP to extract the protein atoms that could be forming hydrogen bonds with ligand atoms for every bound structure.
We then defined any protein atom that was highlighted more than five times across the 152 bound structures as a PLIP hotspot.
This cutoff of five interactions resulted in only four hotspots being extracted.
These top four are shown in Fig 2.5c, and correspond to protein atoms that were highlighted by PLIP 146, 40, 9 and 5 times out of the possible 152.
All but one of the PLIP hotspots are within 2Å of one of the top five PointVS hotspots.

However, the top-ranking PLIP hotspot (which corresponds to a protein atom that forms a hydrogen bond in 146 of the 152 bound structures) is ranked second by PointVS, and the second PLIP hotspot (which PLIP identifies as interacting with ligand atoms in 40 structures) is ranked top by PointVS.

As the first PLIP hotspot is at most the length of one hydrogen bond away from a ligand acceptor in almost every structure, we would expect a geometry-based method to clearly identify it as the top hotspot, as PLIP does.
This is some evidence that PointVS is identifying important protein atoms with a more nuanced approach than simply counting interactions identified with geometric rules.

These results do not mean the PointVS hotspot extraction method is immune to being biased when supplied with fragment screens containing clusters of ligand donor and acceptor atoms, but it is a promising sign that it is not entirely biased by such clusters, and that PointVS is still able to look past them and identify other areas in the pocket as important.

This is a particularly useful finding, given that recent research into fragment screen libraries has highlighted that even screens designed to be diverse structurally still offer a limited exploration of protein pockets .

Given that PointVS identifies sites that are different from a traditional hotspot method and a geometry-based method, we next tested whether the high-scoring sites identified by PointVS are dependent on the size of the input fragment set.
To do this, we performed the same hotspot extraction process as before, but instead of using all of the bound structures of Mpro at once, we randomly sampled smaller sets from the collection.
We varied the size of the set sampled between 10 and 80.
This random sampling process was carried out 40 times for each dataset size.
We then performed the hotspot extraction process as before, and took the top five highest-scoring hotspots generated using PointVS with each randomly sampled set of fragment hits.
The results of this are shown in Fig 2.6, where we took samples of size 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80 from the available bound structures.

We see that when the hotspot maps are extracted from a smaller number of bound structures, a wider range of protein atoms are identified as being important; PointVS is less capable of consistently picking out the same five protein atoms every time, and increasing the number of bound structures given to PointVS results in more consistent hotspot maps being generated.

Nevertheless, we note that even when using the smallest datasets containing only 10 bound structures, the five hotspots that are identified when using the full fragment screen are the most commonly included, hence their darker colour in Fig 2.6.
This is a promising sign that attribution with PointVS could still be a useful tool for less well-studied targets.

Having demonstrated that the PointVS hotspots are consistent amongst themselves, and that they highlight different areas in the Mpro active site to the API hotspots, we assessed whether they correctly highlight important areas by performing fragment elaboration.

If PointVS is successfully identifying important interactions, molecules generated to satisfy the pharmacophoric constraints imposed by PointVS hotspots should be as good, if not better, than the molecules using the API hotspots.
For every target tested, the highest scoring elaborations by our ∆SLE20 metric were generated using the top five PointVS hotspots (Table).
Elaborations made using the hotspots ranked 6-10 by PointVS consistently have worse ∆SLE20 s than those ranked 1-5.

By contrast, the Hotspots API successfully identified ten high- scoring hotspots (indeed, on average, these top ten hotspots produced elaborations with higher standardised ligand efficiencies than the PointVS hotspots), but was unable to successfully rank them amongst themselves.
The accurate ranking of hotspots is important, as in real-world fragment-to-lead campaigns, only a small number of them can easily be targeted.
Within the PointVS hotspot scores, we see that the Mpro hotspots are lower scoring than those for the other two targets.
This can be attributed to the 109 starting fragments for Mpro being of higher quality, having been extracted from curated follow-up compounds rather than fragments.
The improvement that is made on them by elaborating is thus less significant.

This chapter covered the development of PointVS, an EGNN-based method for affinity prediction, and the first ML-based method for extracting important binding information from a target for molecule design.
During the development of PointVS, a commonly used benchmarking protocol for MLBSFs, CASF16, was found to overestimate their accuracy.
In light of this, PointVS was trained and tested on a filtered dataset, and hence encouraged to learn the rules governing intermolecular binding rather than memorise training data.

We showed that when trained on this filtered dataset, PointVS achieves comparable results to other leading scoring functions, providing some evidence that it is successfully identifying important binding interactions.

We provide further proof of this by performing attribution, and showing that PointVS is able to identify important interactions in line with those found by PLIP, a distance-based tool for profiling protein-ligand interactions.
Finally, we investigated how knowledge of important binding regions could be leveraged in other stages of the drug development pipeline; namely fragment elaboration.
We show that when provided with a set of bound structures, performing attribution on such structures yielded hotspot maps describing important protein atoms.
Using these in unison with a fragment elaboration tool, STRIFE, resulted in improved docking scores for the elaborated molecules compared to when hotspots were obtained with a data-based method.

This is further evidence that PointVS is not learning to memorise ligand information but to recognise important interactions, and additionally constitutes the first ML-based method of extracting structural information from a protein target in a way that is useful for fragment elaboration.

More broadly, our work demonstrates that attribution techniques, when applied to debiased models, can be useful for extracting structural information in a way that can be useful in molecule generation.
The success of FBDD depends on access to high-quality structural data and suitable fragment libraries.
In settings where this data cannot be generated (say, due to cost), or where exploring a broader swathe of chemical space is desirable, researchers use de novo design approaches.
These methods aim to generate entirely new molecular structures with desirable properties, offering a complementary path to fragment-based strategies (see chapter 1).
Among the most promising frameworks for de novo design are diffusion models, which have recently emerged as state-ofthe-art generative methods in both chemistry and beyond .
The following chapter explores how diffusion-based methods can be used for molecular design, and in particular, how the plausibility of the molecules they generate can be improved.
Unlike fragment elaboration methods like the one covered in the previous chapter, de novo drug design involves generating new molecules from scratch.
Diffusion models have recently gained popularity as a viable approach to this task thanks to their successful application in fields such as image and video generation .
However, they have been shown to have issues generating molecules of druglike sizes, struggling in particular with correct bond lengths, angles, and the overall internal energy of the molecules .
Addressing the fundamental challenge of generating physically plausible molecules is, therefore, a necessary first step towards effective diffusion-based de novo design.
In this chapter and the next, we focus on methods to increase the feasibility of druglike molecules generated by diffusion models.
The method we present in this chapter exploits the well-known utility of negative data as a resource in machine learning .

By including both positive and negative examples, the dataset teaches the model to recognise the boundaries of the valid chemical space, allowing it to distinguish reasonable structures from physically impossible ones and sample more effectively from the desirable regions.

While many generative molecular design models historically operated in 1D or 2D space , focus has recently shifted towards developing models capable of directly outputting both atom types and coordinates in 3D.
As covered more extensively in Chapter, autoregressive models were once prominent in this domain, generating 3D molecules by adding atoms and bonds iteratively .

However, such models suffer from an accumulation of errors during the generation process and do not fully capture the complexities of real-world scenarios due to their sequential nature, potentially losing global context.
To address these limitations, recent studies have turned to diffusion models, which iteratively denoise data points sampled from a prior distribution to generate samples.
Unlike autoregressive models, diffusion-based methods can simultaneously model local and global interactions between atoms.
Nevertheless, diffusion in molecule generation has faced criticism for yielding implausible outputs .

There have been ongoing efforts to improve the performance of models trained on small molecules such as those found in the QM9 dataset, and as such the models currently available are capable of reliably generating molecules of this size .

However, achieving success in generating larger molecules, as encountered in datasets like GEOM , remains challenging without incorporating additional techniques such as energy minimisation or docking.
In the work presented in this chapter, we focus on enhancing the ability of a diffusion model to generate plausible 3D druglike molecules.
To achieve this, we use the property-conditioning method developed by Hoogeboom et al. .

Instead of conditioning a model on pre-existing properties, we condition on conformer quality, training the model to not only generate molecules, but also to distinguish high- and low-quality chemical structures.
To achieve this, we generate distorted versions of each of the three datasets we evaluate the method on: QM9, GEOM, and a subset of ZINC.
We sample molecules from each dataset and apply random offsets to their original coordinates, based on a maximum distortion value.
Each distorted molecule is assigned a label representing the degree of warping applied and is added back to the dataset.
Nondistorted molecules are also labelled, identifying them as high-quality conformers.

Using these datasets of molecules with varying levels of quality, we train propertyconditioned models, encouraging the model to learn to label molecule validity while simultaneously training it to generate molecules.
First, we evaluate our conditioning method with EDM, the first E(3) equivariant diffusion model for molecule generation .

We experiment with two labelling methods: one, a distance-based metric representing the extent of the applied distortion, and two, an internal energy approximation calculated with the eXtended Tight Binding (XTB) program.
We then test it on two additional models: a geometry-complete diffusion model and a flow matching method , both designed to enhance the structural plausibility of generated molecules.

Since existing models already achieve strong performance on QM9, leaving little room or need for improvement, we focus on evaluating our approach on slightly larger, more chemically complex molecules.
To this end, we employ two datasets of druglike molecules: the GEOM dataset, and another derived from the ZINC database.
Our findings demonstrate that across the models tested, conditioning a model with low-quality conformers enables it to discern between favourable and unfavourable molecular conformations.
This allows us to target the area of the learned space corresponding to high-quality molecules, resulting in an improvement of the validity of generated molecules.
More broadly, this demonstrates the potential of supplementing molecule generation methodologies not solely with examples of desired molecules but also with instances exemplifying undesired outcomes.
Hoogeboom et al. introduced the first E(3) equivariant diffusion model (EDM) for generating 3D small molecules.
Since then, significant efforts have been made to modify the original EDM, whether to adapt the method for structure-based drug design or to enhance the validity of the generated molecules .
Notable examples of the latter include GCDM (Geometry-Complete Diffusion Model) and MolFM .
GCDM addresses the limitations of diffusion models that rely on molecule-agnostic and non-geometric graph neural networks (GNNs) for 3D graph denoising by introducing a geometry-complete approach.

The authors of EDM developed an extension to their method to carry out conditional molecule generation.
In this instance, property annotations are included alongside each of the molecules in the training dataset, and at inference, molecules can be generated with a desired value of this property.
We use this property-conditioning method to train models conditioned on conformer quality.
To implement this, we first generated datasets with 3D conformers of molecules of variable quality levels, and corresponding annotations.
We generated distorted versions of a subset of molecules from each of the datasets we used.
For each molecule, its 3D coordinates, represented as C = {(xi , yi , zi )} where i denotes the atom index, were obtained.
Subsequently, a random number D within the range of 0 to Dmax angstroms, labelled as the maximum distortion, was sampled:

This value represents the maximum distance in angstrom that could be added to atoms in that molecule: in other words, the sampled distortion value determines the maximum extent of perturbation to be applied to the molecule’s structure.
Following this, random offsets were generated within the range of 0 to the sampled distortion, D, for each dimension of every atom’s coordinates:
These offsets were then applied to the original coordinates:
Resulting in a ‘distorted’ version of the molecule.
This distorted molecule, along with its corresponding sampled distortion value D, was subsequently added to the training set.

Following the generation of the distorted datasets, we use the property-conditioning training protocol outlined by Hoogeboom et al. to train on them, using the distortion factor D as the property of interest, and follow the sampling protocol to generate molecules corresponding to D = 0Å .

When testing the internal energy conditioning approach, we used the same distorted dataset and employed XTB to calculate approximate internal energy values for all molecules, both distorted and non-distorted.
We then conditionally sampled from the model, this time enforcing D = Emin , where Emin is a fixed value for each dataset corresponding to the lowest internal energy annotation of any molecule in it.

For each model architecture, we follow their respective guidelines for training and sampling models, with the exception of cases for which pretrained models have been provided (EDM - QM9, GCDM - GEOMno h , and MolFM - GEOMno h ).

We then use each trained model to generate 1000 molecules, with the exception of models in the ablation tests, where we sampled 100 molecules per model to efficiently screen the effects of varying both distortion magnitudes and the ratio of distorted to non-distorted molecules.
Since these models output only atom types and coordinates, we adhered to the standard practice of using OpenBabel to assign bonds based on interatomic distances.
These post-processed molecules were first passed through RDKit’s sanitisation checks, giving an RDKit sanitisation pass rate.
All molecules were then evaluated using the PoseBusters test suite, which begins with its own sanitisation step - molecules failing this initial check automatically fail all subsequent tests.
PoseBusters then tests the physical validity of the molecule by bond pattern matching, correct tetrahedral chirality specification, and appropriate double bond stereochemistry.

The suite also assesses intramolecular validity through multiple geometric checks: bond lengths must fall within 0.75-1.25 times the expected bounds from distance geometry, bond angles must similarly be within 0.75-1.25 times their expected ranges, aromatic rings (5 or 6-membered) must maintain planarity within 0.25 Å , and aliphatic carbon-carbon double bonds must show appropriate planarity with their neighbouring atoms (within 0.25 Å ).
Additionally, PoseBusters checks for internal steric clashes by ensuring interatomic distances between non-covalently bound atoms exceed 0.7 times their lower geometric bounds.

Finally, it evaluates energetic feasibility by comparing the molecule’s calculated energy (using RDKit’s UFF) against an ensemble of 50 conformations generated via ETKDGV3 and relaxed using force field optimisation.
We report both the initial RDKit sanitisation pass rate and the number of molecules that successfully pass all seven non-sanitisation PoseBusters tests.

Additionally, we assess structural diversity among the generated molecules using the MOSES framework , and check for the presence of undesirable functional groups in each molecule using the REOS (Rapid Elimination of Swill ) functionality in the useful_rdkit_utils toolkit (see Appendix B.3).
For every statistic, we provide 95% confidence intervals computed using SciPy’s stats.bootstrap with 1,000 samples and the ‘percentile’ method .
To ensure consistency in our comparisons with pretrained baseline models, we use the same dataset splits and versions as those in the EDM paper.
For QM9, this corresponds to the train/validation/test split introduced by Anderson et al. , based on the 2014 version of QM9 .
For GEOM, we follow the split introduced by the EDM authors , which uses the 2022 version of the dataset .
To maintain consistency and allow for comparison with the models trained on these datasets, we follow the same splitting regime as proposed by Anderson et al. for our ZINC subset.
The QM9 dataset is a widely used benchmark dataset in quantum chemistry and machine learning research.
It consists of quantummechanical properties and 3D conformers of 130,000 small organic molecules with an average of 17.5 atoms (8.2 heavy atoms).
The QM9 dataset has been extensively used to develop and validate machine learning models for molecular property prediction.

However, it has also recently become the central benchmark for de novo molecule generation, particularly in the development of diffusion models , and as such, new diffusion models are capable of reliably generating molecules similar to those found in QM9.
While QM9 features only smaller-than-druglike molecules, GEOM is a larger-scale dataset of molecular conformers.

It features 430,000 molecules, of which 317,928 are mid-sized organic molecules from AICures and MoleculeNet , and 133,258 molecules are from QM9, resulting in an average molecule size of 44.4 atoms (20.1 heavy atoms).
For each molecule, a variable number of conformers are given along with their approximate internal energy as calculated with the XTB program.
From this dataset, Hoogeboom et al. retain the 30 lowest energy conformations for each molecule in their work.
Similar to Peng et al. , we use a version of GEOM from which hydrogen have been removed (GEOMno h ), as the positions of hydrogen atoms can often be inferred with a high level of confidence .
This not only reduces the computational demand of training, but also facilitates more effective learning of heavy atom placements.
This leads to the GEOMno h dataset becoming the quickest to train on among the druglike datasets.
We therefore use the GEOMno h dataset for conducting ablation tests.
ZINC is a database of commercially-available compounds containing over 230 million purchasable compounds in ready-to-dock, 3D formats.
We generate a training set by selecting a subset of 660,000 molecules from the druglike catalogue of the ZINC database.
Unlike GEOM, this subset is curated without repeat conformers.
Hydrogen atoms are not included, and the average molecule comprises 26.8 heavy atoms.
This section evaluates our proposed quality conditioning method.
First, we the present ablation tests carried out on the GEOMno h dataset to determine the optimal ratio and distortion level for our negative training examples.
Next, using these optimised parameters, we evaluate the performance of a conditional EDM on the QM9, GEOMno h , and ZINC datasets, comparing it directly to the unconditional model.
Finally, we assess the broader applicability of our quality conditioning approach by testing its effectiveness on two different models, GCDM and MolFM.
To identify the optimal proportion of distorted molecules and the required degree of distortion for effective conditional training, we performed ablation studies using the GEOMno h dataset.
This dataset was selected due to its inclusion of drug-like molecule sizes, unlike QM9, whilst being a more computationally tractable set to train than the ZINC dataset.
For these ablation studies, we sampled 100 molecules per model to efficiently screen the effects of varying both distortion magnitudes and the ratio of distorted to non-distorted molecules.

We introduced varying numbers of distorted molecules at different distortion levels (ranging from 0Å , indicating no distortion, to the maximum distortion, Dmax Å ) into the original GEOMno h dataset.
We defined dataset ratios based on the number of distorted and original molecules: for example, a 1:50 ratio indicates one distorted molecule was added for every fifty original molecules.

We evaluated each model’s performance by training conditioned models and sampling 100 molecules, ensuring that the samples were from the low-distortion-factor region of the learned space (formally, enforcing D = 0Å ).

The model trained on a dataset with a ratio of 1:50 distorted molecules and a maximum distortion of 0.25Å exhibited the joint highest RDKit parsability rate of 97%, and the highest PoseBusters pass rate at 81%.
While several models reached 97% RDKit sanitisation rates (namely 1:20, Dmax = 0.5Å and 1:50, Dmax = 0.5Å ), these models exhibited slightly lower PoseBusters pass rates (75% and 78%, respectively).
Increasing or decreasing Dmax further resulted in PoseBusters performance decreasing across all ratios, primarily due to failures in the internal energy test.

This observation suggests that if the training includes molecules that are too distorted, the model does not effectively learn to distinguish between subtly flawed and acceptable molecular structures.
Distorted molecules should therefore still bear some resemblance to realistic conformers, albeit with deliberately infeasible bond lengths and angles.

On the other hand, insufficient distortion compromises the effectiveness of the conditioning classifier, and the models struggle to distinguish between high-quality and low-quality conformations, leading to poor performance in generating desirable molecules.
These results demonstrate the concept of conditioned training on negative data, and give an idea of the extent of distortion and frequency of distorted molecules to add.
We used a ratio of 1:50, and Dmax = 0.25Å for all subsequent tests, but note that any dataset would likely benefit from different exact values of these parameters.
Dmax (Å ) We also examined the quality of molecules generated when sampling from the low-quality region of the learned space (formally, D = Dmax Å ).
The results of this are shown in Appendix B.1.
The molecules sampled using D= Dmax Å are, as expected, worse than both the conditioned models and the baseline model in terms of PoseBusters pass rates, with the highest reaching only 53%.
This poor performance is mainly attributed to failures in the internal energy test.

Having established the parameters for conditional training datasets in terms of quantity of distorted molecules and extent of distortion, we move on to testing this approach with the other datasets, QM9 and ZINC.
Following the results of the ablation tests, we generated conditional versions of each dataset using parameters Dmax = 0.25Å and a distorted:non-distorted molecule ratio of 1:50.
After training conditional models on these modified datasets, we sampled 1,000 molecules from each and evaluated their quality using RDKit and PoseBusters.
The results of this evaluation are presented in Table.
Our baseline analysis reveals a clear relationship between molecule size and model performance.
The QM9 dataset, comprising molecules smaller than 9 heavy atoms had the highest baseline performance with RDKit and PoseBusters pass rates of 92.2% and 81.1%, respectively.
The non-conditioned EDM model performed exceptionally well with QM9, surpassing all conditional variants across both evaluation metrics.

This superior performance may be attributed to EDM’s specific development for QM9, coupled with the dataset’s smaller molecular size, which appears to enable better discrimination between high-quality and low-quality conformers without requiring examples of the latter.
The GEOMno h dataset also showed strong baseline performance as assessed with RDKit, with generated molecules achieving a pass rate of 84.7%.
However, the more stringent PoseBusters tests presented more of a challenge, with generated molecules presenting a pass rate of 62.2% for PoseBusters.
This can particularly be attributed to the tests concerning bond lengths (65.6% pass rate), bond angles (73.8%), connectivity (74.4%) and internal energy (75.2%).
Conditional training improved these metrics substantially, reaching pass rates of 96.6% (bond lengths), 93.7% (bond angles), 89.4% (connectivity) and 87.7% (internal energy).
Minor improvements were also seen in the steric clash tests (97.8% to 100%).
The baseline model trained on the ZINC subset exhibited markedly lower performance than the other two datasets, with RDKit sanitisation pass rates of 70.6% and PoseBusters pass rates of 40.0%.
The most prevalent failures occurred in bond lengths and atom connectivity, with pass rates of only 65.0% and 62.4%, respectively.
This performance decline relative to GEOMno h may be attributed to two factors.

Firstly, the ZINC dataset’s increased diversity, featuring unique conformers rather than multiple conformers per molecule (as found in GEOMno h ), may cause the model to prioritise learning atom types over optimising 3D conformer generation.
Secondly, and perhaps more significantly, the compositional differences between datasets may play a crucial role.
While the ZINC subset exclusively contains medium-sized compounds, GEOMno h incorporates the entire QM9 dataset, resulting in a smaller average molecule size.
Conditional training on the ZINC dataset yielded improved RDKit sanitisation rates and PoseBusters scores.

The most notable improvement was observed in the ZINC model’s atom connectivity pass rate, which increased from 62.4% to 95.7%, but improvements were also seen in the pass rates of the tests assessing bond lengths (65.0% to 94.1%), bond angles (75.3% to 93.7%), internal steric clash These results indicate that the baseline EDM’s performance degrades when generating larger molecules, often yielding implausible structures.
Our conditioning method at least partially helps mitigate this decline, increasing the output proportion of high-quality molecules.
We next investigate the use of a more scientifically grounded labelling of the molecules—specifically, using internal energy approximations—for this conditioning process.
The XTB program is a computational chemistry software package used for molecular modelling and simulations.
It is based on the semiempirical tight-binding approach, which approximates the electronic structure of molecules using a simplified set of parameters derived from quantum mechanics.
XTB extends traditional tight-binding methods by incorporating additional empirical corrections to improve the accuracy of calculated properties.
It is well-suited for studying large molecular systems where the computational cost of more accurate methods such as density functional theory (DFT) becomes prohibitive.
We use the default implementation of XTB (GFN2-xTB) to perform singlepoint energy calculations for each of the molecules, both distorted and original, for QM9, GEOMno h , and our ZINC dataset.
For the original GEOM dataset, the original conformers have energy annotations calculated with the same method, so we only carry out this calculation for the distorted molecules.

We carry out this process using two different annotation types: a ‘distortion factor’, a quantity that represents the extent to which the coordinates have been altered, and an internal energy value, obtained by scoring both original and distorted conformers with the extended tight binding program (XTB) .
We’ve observed that for medium-sized, drug-like compounds, conditioning on a distance-based distortion factor results in improvements for RDKit sanitisation and PoseBusters tests.

To investigate whether using a potentially more meaningful label (specifically, an internal energy value obtained using XTB) improves the conditioned models, we used the datasets generated with the previous distortion process.
The distorted molecules were then passed through an XTB single-point energy calculation.
The same calculation was applied to all high-quality, non- distorted molecules in all datasets, excluding the original GEOM dataset, which already has energy annotations calculated with XTB.

We then trained each of the models conditionally, and once trained, we sampled 100 molecules from each, this time enforcing D = Emin , where Emin is a fixed value for each dataset corresponding to the lowest internal energy annotation of any molecule in it.
Then we once again assessed all 100 molecules using RDKit and PoseBusters (Table).
As observed when conditioning on distortion factor, the model trained on QM9 generated lower quality molecules when conditioning with internal energy was carried out.
Conversely, conditionally training EDM on GEOMno h with internal energy resulted in increased performance compared to both the baseline and the conditioned model using the distance distortion factor.
The RDKit and PoseBusters pass rates reached 98% and 84%, respectively.
The model trained on ZINC, however, exhibited a decrease in both RDKit and PoseBusters pass rate.
These pass rates were also lower than those of the molecules generated with the ZINC model trained conditionally on distortion factor.
When using the distance-based distortion factor, we enforced D=0Å when sampling, as this represented molecules that had not undergone any distortion.
The distortion factor, ranging from 0Å to Dmax Å , provides a straightforward measure of how much the structure of a molecule has been altered.
In contrast, internal energy values, although physically meaningful, are challenging to compare directly between different molecules.

Each molecule can have a low internal energy corresponding to a high-quality conformer and a high one corresponding to a low-quality conformer, but the lowest energy conformers of some molecules may still have higher energy values than the highest energy annotations of others.
This inconsistency likely contributed to the observed performance decreases when conditioning on internal energy.

In this work, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of including low-quality conformers in a training set and conditioning a diffusion model on a label representing conformer quality to enhance the generation of high-quality druglike molecules.
By leveraging datasets derived from GEOM and ZINC, alongside a conditioning method proposed by Hoogeboom et al., we have successfully improved the validity of generated molecules.

Our approach, which focuses on sampling molecules with labels corresponding to low distortion factors, leads to enhancements in RDKit parsability and validity as assessed by PoseBusters for the original EDM, as well as for a subsequent diffusion model, GCDM.

We also explored conditioning on internal energy calculated with XTB as an alternative to the distortion factor, but found that the distance-based distortion metric proved more effective, likely due to challenges in comparing absolute energy values across diverse molecular structures.
The method shows strongest improvements for diffusion-based models, particularly those built on the EDM framework, which comprise a significant portion of current 3D molecule generation approaches.

Testing on MolFM, a flow-matching architecture, yielded inconsistent results across datasets, suggesting that the conditioning approach may interact differently with non-diffusion-based generative models.
The approach is most effective for datasets containing larger, drug-like molecules, as demonstrated by our results with GEOMno h and ZINC.

This can be explained mechanistically; larger molecules have more complex conformational spaces where explicit examples of invalid states help define the boundary between high-quality and low-quality conformers.
Conversely, the method provides limited benefits for datasets like QM9 where molecules are small (fewer than 9 heavy atoms) and have constrained conformational spaces.
In these cases, it appears models can effectively learn to distinguish valid from invalid conformations from the training data alone.
Our findings underscore the importance of considering the quality of conformers in molecule generation processes.

The results show that by training models to discern between favourable and unfavourable molecular conformations, we can selectively sample from the high-quality region of learned space, resulting in significant improvements in the validity of generated molecules.

Moving forward, further research could explore why quality conditioning is effective for certain architectures but not others, and investigate alternative labelling schemes that might generalise across different generative modelling approaches.
Additionally, investigating the applicability of our approach to other areas of molecular design and exploration could yield valuable insights for drug discovery and beyond.
Overall, our study provides a promising avenue for generating valid drug-sized molecules efficiently and effectively using diffusion-based architectures.
Having established the effectiveness of this strategy, we next explore a complementary approach that addresses the same challenge from a different angle.

The following chapter covers a fragment-based method that aims to enforce validity not by refining the training data, but by directly constructing molecules from pre-validated chemical building blocks during the generation process itself.
As highlighted in the previous chapter, diffusion models applied to molecule generation tasks frequently produce molecular structures with physically unrealistic bond geometries.
Post-processing techniques and filtering have been used as a practical workaround, but do not solve the underlying problem: the inability of diffusion models to learn fundamental chemical principles.
A possible explanation for this is that the generative task itself (arranging individual atoms in 3D space while respecting physical laws) is too complex for the models to learn.
This chapter documents an attempt to test this hypothesis and help resolve the issue by simplifying the problem.
The proposed method uses pre-assembled, chemically valid fragments, or ‘blocks’, as the primary building units instead of individual atoms.

The goal was twofold: first, to reduce the geometric complexity the model needed to handle, and second, to potentially improve the synthesisability of the resulting molecules by using known chemical fragments.
However, this approach presented its own challenges, particularly in developing an effective spatial representation for these non-symmetrical, inconsistent blocks.
This chapter details the different approaches tested, and then provides a brief review of the relevant papers that have been released since this work was carried out.
Generative diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable success in diverse domains, for example, being capable of producing high-fidelity images and text from latent noise .
However, their application to 3D generative chemistry has been met with challenges.

A primary limitation of current atomistic diffusion models is their frequent generation of molecules with unrealistic bond lengths and angles, resulting in chemically and physically implausible structures .

While computational methods such as energy minimisation or redocking can be employed as post-processing steps to correct these geometric inconsistencies, they do not address the fundamental deficiency: that the models have failed to internalise the basic principles of molecular geometry and stereochemistry.

This failure raises questions about their utility for more sophisticated tasks, such as SBDD, as a model that cannot generate small molecules obeying the laws of physics is unlikely to effectively extract and utilise the binding information of a protein pocket.
This chapter covers an alternative approach designed to mitigate this core problem by fundamentally simplifying the generative task.
We hypothesise that the difficulty of arranging a large number of individual atoms in continuous 3D space is a primary contributor to the poor quality of generated geometries.
Consequently, we propose a shift in the generative unit from atoms to molecular fragments or ‘blocks’: rigid, common substructures found within druglike small molecules.
This fragment-based approach is motivated by two key potential benefits.
The first and most central benefit is the reduction of the problem’s dimensionality.
By assembling molecules from larger, pre-validated substructures, the model is no longer required to learn the precise bond length and angle for every atomic connection.
Instead, it must learn the relative position and orientation of a smaller number of blocks.
The ineffectiveness of many atom-based models suggests that the simultaneous optimisation of all atomic coordinates is a task of prohibitive difficulty.
Our approach aims to make the problem more tractable by abstracting away the low-level geometric details, allowing the model to focus on the higherlevel organisation of the molecule.
While this may inherently limit the chemical novelty of the generated outputs, it provides a more constrained and potentially more learnable generative pathway.
The second motivation is grounded in the practicalities of the broader drug discovery pipeline.

A persistent criticism of many in silico design methods is the poor synthesisability of the molecules they produce, an issue which is in part due to the computational prediction of synthetic accessibility, cost, and complexity remaining a largely unsolved problem .

A fragment-based method offers a potential avenue to address this; by constructing molecules from a library of known, readily available, and inexpensive building blocks (such as a commercial library like the Enamine REAL database ) the resulting compounds could be inherently more amenable to practical synthesis.

Although the model could still propose challenging or unfeasible linkages between these blocks, this strategy should, on average, reduce the synthetic cost and complexity of the generated molecular library.
To tackle this task, we adapted the Equivariant Diffusion Model, or EDM , the same architecture used in Chapter, to operate on substructural blocks instead of individual atoms.
This required several modifications to the modelling pipeline.
First, a molecular dataset, GEOM, was processed to deconstruct each entry into a set of constituent fragments.
Subsequently, the model’s input features were redefined; the categorical variables were expanded to encode the identity of each block type, rather than just atom types.

The continuous spatial variables were also modified to represent the position and orientation of these blocks, moving from a simple centroid representation to a more complex descriptor incorporating rotational information.
The model was then trained following the same method as the atomic model.
Ultimately, this investigation revealed that replacing the atomistic representation with a substructure-based one is a non-trivial task that presented its own challenges.
Despite exploring multiple representational strategies, the highest-performing fragment-based model demonstrated inferior performance compared to the original atomistic baseline.

A central difficulty was the geometric complexity of the fragments themselves; they are not simple, symmetric points that can be adequately described by a centroid alone, yet representing their rotation in a consistent and learnable manner across a diverse set of shapes proved difficult.
This chapter describes the various approaches tested, a brief overview of the results obtained, and a concluding overview of related work that has since been pursued in this area.

At its core, the EDM model treats a molecule as a collection of atoms, where each atom, i, has two key properties: coordinates, xi , and categorical information hi , encompassing discrete features like charge and atom type, represented as one-hot vectors.
An entire molecule is therefore a set of these coordinate and feature vectors, and the goal of the model is to learn the joint probability distribution p(x, h).
To learn this distribution, the model uses a diffusion process.

It first learns a forward process that systematically corrupts the molecule’s two variable types: it adds Gaussian noise to the continuous coordinates and applies random transitions to the discrete categorical atom types, until only a random cloud remains.
The core of the model is an E(3) equivariant neural network trained to reverse this dual noising.

Starting from random noise, this network simultaneously denoises the continuous positions and predicts the correct discrete atom types, step-by-step, to generate a new, physically plausible arrangement of atoms.
At inference, the generation of a molecule starts by sampling a cloud of random 3D coordinates from a Gaussian distribution and assigning a random chemical type to each point.
This initial noisy state is then iteratively refined by a pre- trained E(3) equivariant network that runs a reverse diffusion process.

At each step, this single network takes the molecule’s current noisy coordinates and atom types and simultaneously predicts two distinct outputs: the noise vector for the continuous coordinates and the probability distribution of the original, ‘clean’ discrete atom types.

This information is used to update the state to a less noisy version for the next step—calculating the new coordinates and sampling the new atom types from their respective reverse distributions—until the process finishes and yields a complete 3D atomic structure, from which bonds are inferred using Open Babel .
Adapting our diffusion method from an atomistic to a block-based representation involved several key changes.
First, we redefined the coordinates, xi , to represent block centroids instead of atoms.
Our initial model used a simple 3D vector for each block’s position, though this was later changed to three 3D vectors to model both position and orientation explicitly.
The feature space was also updated.

The one-hot encoding scheme was changed from handling a few atom types (5 different types for QM9 or 16 for GEOM) to at least 50 unique block types (see section 4.3.2.2 for more details), significantly increasing its dimensionality.
The most significant adaptation was to the final reconstruction process.
Unlike the atomistic model where bonds are directly inferred from generated atoms using Open Babel , the block-based model requires an extra step.
After sampling, a 3D conformer for each block is generated with RDKit.

This conformer is then either translated to the sampled centroid coordinates (centroid-only method) or transformed to align with the plane and in-plane vectors (rotation-aware method) to place and orient it.
Finally, after assembling all the positioned blocks, their existing bonds are stripped, and the complete atomistic structure is passed to Open Babel to determine the final molecule.
The first decomposition was carried out on the QM9 dataset .

However, the small size of QM9’s molecules, which average 8.2 heavy atoms (see chapter 3 for an in-depth description of QM9 and GEOM), meant they rarely decomposed into more than two blocks, limiting the model’s ability to learn complex arrangements.
Consequently, the larger and more structurally diverse GEOM dataset was adopted.
GEOM’s inclusion of larger, drug-like compounds provided the necessary molecular complexity to try and train a robust model capable of generating more elaborate multi-block structures.

Regular BRICS decomposition The Breaking of Retrosynthetically Interesting Chemical Substructures (BRICS) algorithm provides a rule-based method for molecular decomposition by identifying and cleaving 16 types of chemical bonds that correspond to common and synthetically feasible reactions.

This procedure breaks down a chemical compound into a set of fragments, which are then classified into ‘bricks’, significant chemical moieties with at least four heavy atoms, and the ‘linkers’ that connect them.
For this work, the decomposition was implemented using the RDKit library .
The BRICS.BreakBRICSBonds function was first applied to each ligand, followed by Chem.GetMolFrags to separate the resulting structure into a list of individual fragment molecules.
As per the RDKit implementation, this process leaves isotopically-labelled dummy atoms at the cleavage points.
To ensure this additional information wasn’t passed into the model, these dummy atoms were removed.

Carrying out BRICS decomposition on the full GEOM dataset results in over 14,000 unique blocks (with just under 30% appearing only once), a prohibitively large number of types to expect the model to learn to place.
To try and reduce this, we filtered blocks according to how many times they appeared, ultimately choosing to only keep blocks which arose more than 100 times, resulting in 172 different block types.
The molecules in GEOM were then filtered such that any containing blocks outside of these 172 types were removed from the dataset, resulting in a dataset size of 56,281 molecules.

Decomposition with standardised fragments As an initial exploration into a more hierarchical generative strategy, we developed a method to standardise the raw BRICS fragments into a more manageable set of building blocks.

The primary motivation for this was to reduce the dimensionality of the categorical feature space for the model’s one-hot encoding, avoiding the complexity of treating every unique BRICS fragment as a distinct category.
The process began by filtering out molecules containing overly complex fragments, such as those with large ring systems (more than 7 members).
All acyclic structures and exocyclic atoms were then decomposed into their constituent individual atoms.
Ring systems were preserved as single units but were standardised into a small set of canonical types based on their size and aromaticity.

This strategy yielded a very simplified representation where each molecule is described as a collection of these fundamental building blocks (either canonical rings or individual atoms) each retaining its original 3D spatial information.
Carrying this process out on the GEOM dataset resulted in a final dataset of 62,746 molecules, described with only 23 block or atom types (shown in Fig 4.2).

Example molecule to decompose Method 1: standard BRICS Method 2: reduced block library BRICS This standardisation approach was conceived as the foundation for a potential two-stage generative strategy.

In this hierarchical framework, the primary diffusion model would first be responsible for generating a valid molecular scaffold using the simplified vocabulary of canonical rings and individual atoms.
A subsequent, specialised process could then be used to refine this basic structure by replacing the generic canonical rings with more specific, chemically diverse analogues.
This ‘decoration’ step could be guided by additional data, such as pharmacophoric hotspot maps from a target protein pocket, to tailor the final molecule to a specific objective.
This separation of tasks aims to deconstruct the complex task of molecule generation into the more manageable sub-problems of scaffold assembly and subsequent conditioned refinement.
To equip the model with a more detailed understanding of each fragment’s orientation, we moved beyond a simple centroid representation.

Inspired by the local coordinate frames used in models like AlphaFold , our goal was to explicitly encode both the position and the 3D orientation of each building block generated by our decomposition strategies.
Each fragment was encoded as three 3D vectors.
The first represents the geometric centroid (mean atomic coordinates), while the other two provide an approximate orientation.
For fragments with three or more atoms, a best-fit plane was computed from atomic coordinates using the scikit-spatial library.
The plane normal served as the first orientation vector.
To define an in-plane axis, we projected the vector between the two most distant atoms onto the plane.
For fused ring systems of different sizes, the direction was defined as pointing from the larger ring to the smaller ring.
This procedure is intentionally simple and comes with limitations.
For many fragments there are multiple equally distant atom pairs, so the chosen in-plane axis is not unique.
In symmetric cases such as benzene, three equivalent atom pairs exist, meaning the same fragment can be represented with orientations rotated by 60°from one another.
For less symmetric fused systems, two solutions exist, leading to an uncertainty of around 20°.
These ambiguities are not unstable but non-deterministic, reflecting the fact that no single canonical orientation can be defined without hard-coded rules for each fragment.
For very small fragments (fewer than three atoms), where no plane can be defined, we assigned placeholder values for the orientation vectors and masked them during training.
Overall, this heuristic is a rough approximation: it does not resolve chirality and introduces rotational ambiguity for many blocks.

Nevertheless, it provides a richer description than centroid-only features, enabling the model to access useful information about relative orientation that would otherwise be lost, while remaining tractable for a large and diverse fragment library.
To assess the quality of the generated molecules, our initial strategy was to employ the same quantitative metrics used in Chapter, namely PoseBusters and RDKit sanitisation checks.

However, in practice, the pass rates for both assessments were very low, so most of our analysis shifted to rely predominantly on qualitative visual inspection to diagnose the specific structural and chemical issues responsible for these failures.

Initial experiments were conducted using only the basic BRICS decomposition method, as preliminary results quickly highlighted significant issues arising from the lack of rotational information (see Figure).
To isolate and quantify this problem, we performed a control experiment to establish the theoretical upper bound on reconstruction accuracy for a centroid-only approach.

For this, we took a subset of 100 molecules from our pre-processed GEOM dataset and fed their ground-truth BRICS fragments and centroid coordinates directly into our reconstruction pipeline, bypassing the generative model entirely.
Even with this idealised input, only 48 of the 100 molecules passed RDKit sanitisation checks.

This 48% success rate reveals a fundamental limitation of the representation itself; even with perfect block placement, the ambiguity in fragment orientation leads to chemically invalid structures more than half the time.
This finding provides critical context for the much lower RDKit sanitisation pass rate of approximately 4% observed for molecules generated by the full diffusion model.
This lower rate is a product of two compounding factors: the model’s own errors in learning the placement task, and the inherent flaws of the centroid-only representation.
To address this primary limitation, it became clear that explicitly incorporating rotational information was an essential next step.
As an initial attempt to address the rotational ambiguity observed in the centroidonly approach, we tested a simple geometric post-processing step.
Rather than encoding orientation as additional model inputs, this method attempted to standardise fragment orientations during reconstruction.
For each generated fragment, we computed its best-fit plane using the same procedure described above.
This plane was then aligned to a global plane—found by fitting a plane to the sampled centroids—using a rigid rotation.
The fragment was then translated to place its centroid at the model’s predicted coordinates.
This approach aimed to remove rotational degrees of freedom entirely by imposing a standard orientation on all fragments.

However, as shown in Table, this method achieved only a 10.8% RDKit sanitisation pass rate; an improvement over the 4% of the unaligned centroid-only model, but still substantially worse than the atomic model.
Visual inspection revealed that the primary failure mode was incorrect connectivity between fragments.
While individual fragments were now consistently oriented, the fixed canonical orientation was often geometrically incompatible with the correct bonding geometry required to connect adjacent blocks.

This result demonstrated that fragment orientation cannot be handled through post-processing alone; the orientation must be learned and predicted by the model as part of the generative process, motivating the development of the full rotation-aware representation tested next.

Following the analysis of the centroid-only models, we incorporated the position and orientation vectors into two existing frameworks: the full BRICS decomposition and the reduced-library BRICS method.
To directly measure the impact of this new representation, we first repeated the reconstruction control experiment described previously.

Using the ground-truth coordinates and the new orientation vectors for 100 molecules from the full BRICS dataset, our reconstruction pipeline successfully produced 89 molecules that passed RDKit sanitisation checks.

This represents a dramatic improvement from the 48% success rate of the centroid-only approach and confirms that our orientation descriptor, while imperfect, provides substantial and valuable information for molecular reconstruction.
Next, we assessed the performance of the full generative models.
For each of the two methods, 1000 molecules were sampled and subjected to the same RDKit sanitisation check.
The model using the full BRICS library achieved a pass rate of 27.2%.
The model trained on the more constrained, reduced-library BRICS dataset performed significantly better, achieving a pass rate of 51.7%.

While the inclusion of rotational information yielded a marked improvement over the centroid-only models, these results still fall well short of the 84.7% pass rate achieved by the fully atomistic model.
The large gap suggests that the primary challenge lies not just in the model’s ability to place fragments, but in the inherent inconsistency of the fragments themselves.

The geometric diversity of the substructures produced by BRICS decomposition appears too great to allow for the definition of a consistent and reliable local coordinate system using simple geometric heuristics.
Since the completion of this work, significant progress has been made in block-based and hierarchical generative models.
Several key approaches have emerged that successfully address the challenges identified in our study, which are outlined below.
HierDiff introduced a ‘coarse-to-fine’ hierarchical strategy that directly addresses the atom-bond inconsistency issues inherent in simpler fragment-based models.
Its fragment vocabulary, in contrast to our use of reactionbased BRICS rules, is constructed by decomposing a large chemical dataset at all rotatable, non-ring single bonds.
The generative process first uses diffusion to arrange these coarse nodes in 3D space.
Subsequently, a decoder module, built with an E(n)-Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN), is tasked with generating the final atomistic structure.

This decoder takes the 3D positions of the coarse nodes as input and directly generates the coordinates for all constituent atoms, thereby solving the orientation problem through a learned, end-to-end process rather than a predefined geometric heuristic.
This approach proved highly effective, achieving over 94% molecular validity on standard benchmarks when trained on GEOM.
Another successful implementation of a block-based philosophy is found in CMD- GEN , a structure-based design tool that uses a hybrid, multi-stage pipeline.

Similar to our work, it begins by arranging coarse-grained pseudo-atoms in 3D space using a diffusion model; however, rather than representing arbitrary fragments, these represent pharmacophoric points.
Following this, the framework switches to an autoregressive model, which takes the fixed pharmacophore points as a blueprint and constructs the 2D molecular graph atom-by-atom.

This separation of tasks—using diffusion for the continuous spatial problem and an autoregressive model for the discrete graph problem—enables CMD-GEN to tackle the complex task of conditioned, in-pocket generation, achieving validity rates of 97.5%.
Finally, the principle of a substructure-aware process was extended beyond de novo generation to the task of conformer generation in SubGDiff .
Its method involves adding noise to randomly selected connected subgraphs rather than to individual atoms.

By forcing the denoising network to predict the original state from this partial corruption, the model learns the internal geometry of stable chemical sub-units, leading to a more accurate representation of local chemical environments.

While this demonstrates the utility of a substructure-aware approach, it is important to note that conformational generation is a distinct task from de novo generation, making a direct comparison of success rates with the other methods impossible.
This work investigated the adaptation of a successful atomistic diffusion model to a block-based framework for molecular generation.
Our exploration revealed that the choice of fragment representation is a critical determinant of model performance.
Initial models using a simple centroid-only representation were fundamentally capped, unable to exceed a theoretical reconstruction accuracy of 48% due to rotational ambiguity.

The introduction of an explicit 9-dimensional orientation vector helped somewhat alleviate this issue, improving reconstruction fidelity and boosting the final model’s RDKit sanitisation pass rate to a peak of 51.7% with a reduced BRICS fragment library.
Despite these advances, the block-based models did not approach the 85% pass rate of the original atomistic framework.
Our analysis indicates that the primary bottleneck is the high geometric variance within the chemically-derived BRICS fragments.
This diversity prevents simple geometric heuristics from defining a consistent and reliable local coordinate system, which is essential for accurate placement and reconstruction by the model.
The challenges encountered in this work are reflective of the broader difficulties in fragment-based generation, and the successes of subsequent models offer a clear path forward.

The consistent theme among effective hierarchical models like HierDiff is the use of a dedicated decoder module—typically an equivariant neural network— tasked specifically with translating the coarse-grained representation into a valid atomistic structure.
This learned, end-to-end approach to assembly and orientation proves more robust than the predefined geometric heuristics we employed.
Therefore, future research in this area should prioritise the development of these hierarchical architectures.

Combining a simplified and standardised fragment vocabulary, as explored in our own work, with an equivariant decoder represents a promising direction for realising the full potential of block-based molecular generation.
The process of fitting an atomic structure to the 3D density map produced by cryo-EM demands high levels of expertise, time and labour.

One way to increase speed and improve quality of output can be to use an in silico prediction as a starting point, and recent advances in protein structure prediction have made high- quality starting points readily available.

However, when structure prediction models perform poorly on targets that are large or outside of their training data distribution, and these types of systems are some of the primary use cases for cryo-EM.
In this chapter, we provide an overview of our preliminary work on conditioning the inference of models based on AlphaFold 2 (OpenFold) and AlphaFold 3 (Boltz-2) with cryo-EM data.
For the first of these, we explored interventions within the structure module, targeting various levels of protein representation—from the single representation to the Cartesian coordinates.

Ultimately, we found this method to be insufficient in instances where the model’s unconstrained prediction was poor, as large-scale rearrangements proved impossible without causing the model to generate disordered or non-physical conformations.
Next, we investigated a similar approach using Boltz-2.

We again implemented conditioning within the structure module, and found this implementation to be slightly more robust, but still ultimately incapable of making the necessary large-scale rearrangements.

We next took inspiration from the work of Fadini et al. 2025 and Raghu et al. 2025, two implementations of similar, cryo-EM conditioning of structure prediction methods, who reported greater improvements when focusing on earlier stages in the pipeline.
We therefore introduced an MSA subsampling approach, similar to that of ROCKET , which allows randomness to be injected into Boltz-2.

While this allows the model to escape local energetic minima and explore conformations more consistent with the experimental data, our method still struggles to induce the large-scale improvements required for certain targets.
Our current investigation is also limited by key simplifications, such as the use of simulated maps and pre-alignment with the crystal structure, which must be addressed for a robust assessment.
In this chapter, we report our initial findings and highlight the future directions for this project.
As described in Chapter, resolving the 3D structure of a protein is important for many applications in biology and medicine, and particularly in the field of small molecule drug design.

A high-resolution model of a target protein not only allows researchers to understand the precise geometry of its binding sites, enabling the informed design of small molecule binders, but is also important earlier in the drug design pipeline at the target identification stage: seeing the structure helps shed light on the protein’s mechanism of action, helping researchers to validate its suitability as a therapeutic target.
Cryo-EM has become an increasingly popular method for structure determination, with the number of new structures available in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) growing exponentially .
This experimental technique relies on averaging data from thousands, or even millions, of projection images of identical macromolecular particles frozen in vitreous ice.
This averaging process limits the final resolution of the map, making it challenging to resolve the precise location of individual atoms.

Huge progress has been made in this resolution challenge (75.7% of the structures reported in 2024 had resolutions better than 4Å ), but at worse resolutions, placing all atoms correctly is near impossible .

Furthermore, many large and dynamic biological systems may never reach atomic resolution due to inherent flexibility, meaning that methods for model building at resolutions worse than 4Å remain essential.
To move from a low-resolution density map to an atomic structure, experimentalists have traditionally relied on manual intervention.
This often involves using a starting model, which is then refined using interactive 3D visualisation software .
The appearance of accurate structure predictors, most notably AlphaFold2 , has popularised fully automated implementations of this “predict then refine” strategy.
In this paradigm, an AlphaFold prediction is used as a starting model, which is then refined to fit into the experimental density .

However, these methods can face issues like mis-assignment of peptide-bond geometry and local sequence misalignment, particularly if the initial prediction differs substantially from the conformation captured in the map .
An alternative paradigm, which we explore in this work, is to move beyond these serial “predict then refine” methods.
Instead of using the experimental map as a final target for refinement, we directly integrate it into the AlphaFold prediction process itself.
By conditioning the prediction with the map, we aim to guide the model towards the experimentally observed conformation from the outset, rather than attempting to correct it post-hoc.
This concept of conditioning the inference stage of AlphaFold with cryo-EM data has been demonstrated by two recent studies.

The first of these, ROCKET , performs structure optimisation in AlphaFold 2’s internal coevolutionary embedding space, rather than Cartesian coordinates, to better sample large-scale conformational changes.
The second, Cryo-Boltz , guides the sampling trajectory of the diffusion-based structure model using constraints derived from the density map.
We present an early-stage exploration of conditioning strategies using both an AlphaFold 2-based model (OpenFold) and an AlphaFold 3-based model (Boltz-2).

We first show that interventions within the structure module, while effective for local refinement, are insufficient to induce the large-scale conformational changes required to match the experimental density, frequently leading to disordered or non- physical structures.
Inspired by the recent findings in ROCKET and CryoBoltz that highlight the importance of earlier pipeline stages, we introduce a different approach.
By implementing an MSA subsampling strategy similar to that of ROCKET, we inject stochasticity into the Boltz-2 model.
We find that this method can help for the model to escape the local minima of its unconstrained prediction, and sample alternative conformations that are consistent with the provided cryo-EM data.
We first implemented a gradient-based conditioning step within the structure module of the OpenFold implementation of AlphaFold 2 .
We next adapted this strategy to the Boltz-2 implementation of AlphaFold 3 , and added an MSA subsampling similar to the approach in ROCKET .

Below, we provide an overview of these two main conditioning methods (structure module gradientbased optimisation and MSA subsampling) and then more in-depth explanations of the implementations of both.
The aim of our method was to guide the prediction to better fit a given experimental density map during the model’s internal recycling iterations.
The first way we attempted to achieve this was through a gradient-based update applied directly within the structure module.
For both the OpenFold and Boltz-2 implementations, upon the initial generation of 3D coordinates in the structure module, we align the prediction to the target cryo-EM map’s frame of reference.
A simulated density map is then generated from the prediction’s 3D coordinates.
Using a simple dot-product between this simulated map and the experimental map, we estimate the agreement between the current prediction and the experimental target map.

In the OpenFold implementation, the gradient of a loss function, defined by this correlation score, is calculated with respect to one of three key internal representations: the 3D coordinates, the intermediate frame representations, or the single representation.
In the Boltz-2 implementation, it is calculated with respect to the coordinates.
Finally, this gradient is applied as an update to the chosen representation, nudging the model’s internal state towards a conformation with a higher correlation to the experimental data.

In the OpenFold method, the update is also passed onto the other non-chosen representations: for example, if the update is calculated and added to the frame representation, single and coordinate representations which correspond to the new frames are also calculated and updated.
For the OpenFold implementation, this process takes place at each recycle through the whole structure module, and for the Boltz-2 implementation, at each timestep in the diffusion process.
This means that after each push, the updated structure is fed back to the model, which aims to continue to refine it into a plausible protein structure.
Below we cover in more detail the specifics behind this process.
As this work is in a preliminary stage, the alignment between the prediction and the cryo-EM map is currently performed by using the ground-truth PDB structure and aligning based on Cα atoms.
This approach would not be applicable in a real experimental setting with a novel cryo-EM map, but it is adopted here to keep the procedure simple while the rest of the method is refined.

norm_text: In order to quantify the agreement between the prediction at each stage of the method and the cryo-EM density map, we must first generate a simulated map of each prediction.

norm_text: For each atom type, the method creates a small 3D kernel that represents the electron density contribution of that atom type.

subsection: 5.3.1.2 Simulating a map from the prediction
norm_text: We then place these kernels at each atom’s position in a 3D grid, where the occupancy value scales the intensity of each atom’s contribution.

subsection: 5.3.1.2 Simulating a map from the prediction
norm_text: The coordinates are normalised and denormalised appropriately to ensure correct placement in the grid, and multiple atoms’ contributions are accumulated to build up the final density.

subsection: 5.3.1.2 Simulating a map from the prediction
norm_text: The result is a simulated electron density map that approximates what we might see in a cryo-EM experiment, where regions of high electron density correspond to the locations of atoms in the protein structure.
After generating a simulated density map from the predicted structure, we quantify its overlap with the experimental cryo-EM map by calculating their dot product.

Gradient-based optimisation is then performed with respect to the prediction (in either the single representation, frame representation, or coordinate representation) to obtain an update that should be added to the representation of choice to maximise this overlap.
Once the update is calculated, it must be applied to the chosen representation to adjust the predicted structure so that its simulated density more closely matches the experimental map.
However, directly applying the full update to any of the representations led to severe structural distortion.
To mitigate this, the update was scaled by a constant <1 before being added.
The maximum tolerable scaling factor was determined empirically by testing different orders of magnitude and selecting the largest value that did not result in structural collapse.
For the OpenFold conditioning method we tested three distinct gradient scaling schedules.
These schedules modulated the strength of the updates based on the model’s internal processing steps, using the default structure with nrecycle = 3 global recycles and nblock = 8 blocks per recycle.
Block Scheduling The scaling factor, s, decays with the block index i within a single structure module pass.
It resets to 1 at the beginning of each new recycle.
The scaling factor ranges from a maximum of 1 to a minimum of 1/8.
Global Scheduling The scaling factor is held constant for all blocks within a recycle pass but decays with the global recycle index r.
In this scheme, the scaling is 1 for the first 8 blocks, 1/2 for the next 8, and 1/3 for the final 8, with the value dropping from 1 to 1/3.
Block and Global Scheduling The scaling factor decays continuously across the combined block and recycle indices, never resetting.
This creates a monotonic decay across all 24 steps, with the scaling factor decreasing from 1 to 1/24.
A limitation of the gradient-based optimisation approach is its tendency to become trapped in local minima.
To mitigate this, we introduced stochasticity by carrying out inference with five separately sampled starting MSAs in parallel.
Each MSA provided a distinct conditioning context, thereby initiating the diffusion process from multiple, diverse starting points.
This strategy increased the likelihood of at least some trajectories escaping local minima and progressing toward higheroverlap solutions.

Unlike ROCKET, we randomly sample MSAs at their full size (a maximum of nmax seqs = 8192), half size (nmax seqs = 4096), and quarter size (nmax seqs = 2048), whilst they implement a more varied subsampling strategy designed to systematically weaken the model’s evolutionary prior.
Their approach involves creating a ‘ladder’ of MSAs with very shallow depths, often containing as few as 1, 2, 4, or 8 sequences.

The goal of this is to make the model’s output more dependent on external experimental data, whereas our method intentionally preserves a strong evolutionary signal whilst adding some diversity to each parallel run to guide the search.
As running multiple MSAs in parallel is computationally intensive, we implemented a pruning strategy to focus resources on the most promising candidates.
Specifically, after every 20 optimisation steps, the trajectory with the lowest overlap score was discarded, until only one remained.
This ensured that computational effort was concentrated on higher-quality candidates while retaining sufficient diversity to avoid premature convergence.

We selected 10 small monomer targets for which the vanilla OpenFold and Boltz-2 methods produced moderate- to poor-resolution predictions, defined as structures with a Cα Root Mean Square Deviation (Cα-RMSD) between 3–20 Å from the ground truth crystal structure.
Our method is designed to improve intermediatequality predictions.
When the initial structure is already accurate (RMSD < 4 Å), little or no refinement is needed.
Conversely, when the prediction is very poor (RMSD > 15Å), our approach alone is unlikely to correct such large-scale errors.
As this research is in its preliminary stages, we are currently testing the method using ideal, simulated density maps generated from the ground-truth structures.
This allows us to first establish the method’s core viability before addressing the additional challenge of noise and artifacts present in experimental maps.

For this initial assessment, performance is being evaluated solely by the Cα-RMSD of the refined model to the native structure, but more comprehensive validation metrics should be incorporated in future work.
